ladies and gentlemen, once again, i would like to thank you very much for the confidence you showed in me yesterday when you elected me president of the european parliament. to succeed the various presidents who have marked the history of our parliament since it was elected by direct universal suffrage, to succeed you, dear josé maria gil-robles, who has so well guided our parliament along the path of democratic progress, (applause) invites me to modesty rather than pride. for my pride now fails me in conscience to the burden we shall bear together, and which i know, as far as i am concerned, to be good, as well as bad. i would like to say to those of our colleagues who voted otherwise, and i am not saying this on the spur of the moment, that once elected the president must be the president of all. primus inter pares . i 'm not sure . it is only a servant of the proper functioning of parliamentary democracy. to remain true to my convictions and to the group which nominated me for the presidency, but to assume the office with integrity and impartiality, respecting our political or national differences, is how i conceive my role and its ethics. as the vice-president to whom the assembly has entrusted me in recent years, i have always tried to do so. i will continue to act in the same spirit. the conditions under which this election took place have marked a step forward in the democratic functioning of the european parliament. it allowed all members, regardless of the size of their group, to participate in an open way. it has taken account of the report of the political forces which the citizens themselves, who elected us, drew up on 13 june. it has allowed each individual to express his or her own choice of conscience. as i said yesterday, i am grateful to the house for having taken into account another aspect of this democratic balance. in the previous parliamentary term, 23% of meps were women. today, it has about 30%. (applause) i would like to thank since simone veil, who was elected in 1979 as the first president of the new parliament elected by direct universal suffrage, the efforts made over these 20 years to achieve fairer representation have now been brought to fruition in the elections which have just taken place. i'm certainly happy and proud of it. but beyond myself, i would like to say to our female colleagues in parliament that this promotion is also theirs. our constituent part-session coincides with the actual taking over of the new building which, after and with luxembourg and brussels, will now be the shared home of our parliamentary work and which is so appropriately named after a great european, louise weiss. the official inauguration will take place a little later, but this coincidence is symbolic of the fact that our parliament is rooted in facts and in minds. architecture has always magnified a human project and remains, through the passage of time, the lasting and privileged memory of civilizations. it has a strong meaning here today. by becoming independent of the council of europe, to which we are, of course, grateful for the long hospitality it has shown us, an era is ending and another is beginning. the gordian knot which bound the european parliament to the days when it was only an advisory assembly has now been severed significantly. unfortunately, colleagues, this building is not free from the sins of youth, which call for our indulgence and that of the media. in a sense, we wipe the plaster off. but i can assure you that at the end of this week we will make a very close inventory of all the malfunctions we have observed and we will do everything possible to remedy them as effectively as possible for the next session. i am aware of the enormous task that lies ahead of us during the two and a half years of this presidency. our first common duty, as i feel it today, will be to demand the full and effective recognition of the new responsibilities which the treaty of amsterdam has now given to the european parliament and which must now be translated into action without delay or reticence on the part of the other institutions. the interinstitutional cooperation between the council, the commission and parliament is essential and we want it to be harmonious, but there is still a need to balance better the two democratic legitimacies on which the adoption of community legislation is based, that of the states, which express themselves through the council, and that of the assembly, which proceeds from the direct universal suffrage of all the citizens of the union. (applause) i would like to thank a new era is opening up on the threshold of this parliamentary term, the european parliament is now a parliament in its own right. since the maastricht treaty, our prerogatives and influence have been steadily increasing. these are now reinforced by the treaty of amsterdam. this is the result of the efforts which our assembly has made at every stage of this conquest for a more democratic functioning of the union. this was the case after the ratification of the single european act in 1986 in order to maximise the achievements, albeit modest, of the cooperation procedure. the same was true after the ratification of the maastricht treaty in 1992, to accompany with meticulous care the implementation of the codecision procedure, which was far more far-reaching. all of us, and there are many of us, who have been involved in the various delegations to the conciliation committee, which brought parliament and the council face to face, in the presence and with the help of the commission, have been able to see how much this new procedure has increased the influence of our assembly during the last parliamentary term. in this way, almost all the disputes submitted to it have been resolved in a way that reflects parliament's main concerns. this positive result is due in large part to the strength of cohesion which i have always found in the successive parliament delegations to the conciliation committee, which i had the honour of co-chair ing, together with our friend renzo imbeni and mr verde. the faithfulness to the vote of the assembly, the internal solution to possible differences of opinion, the sense of reasonable compromise and responsibility, the perfect control of the files on the part of the rapporteurs and committee chairmen, have been decisive and have forced the council to comply. i would like to pay tribute to all the colleagues who have contributed to this. optimizing the powers we had conquered, but at the same time moving towards new democratic conquests, has been our constant objective. in this connection, i should like to pay a sincere and warm tribute to my four last predecessors, enrique barón crespo, egon klepsch, klaus hänsch and josé maria gil-robles, regardless of their political affiliation, for the considerable work of persuasion which they have been able to carry out with the heads of state and government, particularly in the european councils in which they participated. it is largely thanks to their diplomacy and moral authority that the maastricht and amsterdam treaties included the new powers of parliament that we can now put into practice. from now on, no legislative act on almost all areas of community competence can be adopted without the formal agreement of parliament. i would like to say to the council that i am convinced that our assembly is in the mood to do everything possible to ensure that agreement between the council and parliament can be reached, whenever possible, at the first reading. but i must also tell you the truth: the council will have to count on parliament if the concerns of the citizens that we represent are not given their rightful place in the community legislation that will be proposed to us. (applause) as regards the commission, parliament now appoints, first, the president proposed by the heads of state or government and, secondly, the entire college of commissioners, while retaining its power of censure. i am aware that this procedure is a very sensitive watchmaking mechanism. the last months of the outgoing commission's mandate were marked by the serious crisis that everyone remembers. the culmination of this was in december 1998, when parliament dared for the first time to refuse to give the commission discharge. then a chain of events led to her resignation. in the coming weeks, our parliament will hold the hearing and then the investiture of the new college of commissioners. this will be the first act of accountability of our new legislature. in that regard, i must tell you my feeling. it would be inconceivable for us to proceed with the investiture of the commission without first having knowledge of the second report of the wise men. (applause) i will inform the right person, the chairman of this committee, that the european parliament must have this document before we proceed with the hearings of the commissioners-designate. (applause) i would like to say to mr prodi that we do not want a weakened commission. we want a strong, creative commission, which can tackle the major challenges we have to face together. we want the resources made available to him to correspond to the tasks entrusted to him. but in addition to its competence, we expect it to be transparent, based on a revised code of conduct, to respect the political and democratic balances desired by the electorate, to ensure that the procedures for assigning tasks to external bodies prevent the risk of conflicts of particular interests, and to be willing to work in close synergy with our parliament. we are therefore already pleased that the commissioner responsible for relations with parliament is one of the vice-presidents of the commission. despite some substantial progress, we all know that the treaty of amsterdam has not achieved all the objectives it was originally intended to achieve, mainly in terms of institutional reform, which is a prerequisite for enlargement. it is therefore up to our assembly to do its utmost to promote the institutional balance of the union in several directions. the scope of codecision should be extended so that it becomes the community procedure of common law applicable to all legislative acts of the union. the european parliament must be involved in the common foreign and security policy in relation to its operational pillar, the weu. its integration into the institutional system of the union must become effective, as the treaty of amsterdam has confirmed the principle. the european parliament must be closely involved in the preparatory work for the intergovernmental conference on the reform of the european institutions. the citizens who have appointed us would not understand that the european parliament is a minor partner in such an ambitious and necessary reform as the one that has to be undertaken. on the one hand, it must be involved very early on in order to be able to make an active contribution as soon as these preparatory works are started. secondly, we will ask the council to take account of the wish of the assembly, which, in approving the reports presented by mr méndez de vigo and mr tsatsos, requested by a very large majority that the method adopted be the community method, namely a proposal from the commission submitted to both council and parliament. finally, the council must know that parliament would not be satisfied with a minimum reform, if that were to be the case. (applause) i would like to thank the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. parliament will also have to be closely involved in the negotiations which will prepare the enlargement of the union, which will remain the priority for the coming years. and its weight must be increased in the major budgetary choices and the setting of their priorities in accordance with the guidelines of agenda 2000. finally, i am convinced that our assembly must make the voice of the european citizens it represents more widely heard on the world stage of international trade. what has just happened in the world trade organisation with regard to hormone-treated cattle is unacceptable. (applause) we all remember the tragedy of tainted blood or the human risk of mad cow disease. the problem is not to oppose biotechnological progress but to make the requirements of public health prevail. we'll see to it. (applause) i would like to thank the experience i have of this house leads me to believe that we will have to make progress in a number of areas during this presidency, and i will only mention briefly those which seem to me to be priorities, without prejudging today the outcome of the open debates which i shall be happy to encourage on these subjects. first of all, ladies and gentlemen, we must first of all learn the political lesson from the low voter turnout in the last european elections and order our internal reforms in the search for greater closeness to the citizens who elected us. we will also be keen to make progress in this context on the draft uniform procedure for electing members of the european parliament. contrary to the image given here and there, the european parliament works a lot, but it is not sure that we are working as rationally as we could and should. modernization of our working methods and procedures is becoming a necessity if we are to be both more efficient and have sufficient time to be available to our fellow voters on the ground. (applause) i would like to thank in the interests of the treaties, which are our supreme common law, all questions must be able to be discussed without taboo, because our efficiency is at stake, in brussels as well as here in strasbourg. many avenues of thought have already been opened, such as the arrangements for reducing voting time in the assembly, to the benefit of a wider expression of members in the important debates, (applause) the release of time slots to facilitate close relations with our electors - weekdays or on fridays - (applause) the clarification of the respective role of the bureau and the conference of presidents in relation to the prerogatives of the plenary assembly. in this respect i propose to improve the communication of agendas and the recording of decisions to members by electronic mail. i do not prejudge decisions which the house will take democratically after having wisely weighed their consequences or the risk of adverse effects. i simply want to say to you this morning that i will do everything in my power to encourage an open debate and to give priority to the search for the greatest efficiency in our parliamentary work. secondly, we must complete the work that has been started on the common statute for members and, in addition, clarify the conditions of employment and work of our parliamentary assistants. this is based on transparency, fairness and the dignity of the parliamentary function. today, this reform of clarification is necessary in a political environment which has changed a great deal since the treaty of amsterdam finally accepted the principle. our assembly has already made a great deal of progress on the report by our colleague, mr willi rothley. this work must be completed by seeking the widest possible consensus in this house and i, as president, will be keen to achieve this. finally, we must urgently refine our communication strategy, in particular by making a greater effort to decentralize. our information must go beyond the circles of insiders, to whom it is unfortunately often still reserved, in order to be as close as possible to the citizen. in politics, it is not just a matter of doing, but of communicating, and the shortcomings in this area are still considerable. europe is boring, wrote a major daily newspaper these days. this is the challenge we must face, and i will do my best in the role i have been given to do so, with the help of this house and the journalists, who i hope will be increasingly interested in our work, if we can improve its political visibility. this information gap among our fellow citizens cannot be filled by improvisation. it calls for a fundamental political reflection. there is something paradoxical about the current situation. all the surveys show that support for the european project is gaining ground in the minds of many, and at the same time the ever-increasing number of abstentions from the european elections is a reminder that for many europe remains an abstract construct, far from their daily concerns. but democratic life cannot be reduced to a succession of electoral consultations and parliamentary procedures, unless it is, in the famous quip of winston churchill, the worst of regimes, with the exception of all the others. we shall have to take the political measure of the next fact. for too long, the construction of europe has appeared, even wrongly, to public opinion as a machine of cold bureaucratic efficiency. a machine to make the standard where there was diversity, compromise where there was divergence, uniformity where there was difference. the commission has historically been credited with creating the conditions for a large market, but you cannot spread an ideal by means of directives and regulations. for europe to be accepted as something other than a constraint, it must be the bearer of a project that goes beyond the mere construction of an economic and monetary area, even enriched by its social and environmental dimension. (applause) i would like to thank today, there is an urgent need to give the union a new meaning. i hope that, by the appropriate means which we shall have to discuss, our assembly will set itself the objective of reversing the dangerous trend of abstention in the forthcoming european elections, so that the european parliament retains to a high degree, in the very minds of our fellow citizens, the democratic legitimacy it receives from the ballot box. the international influence of our parliament is high beyond the countries of the union. it is particularly so in all the countries which are candidates for accession, as well as in those which have signed cooperation agreements with the union. this positive image is not based solely on the support expected from the european parliament for financial aid to development projects or for the conclusion of economic agreements with the union. what prevails is the order of the mind. the european parliament is identified with the success of civilized democracy on a large, multinational scale in the world. in all the international agreements for which parliament's assent is required, our assembly has never ceased, even under pressure from state interests, to make its agreement conditional on the respect by the partner countries of a more authentic democracy, respectful of freedom and human rights. for all the peoples of the world who are oppressed by dictatorship, civil war or underdevelopment, europe is a great hope for peace, freedom and progress. i hope, ladies and gentlemen, that our assembly will multiply the strong signs which will mobilize the collective consciousness on the universality of the fundamental values of the human community. in this respect, the most pressing and immediate tragedy is, of course, the one which has torn kosovo apart. today, the weapons have fallen silent, the horror has ceased, but peace must be rebuilt. everyone has a vague feeling that the future of a democratic model, protecting all minorities, is at stake. a form of humanitarian sanctuarisation of the european continent has also emerged. it was not acceptable, and it was not accepted, to see human rights violated again in such a barbaric way in the heart of europe. i believe that the joint action of the 15 member states of the union will remain a founding act of political europe, a response to the wishes of the citizens who expect more from us than a single market, a project of humanity. a new europe has begun in pristina, and this europe is being born on the threshold of a new century. now that the arms are contained, (fr) mr president, on behalf of the union for a europe of nations group, i would first like to briefly mention the lessons which can be drawn from the recent european elections. it seems to me that the massive and increasing abstention recorded in all of the european countries indicates the emergence and confirmation of a virtual europe which is distancing itself more and more from european citizens. another apparent sign of the increasing disinterest of the europeans in european construction is the lack of interest in the euro, barely six months after its launch. it seems to me – and this is the second lesson to be drawn from the european elections – that an increasing euroscepticism amongst voters in numerous countries has been demonstrated, particularly in the united kingdom and france, and i believe that by voting for the opposition parties in the large european countries, it is the europe in which their governments participate that the citizens wanted to reject. i see an enormous paradox in yesterday"s election, on the part of the right in this hemicycle, of a candidate who, however admirable, is a known federalist, when this does not apparently reflect the view expressed by the voters – particularly those of the right – in the countries of europe. i do not believe that the legitimacy mentioned by the german foreign minister can be achieved by reproducing, on a european scale, the party systems to be found in the european countries. this legitimacy can only stem from a europe which has been ‘reforged’ on the basis of national democracies rather than trying to create a virtual europe which is ever more distant from the concerns of its citizens. to return to the cologne summit and the consequences of the german presidency, i will make three points. first of all, the employment pact which has been europe"s old chestnut for a very long time. i believe that a certain german chancellor whom we have still not forgotten, helmut kohl, used a phrase which seems to me to sum the situation up exactly. he said, ‘employment – in other words, unemployment – is and shall remain a national prerogative’. this is precisely the definition of this europe which is seen to make plans but leaves the problems to the member nations. the second point concerning the german presidency and the six months that have just passed is the reform of the common agricultural policy. it is clear that this reform has been and still is a precondition to the negotiations to be held with the world trade organisation, which, as we well know, is an instrument of the dominant economy, that is, the american economy. the recent developments that we have seen with regard to the wto, the way in which the new negotiations will be carried out and, particularly, the appointment of the director general preferred by the americans for the first round of the wto, are very bad omens with regard to european interests. it seems to me that this europe, which was born of the idea of the common market, has become a single market and will end up as nothing more than a part of a great global market. that will effectively mean the defeat of the treaty of rome project. lastly, the kosovo affair has also demonstrated the impotence of the european union and its total diplomatic and military dependence on the dominant military power of nato. furthermore, the appointment of the secretary general of nato as a representative of the european common foreign and security policy, appears to complete the picture, and brings to mind that phrase of a french diplomat who said that it is illusory to try to develop a european defence policy while building the european central bank in fort knox. i believe that the kosovo affair and its favourable outcome have eclipsed the six months which have just passed. it is very important – for our group at least – that, in the course of the coming institutional reforms, a far greater importance is afforded to national democracies and national parliaments, instead of allowing europe to sink deeper and distance itself even further from the citizens by creating the kind of democracy that i have described as virtual. president-elect of the commission . – (it) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, thank you very much for this debate, which has been in-depth, clear and in many cases, extremely comprehensive and which has mostly demonstrated open confidence in our future work. i say open confidence because all those who spoke, even those who criticised the composition of the commission, acknowledged the need to work closely together in a major, intense undertaking and recognised the fact that the future of the european union lies in collaboration between the parliament and the commission. it is we and our collaboration which will form the basis for the way out of the current crisis, a crisis so serious as to reduce the number of voters who turned out at the last elections to among the lowest proportions in european political history. i believe that, at the end of this mandate, one gauge of our success will be the numbers who vote in the next elections. that will show whether we have managed to restore the faith of the citizens of europe in the institutions for which we are responsible. this means transparency, a whole cleaning up operation which will not be easy to conduct. it is easy to promise – and i have committed myself fully on this matter – but i also know very well that it is not an easy promise to keep. a little while ago the electoral symbol for my candidacy – a little donkey – was invoked with charming irony, and i was invited to be stubborn, an invitation which was unnecessary as i am pig-headed by nature. however, i would like remind you that i was prompted to choose the donkey while reading a passage from leonardo da vinci, in which, while he is describing the donkey – although i cannot vouch for the truth of the statement for lack of proof – he said that the donkey is a strange animal because rather than drink dirty water it will die of thirst. (applause) it is important for us to take the donkey as the symbol of our politics because, in this five-year term, we must try to do likewise. i am perfectly aware that it is easy to make these resolutions but that it is not so easy to keep them, but the method we used to build the commission, mr poettering, was a very open one. there was no night of long knives, no investiture struggle and no border fighting. it was not an easy task to bring together fifteen countries, north and south, and diverse political situations. as for the result, when i say ‘balanced’ we know full well that there is discontent in some countries, but that is politics: balanced means that the major forces present in the european parliament are very well represented in terms of personality and portfolio size in the commission. you can analyse the composition of the commission in as much detail as you like. i repeat, within the bounds of the treaty of amsterdam, i have taken full advantage of all the power conferred on me, and i believe that one improvement at the end of this mandate may be more advanced ways of forming the commission. nevertheless, please consider the progress made with regard to other areas. please consider the fact that we have arrived here with a commission which will work hard – well or not so well, we will see – whatever the case, which is able to agree on common programmes and the members of which are ready to face their responsibilities, individually and collectively. i reiterate this point because there has been a great deal of discussion regarding the manner in which we will conduct the audiences, hearings and inquiries. i attach very great importance to this aspect of things, as i attach very great importance to the wise men"s report, but i also believe that these inquiries must be made into the history of the commissioners and their programmes, and must be carried out in great depth and with political serenity as, in my opinion, they cannot be the tool to regulate problems which occurred in the past. having said this, i believe that they must be explored in more depth and that there must be hearings which go right to the bottom of the commission"s problems, because, and i am right to do so, i have taken on board the warning that prevention is preferable to the commission being subsequently thrown into crisis. earlier today, in my address, i said that i have asked all the commissioners to give me their word of honour that they would resign should any new event take place or should there be any hidden fact. i believe that this tool will not be used lightly, but with the sense, however, that the problem in question involves not only individual responsibility but also the efficiency and responsibility of the entire commission team which must present itself to you as capable of governing for the next five years. clearly, we have to present ourselves as individuals, but we must also present ourselves as an organically composed group, not as distinct individuals which are separate from each other. this has been the endeavour of the past few months and this is the type of commission which has been introduced to you. please assess it in this way. therefore, i consider that the vote on 15 september will be enormously important. i believe that you have the right to reject the entire commission and consider it inadequate for the great task of leading europe in the next five year period and making its contribution to the great task before us. well then, i invite you to perform this task according to the vision of european common interest, and not in a context, although absolutely legitimate in politics, of individual interest. i will conclude by returning to a couple of points which have been recalled and raised today. firstly, the wise men"s report. i believe that it is very important for us to have read the first of these carefully and to have measured against it many of the thoughts which i have expounded to the parliament on the three occasions in which i have come here. this report does exert an influence, but we have to understand that the political responsibility of the future is our own. the wise men"s report is a wonderful instrument, and we must read it and reflect upon it, but the decision is ours alone to make and its consequences ours to bear, and it is in this sense that the dialogue between parliament and the commission takes on a completely different dimension. secondly, several speakers have invoked the question of international trade, which i did not bring up because it will be discussed in september. i can assure you that it will be very important to maintain a balance between the need for free trade, which is one of the foundation stones of europe, and the protection of important rights, including the fundamental health rights. this is the reason why i have highlighted the example of health with regard to food and medicine as one of the benchmarks for the our future commission. there you are. this is the path we have to follow. as mr barón crespo said, quoting manzoni: ‘adelante ’ but ‘con juicio ’, ‘go on, carefully’. the quotation is not complete, however, because there is another sentence. in fact, manzoni says: ‘adelante, pedro, si puedes ’, that is ‘go on, pedro, if you can’, and this power to move forward is in your hands. (applause)

(fr) madam president, the cologne council launched two processes for institutional reform which, to our mind, avoid the fundamental issues. firstly, it decided to work on a charter which will bring together citizens" basic rights already in force throughout the union, but it did not state exactly what legal basis it should end up having, nor what it would add to current legislation. this is an obvious case of propaganda, with the aim of bringing to the table the idea of a european constitution which would itself legitimise a super-state ready to be constituted. the second cologne initiative was the work towards an intergovernmental conference on improving institutions with the future enlargement of the european union in mind. its mandate has expanded beyond what was foreseen in the first article of the protocol on institutions found in the annex to the treaty of amsterdam, because the cologne european council, without consultation, added the option to extend voting to the qualified majority. this solution strikes us as completely unworkable, for in order to prepare for enlargement, we need institutions which are not more rigid but more flexible, and that is why we feel that this mandate for negotiation must be set right by the helsinki council. the biggest drawback about the cologne conclusions is that they made a huge omission. almost nothing has been learned from the institutional point of view, from the major crisis, prompted last march by the collective resignation of the commission, as a result of irresponsible management. no amendment to the treaty was proposed. the possible reforms are being dealt with by the anti-fraud office and by romano prodi himself, who told us yesterday that he would be able to resolve almost everything by changing the internal workings of the commission and by putting forward a members" code of conduct. we are being taken for a ride, because the problems which led to the resignation of the commission are much more serious. they represent a huge gulf between the union"s institutions and its citizens, which can only be remedied by reform on a huge scale which would establish a europe of nations. by forgetting this, the cologne council managed to dodge the question of democracy itself.

, in writing . – (fr) the issue that we are dealing with during this constitutive session is an extremely serious one: that of the dioxin crisis. i am pleased that it features on our agenda and that representatives of the european commission and the council spoke on this matter this morning at the request of our assembly. the scandal of chickens and other animals being contaminated by dioxin, this carcinogenic substance, brought back very bad memories for all consumers. this is the unpleasant impression for many of us, of having been through this scenario before – a scenario in which consumers are the last to find out what they are eating, and yet whose health is at serious risk. the vote for this resolution is a genuine sign of the will of the european parliament to get to the very bottom of this business and to answer consumers" legitimate concerns. at the time of the mad cow crisis, the european parliament did not spare any effort to have measures adopted for the protection of consumers. through its temporary committees of enquiry, it followed with great vigilance the way the european commission and the member states managed the crisis. its efficiency has been unanimously recognised by all european institutions. this is why i, like many of my colleagues, feel that we must set up a temporary committee of enquiry on the dioxin crisis. short-term solutions must be found in order to resolve problems caused by the contamination of foodstuffs in belgium, and in the longer term, debate must be started on the many questions first thrown up by the mad cow crisis and which are again coming to the fore because of this new food crisis. i am thinking, for example of the belgian government"s lack of transparency in alerting the european commission so late, and of the lack of information which was given to consumers. on a more global scale, the question being asked is ‘what kind of food policy do we want within the european union?’. the european parliament, as well as numerous consumer associations, has been able to give answers which are also ways forward for thinking about a new definition of the european union"s approach to food. this must uphold the interests of consumers, it must ensure that the precautionary principle prevails over all other principles, and it must set up an integrated inspection of the food chain in its entirety, from producer to consumer. this traceability is essential for food safety. this is, therefore, a global debate which we members of the european parliament must sustain throughout the next legislature. it must cover dioxin, hormones and gmos which are all very controversial issues.

(fr) madam president, unlike the previous speakers, who were, it has to be said, all british – well, well, what a surprise! – i would like to protest against the commission"s decision, which i find quite astounding, to penalise the french football federation for so-called discrimination in the sale of tickets during the last football world cup. commissioner kinnock pointed out, and rightly so, that this has been the accepted practice in previous world cups. and why is this an accepted practice, ladies and gentlemen? well, it is quite simply that a world cup like that is organised by a country, and paid for by the tax-payers of that country. given these conditions, it is felt to be courteous and good practice to allocate a slightly larger quota to that country"s citizens. when a company floats shares for example, increases its capital, and then sells the shares, nobody says that it is illegal if it reserves a quota for its own employees, who are a vital component of the company"s lifeblood. this quota is, of course, a form of discrimination and yet, i feel it is a legitimate one. i, therefore, think that the commission was wrong to apply article 82 of the treaty because there was no real abusive exploitation of power, only a quite legitimate and understandable use of a set of circumstances which were highly unusual from a financial point of view. however, madam president, i would like to move on, because this is, when all is said and done, a relatively minor matter which is of no great consequence to life in our country. there are other more serious matters in which the commission has been guided by the same extremist mind set which may bring about very serious imbalances in our country"s economy and also in its employment figures. i am thinking in particular of the sanction imposed, yet again on france, for having allowed certain textile companies to reduce their national insurance contributions at a time when they were taking on new staff in an international climate which, as you know, ladies and gentlemen, is extremely tough, largely because of the international agreements negotiated by the commission itself. so these businesses are now going to have to repay the social grants which they were given because of an extremist, narrow-minded and almost plain stupid way of seeing things. it is an absolute scandal. i think that, in future, this parliament should set an example with a more considered vision, one which is more fair and impartial towards competition. (fr) madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i do not think that the market should be the only factor taken into consideration as regards the organisation of sporting events. during the 1998 world cup, of the two million tickets sold, the largest share was handled directly by fifa, which sent quotas to the 203 national football associations, with a larger share going to the 24 qualifying countries, of which the united kingdom was one. another share, 600, 000 tickets, was handled by the host nation, which reserved 37 % of this quota. the idea of putting all tickets for a sporting event of this size up for sale on the european market has never been put into practice by any country, as commissioner neil kinnock has just pointed out. in euro "96, for example, the football tournament organised in the united kingdom, 42 %, not 37 % of the tickets were reserved for the host nation. secondly, having control of the tickets is to have 90 % control of security. if the world cup was a success in this area too, if we had relatively few incidents, it was largely because this control over the tickets facilitated for example, franco-british co-operation in security matters, and efficiency in handling the arrival of groups of supporters, supervising them, and following up any problems. this allowed us to escape many outbreaks of hooliganism, which we hope never to see again on our continent. thirdly, the more individual sales that are made, the greater the risk of a black market developing. this is the lesson learned by the italians themselves, from organising the 1990 world cup, and it was obviously taken on board by the french organising committee. fourthly and finally, it is understandable to ensure that where a popular sport is concerned, when the host nation has invested nine billion francs in the event, the citizens of the host nation support and participate positively in this event, and this is also a key factor in its success. but it is also understandable group which was most successful and most appreciated by the french people was that of the scots. we, the citizens of france, did not go on holiday to australia in july 1998 because the world came to france, and because we were at the stade de france, at st-denis, at the velodrome, in marseilles with the people from our working-class neighbourhoods. ladies and gentlemen, i think that the european union"s priority in sport today is not to punish a member nation which has managed successfully to organise an event like this, but is rather, as romano prodi said yesterday, to engage in a real pan-european battle against doping, and this means refusing to allow the unique power of money to kill off the beauty and the very spirit of sport. commission . – i should like to begin where ms gill left off, first of all by congratulating her on her maiden speech in this house. she will never feel such fear again or derive such satisfaction. i am sure the whole house thanks her for her contribution. indeed, she summed up the feelings of the commission in many ways when she said that she deeply regretted the existence of discrimination. that is the universal feeling in the commission, which is why my colleague, mr van miert, and his associates in the commission specifically sought to do something effective about preventing for all time in the future and indeed for 1998 the use of discriminatory practices by cfo. i should like to take up where mr vander taelen left off. when he said that football is a valid alternative to war i was reminded of the maxim that the first casualty of war is truth. as i listened to some of the contributions in the course of this debate, i could not escape the feeling that sometimes the first casualty of football is truth because there were one or two contributions that were made passionately, but largely without the recognition of fact. i would like to respond on behalf of the commission, with some repetition of fact. i regret it if i am repetitive, but if at first people do not hear, perhaps they will hear the second time. i begin with mr perry. i enjoyed his recitation of sound-bites about pathetic, appalling and all the rest of it. but what is he really saying when he says that the european commission has the power to impose a eur 20m fine? in theory and in constitutional terms, he is right. but is he really suggesting that the european commission should take eur 20m or eur 30m out of football and put it in the coffers of the european commission? mr ford says ‘yes’, he would rather that the european commission have the money than the cfo. he demonstrated a surprising distance from the realities of public opinion. this man has been my friend for a considerable time. i admire everything but his taste in football clubs. but the fact remains that if that were the course of action taken, he knows what the headlines would be. so does mr watson, who is disturbed about the reputation of the european union. he knows the headlines would say: ‘euros snatched from football’. let us be rational. is it sensible in the circumstances to take the money in large amounts from football and deposit it in the european commission's coffers, or is it sensible to take action that guarantees that on no future occasion will there be discriminatory sales of football or other international tournament tickets? then mr perry says that he wants this action to be absolutely firm and ferocious. i can understand the sentiment. but to be consistent the same action would have to be taken against the organisers of the european cup competition which happened to be in the united kingdom in 1996. football came home, it was said. are we really suggesting in this house, or anywhere else, that we should look back to 1996 or comparable competitions and say that we are dishing out eur 20m fines on those who organised these competitions? come on. let us be rational. let me return very briefly again to mr ford. he said those who make money out of football should put it back in. he knows very well that i am zealous in my support of that view. but i would suggest that we have to do rather more than attend only to international football ticket sales in order to bring about that intelligent and necessary recycling of funds. one point i want to focus on, in what mr ford said, is that the commission, he alleges, is sending out the message to organisers of euro 2000 and maybe future world cup competitions in the european union that they can ignore the rules. the absolute opposite is taking place. i had already said ten minutes before mr ford spoke that the organisers of the belgian and netherlands european championship have been in touch with the commission and not a single ticket will be sold on a discriminatory basis. they are already obeying the rules, setting the precedent, and, at all future times in the european union, that will be the way in which affairs are conducted. the football supporters and supporters of other sports quite rightly will now know that they have the protection of the law and organisers of tournaments will know that they will be the object of real and heavy punishment if they break what are now known to be the rules. this is the point. there was no knowledge of the rules. there is no case-law from the court of justice. there is no precedent of action by the european commission. the money would have been taken out of football if there had been a heavier fine. there would have to be a further effort to levy fines against previous organisers. the fact is that cfo, who i do not paint as plaster saints, the moment that our investigation commenced, stopped the discriminatory sales. everybody would have liked that to have occurred earlier, but it did happen. when mr watson says, therefore, that this is not the first time that organisers have rigged the sales, he may be right. but this is the first time that the legal competition authority has stopped the rigging, stopped the discriminatory sales and the first time that any competition authority in the world has prevented for all future time the use of discriminatory methods in the sale of tickets. mr watson accepted my point when i said that this was a case where consumers were hit but the effect was not on the market as it is generally understood. i think he conceded that because he said that was my claim and the problem was that the reputation of europe had suffered. i would put this point to him, a man for whom i have very high regard, as i do for the other participants in this debate: that reputation can only suffer if what has occurred is misrepresented. i know there is no-one in this house who will ever want to do that. i therefore appeal for attention to the facts. whilst i fully understand and indeed, to a degree, share the passions about the way in which the big business of football so frequently now is operating in ways that contradict the interests of genuine football fans, i accept all that. i ask for fair treatment in this case as indeed in many others. it was uncharacteristically unworthy of one honourable member to say that he could understand why my colleague mr van miert is not here because of the gravity of this case. if there has ever been a commissioner in the forty-two year history of the european union who has publicly demonstrated integrity and guts, it is mr van miert. the reason he is not here this morning is because he has to attend to his work, not from any cowardice. it is infamous for anybody to even infer that is the reason for his absence.

- you will remember that at its meeting on 27 and 28 july the committee on constitutional affairs considered a request for interpretation of rule 29 (1) of the rules of procedure made by the conference of presidents at its meeting on 21 july. the committee on constitutional affairs concluded that 'the declaration on the constitution of the technical group of independent members, mixed group, is not in accordance with rule 29 (1) of the rules of procedure of the european parliament'. the committee on constitutional affairs continues: 'the declaration of constitution of this group, in particular annex 2 to the letter of constitution addressed to the president of the european parliament, excludes any political affinity. it gives the various signatory parties complete political independence within the group.' the committee on constitutional affairs requests that the following interpretation be inserted in article 29 (1) of our rules of procedure: 'the formation of a group which openly denies any political character and any political affinity between its members cannot be accepted within the meaning of that article'. this interpretation will be duly recorded in the minutes of today's sitting. it will then be inserted in the rules of procedure, but if tomorrow, before the minutes are adopted, a political group or at least 32 members object to this interpretation in accordance with rule 180 (4) of the rules of procedure, the matter will then be referred immediately to the house, which will decide, as appropriate, by a simple majority, in the presence of at least one third of its members. that's the rule. if the matter is rejected, it shall be referred back to the committee responsible.

- madam president, my colleague herman schmid will speak on behalf of my group in this debate. i would like to make a preliminary remark and ask mr kinnock a very specific question. reading the second report of the committee of experts makes it clear how right we were in asking the five wise men to continue their investigations and reflections beyond the case of one commissioner in particular, in order to establish a more general diagnosis of the institution as a whole. and that diagnosis is edifying. the title of the report is a strong condemnation of the outgoing commission: to put an end to mismanagement, irregularities and fraud. the old college must be reminded, 42 years after the institution was set up, of the need, i quote, 'to hold the commissioners accountable from the drafting of a proposal to its implementation'. as can be seen from the conclusions of the experts' report, the problem is not so much the malfunctioning itself as a problem of mentality, which is obviously not the fault of the commission's officials, but of the institution's structural shortcomings, which are not technical but political in nature. another paper had already been produced on this subject and had provided an analysis which i considered to be clear and relevant. moreover, the commission itself had commissioned it from its own prospective unit in preparation for the pörtschach european council, and then it closed it without any follow-up. it contained, for example, a substantive criticism of the commission's tendency - like that of other administrations - to, i quote: 'deal with its own area in its own logic, listening to a certain type of lobby and not taking sufficient account of the consequences outside its field of expertise'. this insight into the crisis facing the commission and all the european institutions would help to situate the analyses of the independent experts in their overall political context, which is characterised, in the words of the document of the prospective unit in question, by the exhaustion of a certain way of organising public action, by a crisis of governance that is taking the european union by storm. my question to commissioner kinnock is therefore simple: will you agree to make public this document from the outgoing commission, the urgency of which is shown by our debate?
- madam president, the second report of the independent experts which has just been handed over to us is remarkable for the extent and quality of the work done in a few months and also for the desire to describe frankly the internal dysfunctions of the commission. this is the first time i have read, from official and authoritative circles, such a powerful analysis, without tongue or falsehoods. on this basis we can work on serious reforms. the report finds that there are virtually no rules for granting subsidies. the advisory committee on contracts has only a formal and subordinate role of verification. that the commission used the technical assistance office to escape budgetary constraints. that in shared management expenditure the commission and the member states mutually decommit. that a priori financial control is practically useless. that internal audit is too weak. the financial regulation is not adapted to the requirements of modern management and effective control, or the investigations of the anti-fraud unit tend to take too long, with microscopic results. these findings correspond to what my group has been denouncing for a long time, as do the technical solutions proposed, whether it be the strengthening of internal audit, the fight against fraud, transparency and the obligation for the commission to be accountable. however, it seems to us that the committee of independent experts does not go far enough in its analysis of the political causes of the crisis, but perhaps, after all, that was not its role at this stage. for example, when you read phrases like this, page 64, "why has the commission lost control of technical assistance? because the financial regulation has never sufficiently developed contract law', one cannot help but have the disturbing impression that the reasoning remains unfinished. why was the financial regulation inadequate? why hasn't it been improved? didn't many people find advantages in these imperfections? and, in the end, has not the theory of the commission's independence, which is cultivated by the federalists but which ends up weakening controls, provided a breeding ground for irregularities and fraud which go unpunished? under its cover, organised networks of embezzlement and laundering of community money have been set up, such that fraud is no longer mainly the result of individual misconduct, as denounced in the first report by the experts, but rather of hidden and permanent mechanisms. this is why, according to the europe of nations group, the real political problem facing us today is the status of the commission, a supranational institution with little control and lacking in prerogatives, privileges and immunities. there is a worrying development in this respect. whereas the european parliament has recently tried to strengthen its control over the commission and the theory of independence should therefore logically be set back, it is being revived and asserted with new strength; the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. in the hearing last week, commissioner kinnock clearly supported, in his written and oral answers, two strange principles which i quote from the text. firstly, the principle of management independence, which would be enjoyed by the directorates-general vis-à-vis the commissioners, and secondly, the principle of non-interference, to which the commissioners would be subject vis-à-vis the departments. mr kinnock went on to say that in his experience over the last few years these principles have worked very well. of course, this is not at all the view of my group, nor is it the view of the committee of experts, which in its chapter 7 states precisely that the distinction between policy and management within the commission is not defendable, i quote, either in law or in practice, that it allows political responsibilities to be avoided, that it should logically be eliminated in favour of hierarchical subordination to the politically responsible commissioners. we find a total contradiction between the recommendations of the experts' report and the intentions of the new commission. the consequences of this will have to be drawn from the vote on wednesday on the college's presentation. everyone will have to take responsibility. the privileges and immunities of the commission and its officials are clearly a serious obstacle to the fight against fraud. this is in fact the first difficulty faced by olaf, the european anti-fraud office, when it wants to prosecute european officials before national courts. indeed, i quote the report, 'in order to pursue a criminal investigation against commission officials, a national court must request the lifting of official immunity for suspects, professional secrecy for witnesses and the inviolability of commission premises for searches and access to documents'. such obstacles can discourage even the best of intentions. that is why my group's priority is to abolish them and to bring the commission under ordinary law before looking for other solutions such as the establishment of a european public prosecutor, which would satisfy the federalist whims but would not bring much more compared to the powers of olaf in the fight against fraud. more generally, the control of the commission should be strengthened. the european parliament's control, of course, and for example our assembly should, following this report by the experts, request new audits on specific points or even appoint one or more committees of inquiry to clarify certain areas which are still unclear, for example the evaluation of the real impact of community subsidies. but if it stands alone, the european parliament's control over the commission will be insufficient for two reasons: first, because the european parliament shares the commission's objectives and because it is not subject to pressure from public opinion. this control must therefore be complemented by that of the council. the council must stop allowing itself to be poisoned by the special reasoning of the federalists. it must restore its authority, remove from the commission its privileges and immunities of an earlier age. it must not let itself be deprived of the future intergovernmental conference and must take advantage of it to take back the initiative, strengthen the fight against fraud and subject the commission to a new form of accountability to governments. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to say on behalf of the socialist group that we fully support mrs jackson's report. i think the question is important. we have seen that, although this is not the direct subject of this report, with the dioxin case we can make all the european directives, all the recommendations, all the laws we want, if the inspection does not ensure that they are applied, i believe that the deep doubt of our fellow citizens about the european effectiveness and the interest of these standards is likely to develop. we therefore need to make control and inspection more community-based. of course, a balance must be struck between the responsibility of the member states and european intervention. in this respect, we support mrs jackson's request that we not only adopt recommendations but that we move to a real directive, which sets out specific criteria which each member state will have to respect in the implementation of its inspection. we therefore support all the amendments, and we hope that the commission will be attentive to the need to set rigorous frameworks. we have heard the new commissioner, mrs wallström, whom we have questioned on the question of the effectiveness of the laws. she said the commission intended to be more rigorous so that, finally, inspection would be effective and strictly enforced. we therefore want parliament's amendments to be accepted. finally, after the examples we have had with dioxin, we see clearly the risk we are taking. either we move in a reasonable and rigorous way towards an effective european inspection of the member states, in the framework of a european vision. but the second step is the setting up of european inspectors - when the commission could not really rely on the financial perspective. this gave a rather unreal character to its exercise, because, in particular, it could not, and rightly so, take account of the kosovo tragedy and its financial consequences, and finally because, for reasons which do not seem very satisfactory to us, it refused to respond to the concerns expressed by parliament in the field of administrative reform. we had asked in our guidelines for a gradual dismantling of the bat. we had asked in our budgetary guidelines for a precise assessment of staffing needs and of the capacity for action that it considered it had with the existing staff. in both these respects, we have not found in you much zeal. but we were disappointed, i will not hide it from you, madam president, by the council's budget. disappointed with category 1. we still do not understand why, in the name of what, you are making massive linear cuts in compulsory expenditure. the argument put forward by some delegations, that this is due to monetary developments, seems to us, i remind you, to be contrary to the very precise provisions of the financial regulation. we also do not understand why, in category 2, although there may be a number of technical justifications, you have reduced the payment appropriations. in category 3, we can see that while you have served the major programmes correctly, that is to say all that has been adopted in codecision, on the other hand, everything that directly and specifically concerns parliament has been sacrificed by you. you defend what is ours, you defend what is both of ours, you despise what is ours alone. on category 4, you know the extent of the problem. you are trying to put into this category a whole bunch of things that you cannot put into it: the fisheries agreement on morocco, and especially the massive funds, estimated at 500 million, on kosovo, and this without raising the category. the result is that what you are proposing is, as the french say, to strip james to dress paul, to sacrifice the priorities defined by the legislative and budgetary authorities of yesterday in favour of the priorities of tomorrow. we do not consider that to be good policy. finally, in category 5, we see a great reluctance to tackle the pension problem. this seems serious to us. and we would like to see a little more solidarity from the council in support of the necessary transformation of the commission's administrative structures. i think that, generally speaking, the reproach we make to your draft budget is that it simultaneously insults the past, the present and the future. in the past, for the reasons i have just given. the moment you decide that tomorrow's priorities must be financed by sacrifices on priorities already established, you are making an operation which is not eligible. we know, and you have very rightly said so, that the commission will have increased responsibilities in the field of foreign policy. you have to take them on. the commission has not yet taken the necessary steps to ensure that the appropriations for payments are used. we now know that the commission has already stopped paying. and finally, as regards the future, you ignore, or treat lightly, the major issues that lie ahead of us in the field of administrative reform and pensions. then we shall have a constructive dialogue, madam president. i have confidence in your ability to cooperate. but you should know, we're gonna have a tough conversation. we will not accept that the interinstitutional agreement we have signed and ratified is a trap. cooperation, yes, but not the sacrifice of the fundamental priorities of the european union. we will be able to ask you for a revision of the financial perspective where necessary. - madam president, ladies and gentlemen, we welcome the holding of a european council partly devoted to the area of freedom, security and justice, which shows that the european institutions and the states are aware of the importance of the issues essential to europe's future. these issues are important for all citizens living in this area, as they affect their individual and collective freedoms. tampere will also provide policy guidance on sensitive issues, such as immigration policies, which require a new look at north-south relations, such as freedom of movement, which requires a real harmonisation of visa policies in europe, such as the right to asylum and the right to health for all refugees. other important issues are integration policies, which also affect the cultural rights of minorities, the right to live together in dignity and the political rights for all citizens residing in europe. all these rights must, of course, be included in the charter of fundamental rights, a charter which must be addressed to all those men and women who live in europe and enrich it. it is therefore necessary to strengthen democratic control over the choices we are going to make, because there are still too many shadow areas such as europol. this is why the european parliament, which is the direct representative of the people, must be closely associated with meetings such as tampere. the european council's choices must be transparent, in line with human rights and the wishes of the european parliament.
- madam president, the european council in cologne had the ill-fated idea, without any national parliament to my knowledge having ever asked it to do so, of launching the preparation of a charter of fundamental rights of the european union. this idea, in its apparently restrained form, seems to us both unnecessary and dangerous. this is unnecessary, because, according to the council's conclusions, it should be nothing more than a stylistic exercise combining the rights already in force in a single document. these are rights that already exist and are found in various documents: treaties, the european social charter, the european convention on human rights and above all, of course, national constitutions. moreover, these rights, as far as citizens are concerned, are already well protected by the legal systems in force. the proposed exercise therefore appears to be pointless. it is no less dangerous, because the federalist lobbies will take advantage of the cologne conclusions to try to take the defence of citizens' rights out of national constitutions and to cover them with a higher text, a so-called european constitution. mr barnier also emphasised, during his hearing last week, that the process of preparing the charter should be linked to the process of constitutionalising the treaties. clearly, the cologne council has set in motion a machine that is going to lose control. i believe that it is better to leave the rights of citizens to the national constitutions and their protection to the national parliaments, which have been perfecting them for centuries. the union would do better to devote itself to the first urgent task of the moment: the drawing up of a charter of the rights of nations.

commission - (it) madam president, i apologize for the delay, which i can explain. as is often the case in the european institutions, the italian text of the speech was lost in the hyperspace between brussels and strasbourg. i was expecting it, since i have only the foreign-language text with me, which i used as a note. i have been here for nine hours but i see that i will be forced to read this speech which i will be giving in italian, translating it from a foreign language. i apologize in advance if the translation is not perfect at times. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, we are at a crucial moment in what i believe has been a great exercise in democracy. i have appeared before you many times in the last few days and have spoken to you about the political ideas of my programme and the nature of our future relations. you've questioned the commissioners, both in writing and orally. we are committed to transparency, efficiency, accountability, absolutely and precisely, for every action we take. these principles of transparency, accountability and efficiency are contained in the resolution which has just been adopted. the fundamental point of your resolution concerns the commitments i made to the conference of presidents last week; and this morning, on this solemn occasion, i assure you of my deep and total commitment to these five points. these points constitute the basis for a new beginning in relations between our two institutions, a new culture of openness and, above all, of mutual cooperation. the fundamental element of these questions concerns the problem of individual responsibility of commissioners. i have already stated my position on this matter clearly and honestly. the discussions we have had together in the last few days, in my view, offer the opportunity to deal with any problems that may arise in this area. let us be clear: our firm commitment to collegiality - a fundamental aspect of the role of this commission - will in no way become a screen behind which individual responsibilities are concealed, the problems of responsibility which each of us must assume in politics, which we must assume before this parliament and before the european world as a whole. these principles are, in my view, essential to a strong commission. and even if a strong commission sometimes creates disagreements with parliament - we will often say 'no' - i think, for you and for me, that it is much more useful to have a strong partner than a weak one. let us return to the content of this resolution. i fully agree that the organization of our relations is a fundamental element of the european construction, but it is not the only element. we must appeal to the citizens in this respect and this is a fundamental challenge for all the institutions. therefore, one of my most important tasks is to present my political guidelines for the five-year term in january and we must and will have to give a very high political profile to this january consultation. i said yesterday - and i say again - that i am strongly committed to helping sustainable development meet all environmental challenges. the first and most important of these challenges is, in my view, to regain, as soon as possible, the confidence of the public in the safety of the food we eat and in the protection of the health of all. (applause) i would like to thank i recognize that the preparation of the next intergovernmental conference in front of the european parliament is of fundamental importance. i renew my commitment to you to have a strong and decisive conference. i also want to be clear, because there must be no ambiguity about the nature of the report i have given to mr dehaene and mr von weizsäcker and lord simon. it is not a report from the commission that you will receive, and you and i will receive it at the same time. in the light of the report we will receive together, i understand that we will have to organise a discussion through the european parliament and the commission which prepares a strong intergovernmental conference in preparation for the helsinki summit. the dialogue that has been opened up between us is therefore very important in this respect. you also asked me for an interinstitutional agreement as the basis for a code of conduct to govern our relations and our dealings. i fully agree that we will have to sit down, look at it and organise the details in practice. i also accept the commitments you have asked me to make on the five points in the preamble to your resolution. of course, these must be analysed in detail in the future code of conduct. i would remind you, however, that as president of the commission i will exercise my responsibilities to the full. two points of your intervention should be somewhat moderate. firstly, you are asking that in the event of a serious criminal charge, a member of the commission be suspended from office. i have no power of decision in this matter but, as i have said before, if such accusations were formally made against members of the commission, i would feel obliged to examine the consequences with the utmost rigor, and i can imagine that there are circumstances in which a member of the commission would want to be suspended from office pending judgment. i can also imagine situations in which a possible resignation would have to be considered, but that decision depends on the political assessment of the member of the commission in question and, ultimately, of me as president. it is therefore appropriate, from this point of view, to respect the fundamental principles of law and therefore the presumption of innocence. fundamental freedoms are for everyone, but i can assure you that i will be very strict in this matter. let me make one final comment on this. on the crucial element of accountability, i will never accept that a member of the commission deliberately misleads parliament or lies to parliament. our relationships must be based on mutual trust. secondly, you want to express your views on the codes of conduct for commissioners and high-level appointments which are to be applied by the new commission. as president, i must say that these regulations must be applied on the first working day of the new commission. i do not want there to be any ambiguity about the immediate commitment to the reform process that is signalled within the commission by these codes of conduct. however, this does not mean that these codes are written on stone. you have received them and you can make your comments, which we will take into account: these codes are not immutable. several of the desired points included in the new framework agreement refer to transparency. i told you that the new commission would be open to your suggestions. it has committed itself to attend parliamentary committee meetings and plenary sessions to address all important political issues. it has also made a firm commitment to study, within the limits of its possibilities, how it might be possible to improve the involvement of parliament in all areas. i note the importance you attach to international agreements. however, you must recognize that our commitment to consult you will have to be implemented in a manner consistent with the proper conduct of the negotiations. i can assure consider how best to ensure that information reaches you quickly. i am also prepared to announce the important decisions taken by the commission directly in plenary when it is necessary, when you are making firm preparations for this intergovernmental conference, which is of fundamental importance for our future. this intergovernmental conference is of fundamental importance because we have prepared together for a second objective, an objective which, in one way or another, will really change all our policies: enlargement. once the enlargement process is complete, we will go from 362 million people to almost half a billion. we will have to expand to countries with fundamentally different histories, customs and income levels. this choice is aimed at safeguarding the pillars of our europe, namely peace and freedom, and it is impossible to guarantee these pillars if enlargement is not carried out in the most constructive, open and strongest possible way. finally, we have committed ourselves to a third objective. we are committed to helping the economic recovery that is beginning and to making sure that it serves all citizens: it must serve employment, social justice in pursuit of reform but also to preserve the great foundations of the social protection system created by europe, a system that has had so many problems in recent years of reform and which we refuse to see abandoned, leaving citizens without protection. these are the three major commitments we have made together. i hope, ladies and gentlemen, that the vote that is to follow will enable us, and you, to carry out together this task which, without rhetoric, is truly a great historical task, an institutional innovation never before seen in the world. therefore, to face together these new tasks which represent a great change from the past, we must proceed with great cohesion, the cohesion which must exist between parliament and the executive in all modern democracies. the future of our europe is based on our dialectic but also on our spirit of cooperation.
