- mr president, one question before i explain my vote. i'd like to know what mrs. schreyer's official title is. she's approved, i voted for her, but she's not appointed yet, it's absurd. but i'm very glad that she's listening to what i'm going to say. (interruption by the president: there is a transitional day, mr bourlanges.) i think that all this, and that is the point of my explanation of vote, is absurd. i voted four times in favour of the commission because i have confidence in mr prodi and his team. in this explanation of vote i wanted to draw attention to the fact that this parliament has not behaved properly from a legal point of view. article 214 is formal: it provides for a precise sequence of procedures and a distinction between the moment when the president is appointed and the moment when the college is approved. this is intended to protect the political authority of the president. in this case, by the votes we cast, we approved the commission each time before actually appointing the president. in the first vote we approved the appointment of mr prodi, whereas the act of 19 july had already appointed the commissioners envisaged. we then proceeded with the third and fourth votes, building on the decision of 19 july, which was taken earlier. i think that this parliament has not grown up in this matter. we should have been more scrupulous than the council in respecting the very strict provisions of article 214.
in writing. - like my colleagues in the party of european socialists, who are particularly attentive and diligent in the hearings of the commissioners-designate, i welcome this procedure, which is rich in information on the personality and intentions of those who will be our privileged interlocutors. this 'examination' of the future executive before the elected representatives of the european citizens is an important step in the democratization of the european institutions, which the socialists have made their workhorse. the half-hearted performances of some of the candidates, who seem to always be reluctant to mention social europe or employment, or even the very unconvincing audition of mrs palacio, cannot hide an overall satisfactory impression. unlike the european right, which has obviously tried to hide its divisions by the virulence of its attacks, sometimes personal and insulting, against certain commissioners, i intend to favour the path of consultation and collaboration with the future commission. in my view, the main thing is to find a credible interlocutor, to put an end to an endless transition situation and to enable the european executive to resume its difficult task and finally to move forward, in close consultation with the european parliamentarians, on the decisive issues affecting europe and its citizens. it is with this spirit that i am voting in favour of the investiture of the new commission, without, however, signing a blank cheque. i want to give myself the opportunity to judge the quality of the work done on "pieces".
in writing. - i personally listened to all the speeches by president romano prodi and attended all six hearings of the commissioner-designate. the first conclusion i draw from this is that we have a strong team, with commissioners, the vast majority of whom are competent in their fields. the second conclusion is that the ideology conveyed by this team and many of its proposals are far from my ideas on the construction and management of europe, with a very worrying domination of liberalism over social and citizenship. that is why, if i am voting this afternoon, with no emotion, for the investiture of this commission, wishing it good courage and good luck, i shall be paying particular attention in a few weeks' time to the programme which will be announced for the year 2000 and the legislature. my vote on this occasion and my subsequent votes will depend on the extent to which the proposals which will be put to us correspond to those on the basis of which i was elected on 13 june. for me, more than ever, the challenges for the next five years are four: a democratic, transparent and effective political europe; 2 - a strong and fair social europe which defends the most vulnerable; 3 - a citizens' europe where every citizen feels fully european in his or her daily life; 4 - a europe that knows how to enlarge resolutely and without laxity to guarantee peace.
in writing. - the record level of abstention in the european elections in june, especially in the popular quarters, showed that europe is still far from its citizens. it is not sufficiently transparent in its operation. it is too much about the concerns of the market and big business and not enough about the concerns of the population, especially those who suffer from precariousness, unemployment and poverty. the hearing of commissioners-designate provided an initial response on reforming the way the commission operates and strengthening links with parliament. but it is on the basis of the policies pursued that europe is expected and that citizens' trust must be regained. what are the prospects for a social europe? what are the safeguards against economic forces increasingly dominated by the financial sphere? what new employment policy? what are the major works of collective interest to prepare for the future and support growth? in writing. - i would like to express my great satisfaction at having been able to participate in the great democratic moment we have just experienced, which has no parallel in the european political landscape. the european institutions, particularly the european commission and the european parliament, are coming out of the hearings of the commissioners-designate with a bang, and the european citizens who have followed them (through the press) will, i hope, find reasons to take a greater interest in european construction. for these reasons, and in view of the generally recognised competence of commissioners and the willingness of most of them to work closely with parliament, i voted to invest the european commission. i did so all the more readily because the procedure chosen for these hearings was a reminder of the commission's commitment to present, before the end of 1999, a set of proposals designed to finally give concrete substance to article 299 (2) of the treaty of amsterdam, which enshrines the specific nature of the outermost regions and establishes the right to special derogating provisions for them to enable them to cope with their structural difficulties. on the other hand, with regard to the octs associated with the european union, commissioner nielson recognised the need to present as soon as possible a set of proposals to give these countries a status adapted to their current situation, with a view to the next association convention, with the consequence in particular of renewing the financial instrument for their development. on these two subjects, to which i am particularly sensitive, the comments of the commissioners responsible seemed to me to be a good omen for future cooperation between the commission and parliament.
in writing. - the vote on ratification of the commission is not a vote of approval of its programme, since the european parliament will be consulted at the end of the year. the question now is whether the commissioners-designate are capable of performing their duties with competence and seriousness. nothing we have heard in the commissioners' hearing is likely to justify, at this stage, a veto on this or that. let's say they can benefit from a positive a priori. however, as soon as he was presented to the european parliament, romano prodi made statements that can only disappoint and worry those who expect the european union to give swift, bold answers to reorient europe to the service of the people and the people and not to finance and money, so that europe can assert itself as an alternative to liberal globalisation. mr prodi's silence on the need to defend the european social model, his distressing sobriety, his frequent omissions on a european employment policy and his cautious generalities on institutional change create more than reservations. that is why i voted against mr prodi's appointment. in the meantime, and pending a necessary reorientation of the commission's policies and a debate on future action, today's positive vote must be interpreted as a choice not to multiply the crises and the blockages in our institutions, as a refusal to seek individual scapegoats where europe's political and civilization orientation is at stake. this vote is, in a way, administrative. i am therefore not voting no confidence in the commissioners-designate. it is also not a vote of confidence. i expect the new commission to win this trust. it must know that many of us will not hesitate to punish it if its action proves as disappointing as its present political presentation.
in writing. - mr prodi spoke of the commission as a real government. mr poettering, on behalf of the epp, welcomed this drift. we, for our part, condemn it resolutely. what is mr prodi asking for? more and more powers, more and more areas of competence for the commission, that is to say, more and more centralisation and more and more regulation. mr prodi called for the drift to be continued and extended, which had led to the increase in irregularities and fraud denounced by the committee of wise men and which had led to the resignation of the santer commission. far from proposing a correction of the institutional drift, far from refocusing the commission on the limited tasks assigned to it by the treaties and on the rigorous management with which it should carry them out, mr prodi firmly subscribes to the usual view of perpetually exceeding the powers enshrined in the treaties for the benefit of the commission. the commission is proposing to increase the drift. this is the first reason why we refuse to vote for a commission which sets its objectives in defiance of the treaties. the second reason for our negative vote is a number of worrying statements made by the commissioners-designate at the hearings before the european parliament. what mr prodi and a few others have complacently presented as a model democratic exercise (mr prodi has even just spoken of "an imposing exercise of democracy") was in reality a vast session of mutual encouragement to the federalist bidding. a number of candidate commissioners - of mrs pack, particularly the energy and clarity with which she develops a convincing argument. i shall be more specific about his report at the end of this morning's debate. the commission welcomes the fact that various international civil and military administrations are now in place and have undertaken the very difficult task of rebuilding kosovo. it called on all parties to fully respect security council resolution 1244 and the various military agreements and commitments and hoped that the deployment of kfor and unmik could be completed in a timely manner. the commission supports the creation of a democratic and multiethnic kosovo and deeply regrets the continuation of ethnic violence. it strongly condemns the violence, irrespective of the ethnic group responsible, and calls for every effort to be made to ensure the reconciliation and cooperation which are essential for stability and security in the whole region. the assembly is certainly curious to know what role the commission is playing in the massive efforts to restore infrastructure and civil society in kosovo. the commission's role is broadly twofold: it is engaged in the extensive reconstruction programme and it collaborates with other international donors in unmik's coordination initiatives. the first part will no doubt be the subject of much discussion, particularly in the debate on mrs pack's report, and i shall therefore limit myself at this stage to a few of the main points. firstly, an overall budget of eur 137 million is foreseen for 1999 under the obnova programme; 46 million has already been committed and actions are under way. however, the commission is counting on the active support of this parliament - support which i have no doubt about - to obtain both the remaining eur 92 million for 1999 and the additional funds we will need in the coming years. as i speak, we estimate future needs at some 500 million euros for the year 2000 and 500 to 700 million euros for 2001 and 2002. secondly, it is clear that efficiency is of the utmost importance. the commission therefore proposes the creation of a reconstruction agency in kosovo to ensure the effective implementation of the community reconstruction programme. thirdly, it is clear that the creation of the agency needs to be well prepared and a working group has been set up precisely for this purpose. it has programmed and is in charge of implementing the first tranche of €46 million for reconstruction aid. the main concerns are mine clearance, customs and procurement of supplies for the rehabilitation of housing and public buildings, especially the hospital in mitrovica. the subsequent tranches will be used mainly to prepare the roads for winter, to make connections between towns, for which we are asking the member states to support, and then to finance public services, public buildings, economic reconstruction and institutional development. the second part of the commission's role goes beyond the implementation of community aid and extends to the international effort in favour of kosovo, which involves a whole range of activities. i will give you some examples. first, the commission, together with the other participants in the reconstruction effort and the main international financial institutions, is assessing the damage and needs. in fact, the commission is the sole methodological assessor of physical damage at the provincial level. the first results of this exercise, concerning damage to housing and local infrastructure, were published at the conference organised on the initiative of the commission and the world bank donors last july. a more comprehensive report, focusing on major infrastructures, will be published later this year. secondly, the commission shares with the world bank the task of mobilising donors and we obtained, during this conference in july, pledges for more than 2 billion euros. a second donor conference is scheduled for next month. thirdly, the assembly is aware that the european union has a special responsibility for reconstruction within the framework of the un civilian administration, unmik. the corresponding initiatives are being taken under the so-called fourth pillar, which is headed by a commission official, mr dixon. thanks to the tireless efforts of mr dixon and his colleagues, the fourth pillar is functioning well, even though it faces enormous difficulties due to the legal and institutional vacuum in kosovo. the priorities for the moment are to put the banking system in order, to work closely with the other pillars and kfor to restore the supply of essential goods, housing and transport before winter, to prepare a simplified budget with the world bank and the imf, to resolve the fiscal problems and to establish with the world bank a medium-term investment framework to be submitted to the next donor conference. fourthly, the european union, and of course the commission, will also contribute to the reconstruction effort through the other pillars: through the first pillar, it will cooperate with the unhcr on humanitarian problems; the european union will cooperate with the united nations through the second pillar and with the osce through the third pillar on institutional development and democratisation. we will endeavour to ensure full cooperation between the participants whenever there is an overlap between the civil administration and reconstruction. mr president, following the recent council decision to ease sanctions in view of the crisis in kosovo, the commission is presenting a proposal to spare kosovo and montenegro from certain sanctions imposed by the union on the former yugoslav republic. the oil embargo and the ban on air travel will therefore be lifted. it is certain that good cooperation with all the relevant kosovar authorities will be essential to establish effective controls on the final destination of aid and to avoid in writing. - marine pollution, whether accidental or deliberate, is a particularly serious threat to the maritime and coastal areas of the member states of the european union. in the recent past we have had several tragic examples of accidental pollution in the form of oil spills and other dangerous substances, including chemicals. the members of the union for europe of nations group believe that in the field of accidental marine pollution, the establishment of a community framework for cooperation is justified by the existence of a genuine common interest. the commission's proposal is to bring together, in a single legal framework, the various measures taken so far in this field. as regards the amendments adopted by the committee on the environment, we voted against all those which call on the eu's coastal neighbours to use the phare, tacis and meda programmes to make a financial contribution towards the establishment of this community framework for cooperation. the three programmes do not currently provide for any action in this area and it does not seem desirable to encourage a dispersion of resources to the detriment of priority programmes for the economic development of the neighbouring countries of the european union which are candidates for accession. on the other hand, the members of the union for a europe of nations group voted in favour of all the other amendments, including amendment no 22, which limits the commission's right of initiative and allows the ad hoc committee to set its own agenda, draw up its own minutes and the declarations of interest of its own members. it is essential to put an end to the drift we have seen in other areas: the commission tends to set up committees and systematically seek to control them in their entirety, in order to make them totally dependent on its views. each committee set up by the commission must remain autonomous and independent in order to be able to play its full role as an expert.
in writing. - meps in the union for europe of nations group voted against all the amendments adopted by the committee on the environment, which aim to convert the commission's recommendation into a directive, for three main reasons: bureaucracy, the legal basis and the structure of the control bodies in the member states of the european union. all the members of the union for a europe of nations group are in favour of a europe that promotes coordination between the different member states rather than a bureaucratic europe that advocates strict regulation that is not adapted to the diversity of geographical and cultural situations. on the legal side, we would like to point out that the role of the european parliament is to comply with the existing legal bases and that it must not, under any circumstances, create new ones which are not in accordance with the treaties signed by the governments of the various member states. finally, we would like to point out that the control bodies in the various member states are, for cultural or historical reasons, different. we know that the federalists would tend to replace the control bodies of the member states with a european super-control body that is far removed from the realities on the ground. in our view, the european supervisory body must remain as it is, that is to say, a body to check whether the supervisory bodies of the member states are applying community rules in order to avoid, of course, distortions of competition between the different member states. community rules must be applied fairly everywhere so that all operators can compete in the single market. in conclusion, the members of the union for a europe of nations group will ensure, throughout this parliamentary term, that bureaucratic and technocratic europe does not develop, but that europe develops in a harmonious framework accepted by all the citizens of the member states of the european union.

in writing. - the resolution just voted by the european parliament on the preparation of a charter of fundamental rights for the union is a perfect illustration of the risks of deviation which i denounced in my speech yesterday during the main debate. in virtually every paragraph of its resolution, the european parliament expands the interpretation of the cologne council decision in order to gain importance, marginalise national parliaments and prepare the transformation of the future charter into a european constitution. in paragraph 2, the european parliament claims that the preparation of the charter will be a joint responsibility of the council and itself, whereas it is clear that fundamental rights are now protected by national constitutions and that any exercise concerning them should involve national parliaments as a matter of priority, if not exclusively. in paragraph 3, the european parliament calls for an 'open and innovative approach to the nature of the charter, the nature of the rights which should be included in it, and its role and status in the constitutional development of the union', which clearly shows its desire to go beyond the mere collection of existing rights, as requested by the council. in paragraph 4, first and second indents, parliament requests that the number of its representatives in the 'constituent assembly' responsible for preparing the charter be equal to the number of the representatives of the member states, i.e. at least fifteen; the commission is also proposing that the member states should be able to apply the principle of subsidiarity to all the other member states. in paragraph 4, third, fourth and sixth indents, parliament asks that the future parliament itself determine the responsibilities of its bureau and the organization of its working groups and secretariat, which would give it a very wide independence to then direct the process as it sees fit. in paragraph 4, fifth indent, parliament calls for a 'contribution from ngos and citizens'. we know what this means: the intervention in the debate of persons or bodies without democratic legitimacy, chosen according to obscure criteria, and often heavily subsidized by the european commission. this is the assurance of confusion, which, in view of the preceding premises, only the federalists will be in a position to profit from. we have here a perfect example of the beginning of one of those manipulations of public opinion which the federalists have always been fond of. the most surprising aspect of this manipulation is the attitude of the council: throughout the negotiations of the treaty of amsterdam, it had fiercely resisted the grouping, in a separate title of the treaty, of all the rights of citizens scattered throughout that text. he had won the case. but at the cologne council last june, it spontaneously, abruptly and without reference to anyone, accepted something much worse: the launching of a much wider process of dispossession of national constitutions. we will oppose this undemocratic manoeuvre without compromise.
in writing. - i vote against the guidelines and priorities proposed by the european commission to the tampere european council on rights and freedoms. the simple fact that it is not envisaged to regularize all the undocumented people living and working on european soil is enough to explain my vote. it is not without cynicism to present the european area as an 'area of freedom, security and justice'. capital is not asked for its origin to ensure free movement and free investment throughout the european union. but depending on your nationality and above all your social background, the free movement of persons is regulated, restricted or prohibited. mergers of multinational enterprises are free, but not mergers of immigrant workers' families. full freedom is granted where it is harmful to employment and to society. it is rejected, however, where the most basic humanity is at stake. the 'european charter of fundamental rights' which the tampere european council is expected to draw up will be nothing but a collection of empty words if it does not at least contain complete freedom of movement and establishment for all those who reside and work in the european union, irrespective of their nationality of origin; and full equality of rights, including the right to vote.

- madam president, mr prodi, ladies and gentlemen, after hearing mr prodi's proposals, i am extremely surprised by the position of the epp and the pse on food security. they may not feel ready to make any concrete proposals today, but we do. that is why we wanted to propose a resolution, because throughout europe, the successive scandals have led to consumers no longer trusting their farmers. the argument that the environment committee is planning a hearing on animal feed should not be an obstacle to debate. we can certainly hear experts on a small part of the subject, but we parliamentarians must nevertheless take initiatives. i think that is what the citizens expect from parliament and the commission. adopting a resolution today would have been a strong signal in this regard. the recent past and its staggered productivity have left us with a situation which, in agriculture as - too often - elsewhere, has placed politics at the service of the large agro-food economic groups and the large retailers. the result: mad cows, poison chickens, dioxin-like substances, waste oil in food oil, sewage sludge in livestock meal, and so on. the list of scandals is long and shows that european countries have not been any better than their american counterparts in terms of agricultural production, even though they have banned hormones. it takes courage to say it. recent efforts by some governments to control these industries remain inadequate. in addition, many european countries have taken no action. for that we need rules which give priority to the precautionary principle which has long been dear to the greens. the meaning of this principle has yet to be agreed. for us, it is about restoring the quality of food that guarantees the safety of products fit for consumption. first of all, we ask for an inventory of all the toxic substances that can contaminate our food through pollution: air, water and soil. we are calling for regular testing in sectors which have experienced toxicity problems and for checks in agricultural areas close to polluting enterprises. we want traceability at all levels, not just in the labelling of products that end up in the housekeeper's basket, but upstream. we want to know the exact list of products that go into the feed. finally, in the name of the same principle, it is urgent to wait before accepting genetically modified products whose long-term effects on the resistance of non-cultivable plants are not known, nor is the adaptability of pests to these gmos known. if the european union really wants to show all those who have suffered from the neglect of the past that it wants to involve all actors and that they can trust politicians again, it must make very concrete proposals on food security now. (applause) i would like to thank
- madam president, mr prodi, it is good that we are having a debate today on food safety, as there are many legitimate reasons for consumers to be concerned. the council and the commission would like to take this concern into account, but at the moment they seem unable to provide any other solution than piecemeal but frivolous regulations which the cleverest and least scrupulous will continue to circumvent at the expense of food safety. recent examples show this. i would therefore like to take this opportunity of general debate to urge my colleagues and the other institutions to return to some of the principles of common sense that have been swept away by the great theories that are too economic and not human enough. trust is not something that is decreed, it is something that is created. it can be innate, particularly when it comes to local products that follow sometimes age-old quality rules. so let us take advantage of this opportunity to recognize and give due priority to these trustworthy productions. at least let those who have known them and have always practised them with the confidence of their consumers continue to do so, without putting them under the knife of inappropriate guidelines because this reality too often escapes their author. these products of the land, i tell you, should never be penalized by community legislation, especially when it comes to marketing them as local products, because the quality of these products is the best guarantee of food security. i shall take our farmers' markets as an example. of course, the fruits and vegetables in my house are in non-isothermal cages, but at least we know where they come from. if they're not fresh, they rot. so, in that case, we can do without the cool dates. on the other hand, if you do not have the privilege of being close to the production sites, you must intervene to create trust and never betray it. but i am concerned when i see that the most basic precautions are not being taken. negligence or willful failure is a serious offence, for which all those responsible will have to answer to the people. so, to ensure food safety in the face of the unknown, i believe that, beyond the practice of scientific committees as is done far too often in the united states - and, i regret, even in our own country, in the european union - with decisions taken behind closed doors, we must first of all guarantee true and complete information to the consumer from the sources of production. the transparency of these products, their traceability with production and component data, and comprehensive labelling will enable everyone to be informed. in addition, the use of unnatural ingredients such as gmos or hormones must be clearly indicated, even if we want to ban them. how many more scandals will we have to wait for before we can impose, without risking fines, the recognition of the precautionary principle which, in the field of human health, is the only one capable of guaranteeing consumers the protection to which they are entitled? that is the question you must answer today, so that this debate will not have been in vain.

- the agenda calls for the commission statement on the 11th international aids conference in lusaka.
commission. - i should like to begin by thanking the european parliament for addressing the important subject of aids in developing countries and discussing the conclusions of the international aids conference in africa, which has just been held in lusaka, zambia. the commission is very concerned about the devastating effects of aids in developing countries and the apparent failure to bring the epidemic to a halt and to provide adequate care for all those affected and infected. the statistics and analyses are convincing and show that the aids epidemic cannot be ignored by the developing countries and the international community. in developing countries, where 90 percent of the people infected with hiv live, aids is undermining all efforts to improve the quality of life. in many of the countries where it is most prevalent, aids has already reduced life expectancy by more than a decade. aids is rooted in poverty and inequality and exacerbates these factors. its effects are particularly devastating for the poor, who have the fewest resources to cope with the disease. i would like to emphasize some of the efforts made by the commission and in particular some of the new initiatives envisaged. the commission has been dealing with the aids problem since 1987 and has implemented policies, strategies, actions, financial means and, last but not least, global partnerships and partnerships between countries. by the end of 1997, the european community had allocated a total of eur 200 million to hiv/aids projects in most developing countries. we are determined to go further by allocating more resources and working with countries, member states and international partners to develop effective strategies to stop the spread of hiv, mitigate the impact of the disease on the health sector and provide care for people already infected with aids. however, we cannot tackle aids without first recognising that it is a threat to all countries and that each country has a fundamental responsibility - and capacity - to protect its own people through political leadership, adequate resources and effective and equitable strategies. an increasing number of countries have ignored the aids epidemic, denying that the behaviour of their populations is causing the disease to spread; the facts have contradicted them in a tragic way. it is particularly important that the authorities in these countries make a clear call for the prevention of the spread of the epidemic. hiding the facts won't do any good. the population must be clearly informed of the danger to which they are exposed and of the preventive measures which can be taken. i am thinking in particular of the younger generation. sexual practices and rights, especially among young people, were discussed at the recent cairo+5 international conference on population and development. the commission has already taken a number of initiatives to improve the quality of health care in the community. however, political leadership and recognition of the aids problem is only the first step. our common approach to the epidemic must be broad and equitable enough. the poor and the poor countries face many pressing problems alongside aids, and government aid and international resources are scarce and even declining. in a typical developing country, it costs as much to treat one aids patient for a year as it does to educate ten elementary school students for the same period. it is difficult but essential to strike a balance between these two commendable objectives. all partners should therefore play an appropriate role in a genuine partnership. this has been the spirit of the eu response in the past and will be the principle in the future. countries are trying to develop incentives to find solutions to reduce risk and vulnerability, even in the most difficult situations. countries need to make decisions about sustainable and equitable financing. in addition, the international community, including the eu, can help, for example by reducing the cost of condoms and providing clean needles and essential medicines. these should include medicines that can have a significant impact on reducing the risk of mother-to-child transmission of hiv and medicines that are essential, especially for the poorest, most affected and most vulnerable. as for condoms, they are one of the safest ways of preventing the spread of the epidemic. some have moral reservations about the use and promotion of this type of prevention. however, i would like to stress that given the scale of the public health problem we are facing, the interests of the populations at risk must be put before dogmatic positions of principle. it is most encouraging that a growing number of developing countries have already put the interests of their people first, but there is still a long way to go. aids must be an even more central part of our development and poverty reduction efforts. we know that the greater the inequality, the greater the number of people infected with aids, and this is particularly true in the case of inequality between men and women. aids spreads more rapidly in cases where women are dependent on the income of the spouse, are illiterate and have limited rights in divorce, inheritance and child custody. the eu, together with its international and national partners, has been generous and timely in responding to the aids pandemic in several developing countries. however, the assistance we have provided has not always been directed to the most effective interventions and has not yet reached the level needed to achieve the required results. we will therefore continue our efforts with developing countries to ensure that the knowledge available and the funds we provide produce better results in the future. however, only joint action can achieve the required level and we will redouble our efforts to coordinate our work with all the partners involved. in conclusion, the commission welcomes the declaration of the heads of state or government of the sadc on aids, signed in lusaka. we welcome the signing of an additional financial package for the regional action plan on aids in the sadc region (eur 5 million) and an additional regional initiative on aids for all acp countries (eur 20 million) as soon as possible. these additional funds may seem meager in view of the scale of the problem; however, they must be seen as an additional effort, an additional catalyst for eu and international commitments to combat this devastating epidemic. we must work together and continue these efforts.

- mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the aids epidemic in africa is becoming more and more dramatic. the recent lusaka conference was a powerful demonstration of this. every year, 2 million people die of aids and 4 million more are infected. in total, 25 million people in africa are now living with aids and their deaths are almost programmed. in about ten african countries, life expectancy will not reach 60 or 70 years in 2010, as was expected, but will fall to 40 years, a rate similar to that which we experienced in europe in the middle ages. this epidemic is not only a humanitarian and health catastrophe: it also threatens the social and economic cohesion and demographic balance of african countries. in kenya, for example, 43 of the 50 tax officials who died last year died of aids. according to the zimbabwe farmers union, the virus is responsible for a 60% decline in maize production and 30% in livestock production. in zambia, if the projections are correct, there will be one million fewer children in 2010 than today. in this situation, how can we accept that the appropriations for the fight against aids in developing countries should be cut by a third by the year 2000? - madam president, once again, when voting on the calendar of partsessions for the year 2000, we had to resist an onslaught of amendments aimed at reducing the duration of the strasbourg plenary sessions. this behaviour is all the more intolerable as it is aimed at emptying an intergovernmental compromise whose ink is barely dry of its content, since it is protocol no 12 to the treaty of amsterdam, which has just been ratified by the various member states. the commission's decision to initiate the procedure was based on the principle of proportionality. the opposition in strasbourg, therefore, finding it impossible to reduce the number of sessions, is now seeking to reduce the number of days in each session, which would lead to the same result, by different means. in our opinion, this would also be contrary to the spirit of the treaty and we are therefore pleased that these amendments have been rejected. but we also take this opportunity to reiterate our position in principle on the brussels mini-sessions. as the treaty says, and as the court of justice has pointed out, these are additional sessions - i say 'additional' - which can only be provided for if all the normal sessions in strasbourg have been held regularly. the mini-sessions are therefore supplementary sessions, which obviously means, in our view, that they can only be held if the regular strasbourg agenda is overloaded. in this case, it is clear that we cannot know today, when voting on the calendar for the year 2000, whether the agenda for the november 2000 plenary session, for example, will be overloaded and whether a mini-session will have to be added on 29 and 30 november, that is to say in more than a year's time, in exactly 14 months' time. by taking such decisions, the european parliament is violating the spirit of the treaties and i hope that governments will be found to put things right.
in writing. - on the occasion of these technical votes on veterinary and phytosanitary matters, i would like to stress how important it is that the member states of the european union retain sovereign, national, freedom of assessment and decision-making on all food safety matters. indeed, states must retain the absolute right to protect their population. we have a perfect illustration of this today with the commission's decision to lift the embargo on british beef and the refusal of france and germany to implement this decision. the french believe that if there are still 3,000 cases of mad cow disease in britain each year, despite all the precautions taken, there is something still not understood about the transmission of the disease. in these circumstances, our national agency for food safety, approved by the academy of medicine, has rightly concluded that france must maintain its embargo. if we did not have this national agency, and if we had replaced it with a european agency, as some people are now demanding, we would be deprived of objective information, and we would not even have expert opinions to justify our reluctance. however, the governments of the european countries, and particularly the french government, have put themselves in an impossible situation by adopting the treaty of amsterdam. the new article 95 of the directive, which amends the old article 100a, prevents any member state from taking measures derogating from community rules in the field of public health on its own initiative and obliges it to apply to the commission for any derogations, justifying its case by 'new scientific evidence'. it is clear that in the case of the mad cow we are not bringing forward any new scientific evidence in comparison with the evidence already in the commission's possession. we simply have a different appreciation of the precautionary principle: as often happens, the commission places a high priority on the free movement of products, and it is interesting to note that, for once, france places a higher priority on the food security of its citizens. the fact remains that the contradiction between the european decision to lift the embargo and the french refusal creates an intolerable situation, which proves, less than six months after the ratification of the treaty of amsterdam, the inconsistency of those who supported it. a few more cases like this, and the french may come to understand the usefulness of making the decisions that apply at home.

- mr president, a nuclear accident always provokes reactions of emotion, fear and even irrational terror. what happened in chernobyl has been on people's minds for a long time. but in tokaimura the japanese authorities themselves acknowledged that safety procedures were not respected at both the conversion plant and the fuel production facilities. unfortunately, this is not an unforeseeable accident. beyond our sympathetic and friendly response to the families affected by this tragedy, what are the lessons and consequences that we should draw from this accident? the first lesson, of course, is that it is imperative that the european and national authorities in each of our states ensure that safety procedures are followed. secondly, and this seems very clear to me, the iaea must intervene more regularly, not only to check the wording of regulations, which it does too much, but also to do what it does not do enough, which is to go on the ground and check that these regulations are actually being applied. in the tokaimura case, the iaea should in any event request the japanese authorities not to allow the resumption of reprocessing activities until a thorough investigation has been conducted and public and transparent findings have been made. in any case, we in the european parliament feel that it is more necessary than ever for the european commission, within the framework of its euratom powers, to help japan in the present situation, but also to ask the euratom services to make a full analysis of all the official safety regulations at our plants and around the plants in europe to see whether all the safety conditions are being met; the commission has also been asked whether emergency procedures can be added in the case of regrettable human negligence, which is much worse, at least in recent years, than the unforeseeable accident which, by definition, can cause terror. we are in favour, mr president, of the use of nuclear energy and we know that in the european union the safety regulations and conditions are stricter and more respected. we are told anyway that, for example, the possibility of starting a nuclear chain reaction because of the improper handling of an operator is practically impossible in europe. that's what happened in tokaimura. we want to avoid two pitfalls, mr president. on the one hand, unconditional and unchecked support for nuclear energy. but also, and on the other hand, what some people do too much: the manipulation of public opinion to spread irrational fears and terrors well known a thousand years ago. these were the famous millennial fears of the year 1000. today, these are the fears as we approach the year 2000. no, nuclear does not kill any more than a conventional source like coal has or still kills. that is the meaning of our resolution today.
in writing. - i am voting in favour of this report because there is an urgent need for the european union to take concrete decisions to combat the greenhouse effect. however, the reference in recital g to 'flexibility mechanisms' is unacceptable to me, since the principle of organising a market for polluting rights would be scandalous. the 'right to pollute' cannot be bought and a payment or exchange cannot free the richest from making every possible effort to respect the common law. they should have the greatest means of complying with the constraints necessary to improve the environment. every effort must be made to ensure that each actor reduces its pollution as much as possible by ensuring that the minimum effort set is achieved by all. market regulation cannot replace the requirement of equal rights - and therefore duties - for all. it is a major choice of society that should be the foundation of european identity. but here again we are making serious concessions to american and liberal conceptions which have proved ineffective in protecting the planet and their unequal effects. europe was not able to prevent the adoption of this principle in kyoto, but it is not obliged to implement it in its own country. i hope she can resist it eventually.

- madam president, my group fully endorses the interinstitutional agreement of 25 may 1999 on internal investigations which the anti-fraud office must be able to carry out in the institutions, bodies, offices or agencies of the communities, including the european parliament. we think this is an excellent agreement. we must react strongly to any suspicion of fraud. but we are a little more perplexed by the implementing measure concerning the european parliament which is being proposed to us today and which is in the form of an amendment to the rules of procedure of our assembly which concerns both officials and members. it seems to me that we have gone both too fast and not fast enough. not quickly enough because, as far as officials are concerned, it seems to me that it was pointless to wait until the end of october to take an implementing decision applying to parliament's staff, a simple decision by the bureau on the basis of rule 22 (5) of the rules of procedure might have been sufficient. but perhaps we have also gone too fast with regard to the members of parliament, and here i plead guilty before mr napolitano, the chairman of the constitutional committee, since i am a member of that committee, but perhaps the debate in plenary will enable us to make up for some of the omissions. we should have thought it strange - this does not exist in many parliamentary democracies - that the elected members of the assembly could be controlled by a body which is more or less dependent on the executive and, in this case, even though olaf is controlled by an independent monitoring committee, it is at the same time headed by an official appointed by the commission. this remark should bring us back to the interpretation of recital 4 and article 1 of the interinstitutional agreement, which define the persons whose misconduct may be the subject of administrative investigations by olaf. the staff covered by the staff regulations are officials and other servants of the communities and, i quote, 'members, officials and other staff of the institutions, bodies, offices and agencies of the communities not subject to the staff regulations'. i believe that this wording and in particular the mention of the statute show that the members and staff in question are employees rather than elected officials. moreover, members of the european parliament are subject to a separate statute under the treaty itself. therefore, madam president, i believe that members should be subjected to a rigorous system of internal control - and i am the first to say this - but i do not believe that the text which will put this control in place should simply be set apart from the standard decision applying to the whole range of community administrations. we need a specific decision for members which could perhaps provide, for example, for parliamentary inquiries, a separate supervisory board, which would be elected by our assembly at the beginning of each parliamentary term. this text would naturally be included in an annex to our rules of procedure, whereas the text concerning civil servants would not need to be included. however, if our colleagues thought that it was politically impossible to postpone the adoption of the current draft - and i am not far from agreeing with them - i believe that we should still put a reform in motion fairly quickly.
the rapporteur. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, you will understand that it is a great honour for me to speak today. i have been in this parliament for ten years and i have never had the opportunity to speak for 15 minutes, which, given my temperament, was a long frustration that ends today! i would like to say to you, mr president, madam president-in-office, madam commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, that it is a strange business to prepare a budget for the european union. what kind of budget is this, based on the principle that the budgetary authority and parliament vote on expenditure but not on revenue? what budget is it that makes it necessary to distinguish between two clearly defined categories of expenditure, one - compulsory expenditure - which is arbitrated by an authority, the council, and the other - non-compulsory expenditure - which is arbitrated by parliament? this distinction is obviously absurd. what is this budget which so binds the budgetary authority by legislative acts that certain figures, certain amounts expressed in legislative acts and programmes are so binding that they tend to reduce the budgetary procedure to a collection of legislative arbitrations already carried out? so the situation is strange to say the least. but this is a more strange affair than making a budget within the framework of the interinstitutional agreement and the budgetary perspective that we have. we are working within the framework of the financial perspective agreed in berlin. however, the least that can be said is that the programming exercise that took place there was rather strange firstly in its duration (programming for seven years in two council days was perhaps risky) and uncertain in its amounts. we now find that, regardless of how needs are approached, there is a very uncertain match between budgetary forecasts and the reality of these needs. in category i, 'agricultural expenditure, support for markets', we are already at the marginal limit; in category iv, 'external actions' - we shall come back to this - the category is literally exploding. in category v, we do not know what the administrative reform of the commission will cost, but we see the problem of pensions looming with great concern, without the appropriate expenditure having been planned; the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. already, countries such as cyprus and malta are in a precarious situation. so the budgetary programming exercise was uncertain, but also very restrictive for the european parliament because, for the first time, we are working in a framework where we have obtained, ladies and gentlemen, less flexibility in exchange for not more money as before, but less money. the situation is therefore paradoxical. the matter becomes downright surreal when we approach the 2000 budget year, because the european union is experiencing a real contradiction. on the one hand, the treaty of amsterdam and the implementation of the single currency create new burdens, on the other hand, the planned enlargement does indeed imply an additional financial effort. finally, the increasing responsibilities of the union, particularly in the field of kosovo, are also creating tensions, much greater pressures on the budget. but faced with this situation, institutions, notably the council - i wonder what the commission will do in the end - tell us: we are going to finance more policies, with more partners, assume more responsibilities with less money. i say, mr president, that there is a paradox, a contradiction, which parliament does not want to accept. that is the framework in which we find ourselves. because the 2000 budget is obviously both the story of the paradox i have just mentioned - how to finance more with less money - and also, i hope, the rejection of this paradox by parliament. how do institutions try to deal with this paradox? well, by two very simple and equally reprehensible methods: the first is to reduce spending, and the second is to sacrifice traditional priorities in favour of new ones. the draft budget which the council has submitted to us, and which we reject, seems to me to be very worrying in this respect. when i say cutting expenditure, i am thinking, for example, of expenditure in category i for which a cut has been proposed. the commission has already taken the wrong path, perhaps it regrets it a little today? we are being offered linear reductions which do not correspond to reality. same goes for payments. as regards the structural funds, we have considerable payment needs, due both to the implementation of the new agenda 2000 system and to the enormous weight of the past. this moan, which is the moan of the dying - excuse me, it is untranslatable for the interpreters, moan means remaining to be liquidated - is therefore the remaining to be liquidated of programs of past years, which are expiring. all this involves considerable effort in terms of payment and, on this point, the council does not follow us and does not follow the commission, and proposes a reduction which is totally unacceptable in relation to the apb. the commission, which has shown a certain hesitation on this issue in recent months, seems to have recently returned to a better mood, and we welcome this. so on the one hand we have a reduction in expenditure and appropriations for actual and future needs. the same applies to expenditure in category v. at the same time, yesterday's and today's priorities are being sacrificed - and this is unacceptable - in favour of tomorrow's priorities. i think there's something very wrong with that. in category 4 the council proposes something which is absolutely unacceptable, namely linear cuts without any justification. i would like to stress that we would understand very well that cuts should be made if they were at least justified, but that is not the case. we were told: "we must finance kosovo, morocco, timor, turkey". timor and turkey are not yet in the draft budget, but we shall see them there. we are told: "we must finance this and in return we will cut all traditional development spending for africa, asia and latin america". parliament says no. we will not accept that africa, latin america and asia, everyone but europe, pay for kosovo. this is unacceptable. (applause) i would like to thank more generally, we consider it important that the council should commit itself to this type of approach in the future, because, let us not be mistaken, we must structurally assume new responsibilities. and we cannot hope to make the balkans pay structurally, sustainably, for example, through enlargement, etc. no, we're not getting out of this. you will not fit the foot of berthe the big-footed, mother of charlemagne, into cinderella's shoe. that's not possible. the size of the shoe must be adjusted to the needs we have to cover. that's the situation as we see it. we are waiting for the commission to take a decision on this. the commission's apb obviously did not take into account a number of expenditures, but it was very clear. the question now is whether the commission will defend it. i would caution you, commissioner, against a proposal that could be made to substantially reduce your own apb, because it would be serious if the commission did not even defend its own policy. we would be in an even more paradoxical situation, which i am prepared to accept, namely that parliament would be the defender of the commission's preliminary draft budget, replacing the commission as the guardian of the major policies decided by the european union. i'm warning you about this. this could be serious. what is the reaction of parliament ? parliament's response is simple. he refuses to do that. it considers that the new priorities must be addressed. there are essentially two: first, we must deal with the consequences of the institutional crisis we experienced last winter at the administrative level. this implies active support and even an active demand for administrative reform to the commission. all the provisions on bat are aimed at this, as are all the appropriations for olaf. the call for the creation of a new administrative instrument, a kind of implementing agency or decentralised implementation unit, is a real need. we have had contacts with the commission which seem to have been fruitful. we expect actions after we hear words. on the international level, our second priority is indeed to finance, in one way or another, the major priorities: kosovo with 500 million, the agreement on morocco with 125 million, the programmes for turkey and timor with 50 and 30 million. we voted in this respect an amendment which reflects a strong political commitment of this parliament, even if we vote for it above category 4, which means that it does not have the status of an amendment at the moment, but it reflects a commitment of this house to vote on these appropriations at second reading, particularly as regards the agreement for morocco which is a political priority of this parliament. the second approach adopted by the european parliament is not to sacrifice traditional priorities. that is why we have overwhelmingly rejected all the linear cuts proposed by the council and we believe that we must meet the needs of planning, development, international development, social action and environmental policy. we must face all these expenditure with great energy and we must not accept to sacrifice them. i have not mentioned that there is one essential point: research in the context of administrative reform. we are waiting for the agreement in the pipeline between the commission and parliament to be put into practice and formalised in writing in order to ensure a better budgetary use of the appropriations for this subsection. so we're dealing with new priorities, we're not sacrificing traditional priorities. this implies, and this is the crux of the problem, that, thirdly, we fully respect the provisions of the interinstitutional agreement, but in a dynamic way. we respect that agreement. we respect all the ceilings in all categories and even leave substantial margins in some of them, such as category 1b 'rural development'. but we want a dynamic interpretation, in line with what has been said, and in particular we want a structural revision of category 4 that is sustainable, not annual. there are new expenses, we have to cover them. these are not annual expenditures, they are sustainable. this must be reflected in a net increase in appropriations for section iv over the whole period and not just in the 2000 budget. this is a requirement of this parliament and i hope that it will be taken fully into account by the commission and the council. how are we gonna get out of this? the council has time to reflect and to choose the means: time to reflect, since we are meeting on 25 november - at st catherine's, every tree takes root, and i hope the budgetary tree will take root - and the choice of means is yours, madam president - and yours, because i know that you cannot do everything and i regret it - to choose between two paths: the revision of the financial perspectives for category 4 which will enable us to vote on this budget in the face of the new priorities in accordance with the commitments made when this agreement was negotiated. if you do not want to go down this road, then it will be up to this parliament to return to the strict application of the treaty, article 272, and to give itself the means - which it can do - both in terms of commitments and payments, to vote appropriations commensurate with the commitments which are the political commitments of the european union and in strict compliance with the treaty. madam president, the ball is in your court. - mr president, madam president-in-office of the council, madam commissioner, every budget is, par excellence, the expression of political choices. from this point of view, i think there is a strange contradiction between pushing up the tasks assigned to the european union and pulling down the resources needed to carry them out. the iron logic of the fiscal stability pact is clearly incompatible with the ambition of a more social and united europe. to make the main points of the draft budget submitted to us by the council of ministers clear to the layman, i shall summarize them as follows. agricultural expenditure: a systematic 10% cut in all credit lines compared with the commission's preliminary draft, without even examining the specific needs on a case-by-case basis. structural funds: substantial reduction in the appropriations for regional aid. internal policies, i.e. research and networks aside, all policies in favour of employment, youth, training, the environment, culture: a reduction of almost 18% compared to our current budget. external action, particularly in the field of cooperation with the countries of the south: the cutting edge. examples have already been given, but i will add: food aid - 9% compared to today; cooperation with africa - 12%; aid to ngos - 35%. this choice is, in the eyes of my group, totally unacceptable. the reason given for these deep cuts is the unexpected emergence of new and entirely legitimate priorities, such as aid for the reconstruction of kosovo, contribution to the building of the newly liberated east timor, solidarity with the victims of the earthquake in turkey and financing of a fisheries agreement with morocco. that argument is, in my view, inadmissible. we cannot agree to strip peter to dress paul. as much as my group does not advocate any unreasonable increase in union expenditure, we feel it necessary, if the need arises, which it clearly does, to use the margin for increase in expenditure allowed by agreements between the member states themselves. however, as a percentage of the union's gross domestic product, the volume of the council's draft budget is lower than that of the commission's preliminary draft, which was already lower than that of the berlin agreement, which was itself below the ceiling set by the edinburgh agreements. where will it stop? you have to know what you want and be able to afford it. that is why my group is calling for the financial perspective to be revised for all the chapters i have just mentioned, within the limits laid down by the agreements of the member states themselves. and, mr bourlanges, since whoever can do more can do less, we support the rapporteur's proposal for a revision of the financial perspective for external action. i would also like to draw the attention of our colleagues to certain amendments tabled by my group in favour of a study on the application of the tobin tax to unesco world cultural heritage in the countries of the union, in favour of freezing aid to turkey, with the exception of aid to the victims of the earthquake, as long as the turkish authorities do not change their attitude towards the kurdish people, the cyprus question and the problem of human rights in general. finally, we urge that the appropriations entered in the 1999 budget for the european women's lobby, which brings together 1400 women's associations and does a very good job, be fully repaid in the 2000 budget. as you can see, these are common sense proposals on which all progressive members, if not more, can and should be able to agree.

- the next item is the report (a5-0035/1999) by mr huhne, on behalf of the committee on economic and monetary affairs and industrial policy, on the 1998 annual report of the european central bank (c4-0211/1999). i shall now give the floor to mr duisenberg.
- mr president, ladies and gentlemen, this is the first time that the new parliament has been given the task of monitoring the european central bank. the green group warmly supports the huhne report, not only for its professional quality but also for its general spirit. it is a response to the fundamental problem we face today, namely responsibility for the conduct of monetary policy. what is the nature of this problem ? the central bank is not a fourth power. it is not in a position, for example, to challenge the social rights acquired by europeans. these rights are based either on the universal declaration of human rights, on national legislation or on agreements between the social partners. the central bank, on the other hand, was given a specific task by the europeans: to ensure price stability. the maastricht treaty is not very specific about how it is to report on its mission to the national representation. all the central or international banks of the major countries are bound, in one form or another, to this democratic responsibility towards the socio-economic community, in the anglo-saxon countries through the parliament, in germany through the federated banks of the länder. we must now invent the forms of democratic accountability for the european central bank. the huhne report already provides many clues. we support the two amendments tabled by the rapporteur himself, the publication of votes in the council of the european central bank and the econometric models on which these votes are based. only full transparency in the relationship between the objectives set by the treaty and the actions of the council members will enable the europeans to measure whether the council members are fulfilling their duties properly, which we do not doubt. in this respect, the huhne report rightly welcomes the drop in interest rates in april. in addition to the positive effect of this decision on employment, it is in line with the objective of ecological sustainability, i.e. the refusal to give too much priority to the present over the future. this is why our group is concerned about the rumours of an upcoming rise in interest rates. such a decision would undermine both the recovery of employment in europe and green investments, in particular those related to energy savings and the fight against the greenhouse effect. such a decision could only be taken if there was a threat to price stability. and price stability is a two-way street. for many months the consumer price index has been rising at a rate of 1%, but the industrial price index has been falling at a rate of 1%. this deflation of industrial prices precipitates the preference for the present, which would become dangerous if real interest rates were to rise. it is to avoid this that our group is proposing an amendment which draws the attention of the european central bank to its mandate of ensuring price stability in both directions.
mr president, our parliament is receiving today the president of the european central bank, that is to say the president of the first institution to which the european nations - by some unknown arrangement - have decided to entrust, to give sovereign power, to eleven of them at any rate. mr duisenberg, you are thus succeeding - even if the meagre attendance here today does not seem to be in the spirit of what i am saying - the emperors and popes who, since charlemagne, have dreamed of uniting our continent by faith or by force. in the end, you will probably have more power or influence than they do, although it will be less glamorous, because at the end of the millennium, when money seems to be the ultimate universal value, you are about to hold both temporal and spiritual power within the european union. in the face of this state bank or this holy bank - i do not know how to describe it exactly - of which your vice-president, mr noyer, recently explained to us in english how it felt to be accountable for the long term when governments were succumbing to the whims of the short term because they were subject to the vagaries of universal suffrage, and therefore in the face of the all-powerful nature of this bank, our colleague huhne's excellent report calls for more transparency, without even daring to go so far as to ask you to do what could be considered an exhibition, that is to say to get out of the anonymity of decisions. we can only approve these excellent resolutions, knowing that the more democracy is abandoned or disregarded, the more transparency is spoken of. in russia, transparency is called glasnost. that is why, mr president of the central bank, i believe that today's meeting, and in particular the ridiculous counter-power that this parliament is trying to exert in relation to the considerable power entrusted to you, can only worry all those who are attached to national sovereignty, which is only a way for peoples to control their own destiny. i hope that, in recognition of the power that has been given to you, you will be able to exercise it with all the wisdom that can be hoped for.
