president of the republic of colombia. - (es) madam president, ladies and gentlemen, it is a great honour for me to stand before you, representatives of a europe of hope, which is the most successful model of political integration of this century and which proves that it is possible to move from death to life, from contempt for man to respect for his rights, from pessimism to hope; the european union is a great example of the need to promote peace and democracy in the world, and it is also a proof that peace is possible where development, social justice, the defence of the weakest, solidarity and coexistence are rooted, where they define culture, give meaning to freedom and pave the way to these shared objectives. my country has the privilege today, from this new chamber of the european parliament, of speaking to europe, to the representatives democratically elected by the 15 countries that currently make up the european union. colombia, the country i govern according to democratic principles, is struggling to achieve peace, employment, development and, in particular, social justice. the sovereign people of colombia, through the highest vote in history, have been clear and have given me an unequivocal mandate. a mandate to achieve peace within the nation. i'm not used to raising my hands to protect myself from the sunlight or having a blindfold. the international community is farsighted and watching us carefully. we too, with our own eyes, see what is happening on the territory of the nations and we know that action must be taken now, that there is no time to lose, that the time has come for cooperation and not confrontation or intervention. many of our neighbours in latin america have, over time, found a solution to their conflicts. the european union has always been very much present in this process, acting as a mediator and a bridge between different political and social sectors. the european union played a key role in the negotiation processes in guatemala and el salvador. the traditional concern of europe for peace and human rights and its accentuated tradition in the negotiation process are more than necessary support for my country: they are vital support. it is therefore also vital that europe knows the ins and outs of the colombian conflict. we can no longer allow the discussion of colombia to be based on empty words, on the idealization of conflicts of the past decades, or even less on news reports from the press that are more concerned with the spectacular nature of the news than with the reality they contain. i know the questions you have about our conflict and the peace process. why does the guerrilla persist in colombia when it has disappeared from the rest of the continent? is there a civil war in colombia? what does the "relaxation zone" mean? who is violating human rights in colombia and what is the government's commitment to human rights? is plan colombia a military plan ? i'm here today to inform you of our true situation, without denying the severity of the violence we are suffering. it is impossible to ignore the reality of my country. violence has been rampant in our homeland for years. many colombians have died because of it and many have lost their freedom because of the kidnappings. the colombian conflict, because of its own dynamics, has undergone serious transformations, and the force with which drug trafficking broke into colombia in the 1980s is undoubtedly the main factor in the escalation of violence. it has not only had an effect on the guerrillas, whose funding is increasingly coming from coca leaf rights, but has also caused the violence to spread to other armed groups and organised crime groups. in the face of escalating violence, the population has said, "enough". the protests, which are reminiscent of the spanish response to terrorism, have taken to the streets to demand an end to the violence. the people of my country are now more united than ever to demand an end to the violation of human rights, in particular kidnapping, which is an unacceptable instrument for financing guerrillas and other violent groups. there is no civil war in colombia. the guerrillas are supported by less than 4% of the colombian population. the conflict has changed substantially over the past two decades. while the military capacity of the violent groups is growing, largely boosted by the money from drug trafficking, the civilian population is asking to be excluded from the conflict, because they have understood that they are now the main victims and that their fundamental rights are being violated day after day. our conflict, ladies and gentlemen, is a sui generis conflict requiring a sui generis solution, which is what my government is working towards and is committed to. the guerrilla has occupied the attention of our people for over 40 years. during this period, several insurgent groups were involved in the conflict. but some of them also understood that the best alternative for the country is to lay down arms and embark on the path of political dialogue. in the last ten years, six armed groups with nearly 8,000 insurgents have replaced the use of their weapons with the force of their ideas. today we are moving forward on the path of negotiating the armed conflict with the farc, the oldest guerrilla group. in just over a year, through dialogue, we have agreed on a 12-point negotiating timetable and, on a historic sunday for our nation, we began the process of negotiations that will lead our country on the road to building a real and lasting peace. there has also been much speculation about the "relaxation zone". it is in fact an instrument created by colombian law to create the security conditions necessary for dialogue. this area covers only 3% of the national territory and represents 0.25% of the colombian population. in this area, we have not renounced our territorial integrity, nor the presence of the state, represented by its democratically elected mayors and municipal councillors. we are also making progress in finding a solution with the national liberation army, the eln. last week we made preliminary contacts with a view to resuming the dialogue and i hope that we will soon make progress which will enable us to begin negotiations with this subversive group as well. the whole of colombia and the international community are hopeful that progress will be made through political means. i am aware that our path is difficult and that we will continue to face difficulties, but we will move forward with determination to overcome them. peace processes take time and require patience, a lot of patience. let us recall the case of el salvador and guatemala. let us look at the processes in the middle east or in ireland. none of them found a solution overnight, but the benefits of a negotiated political solution will be clear. i want to reiterate here that i will do everything possible to obtain this vital peace for us. but as i said a few days ago in the united nations general assembly, i do not want peace at any price, but a peace which will really consolidate democracy, preserve the integrity of the territory and enable all citizens to exercise their rights and freedoms fully. i believe that we cannot achieve a dignified and democratic future without a culture of respect for fundamental rights. i know that throughout the internal conflict in colombia there have been serious violations of these rights, and this must stop. my commitment to human rights is absolute. my beliefs, my training, and the mandate of my people confirm it. that is why i have launched a broad state policy to fight within the limits of the law against armed groups that are on the margins of it; to ensure the safety, protection, support and freedom of action of human rights defenders; to address the needs of people displaced by violence; the european union is committed to the protection of human rights and the rule of law, and to the adoption of legal instruments to protect human rights and strengthen our judicial system. in short, a set of specific measures to ensure the application of international humanitarian law. the results of this policy are reflected in the significant reduction in complaints of human rights violations by the police, as acknowledged by reports from intergovernmental bodies and ngos working in this field. we have worked hard to update our legislation. congress is currently debating a bill to criminalize and punish kidnapping, genocide and massacre. similarly, my government has encouraged the approval of a new military penal code that substantially increases the power of civilian courts when they have to try military personnel for crimes such as genocide, kidnapping and torture, and we have signed the statute of the international criminal court. we have also drawn up a presidential directive to encourage respect for non-governmental organizations working in the field of human rights. i also hope that these organizations will develop their noble activity with a strictly humanitarian purpose, without interfering in political life. ladies and gentlemen, my government is working resolutely to protect human rights, and in this respect we need the support of the international community. the violations of human rights by guerrillas and self-defence groups must be denounced and punished. if a state official violates human rights, it is also a crime that cannot go unpunished. so all violations of human rights must be rejected and the perpetrators punished in accordance with the law. the "reason of humanity" must take precedence over the "reason of the state" or the justifications put forward by the perpetrators of violence. it is also important for colombia that europe and the united states understand the links between drug trafficking and violence in colombia. colombia is the nation with the highest number of victims in the world in the fight against drug trafficking. this sinister trade has been and is the main cause of the greatest evils of our recent history. the economic power of these organizations has led to corruption in many areas of our lives. the drug trade has been a major source of violence and has been the cause of the mass killings that have cost our nation a very high human cost. it is currently helping to sustain the wave of violence we are experiencing, by funding various perpetrators of violence. i have already said it and i want to say it again before you: drug trafficking is today the worst and the greatest enemy of peace, and we will not achieve lasting peace unless we dismantle the organizations involved in the odious drug trade and unless we find economically and socially sustainable alternatives and solutions. my country has borne the brunt of the fight against drug trafficking like no other. i therefore wish to take this unique opportunity to call on all countries in the international community to develop the principle of what i have called 'shared responsibility' in order to combat the world drug problem. this principle implies that we must tackle together the serious problem of drugs on a global scale, in every link of the chain, namely production, distribution, consumption, money laundering, the diversion of chemicals and the sale of weapons. it also means that we all contribute to sustainable solutions to the extent of our own possibilities. we have concluded important agreements with the european union recognising shared responsibility in this area. we have made progress in promoting cooperation mechanisms between europe and the andean countries, such as the tariff concessions of the andean gsp, the extension of which is vital for my country. in this context, i also welcome the recent tampere european council presidency conclusion on money laundering, which notes the council's decision to 'ensure that concrete measures are taken to trace, freeze, seize and confiscate the proceeds of crime'. we must confiscate the money and property of drug traffickers and their associates who have acquired it through the trade of death, we must take away all possibilities for them to buy chemicals and weapons and we must prosecute the smugglers who launder the money they obtain. we must continue to move together towards global solutions that take all the links in the chain into account. we must also give priority to education and prevention programmes together to reduce demand. in this fight, ladies and gentlemen, we need you as partners and allies. my country does not ask much of you: we only ask that each member of the international community do its part of the job, according to the principle of shared responsibility. and that we can afford the costs of sustainable solutions wherever possible and with available resources. we should also be concerned about the serious environmental damage that drug trafficking causes every day. in our homeland, one of the eight most biodiverse nations, illegal coca cultivation has destroyed over a million acres of forest, wetlands and uplands. the devastation of nature is so irrational that we are destroying five hectares of forest to grow one coca or one poppy, and that every year 200,000 gallons of herbicides, 16,000 tons of chemical fertilisers and 100,000 gallons of poisons used in these crops pollute the water and soil of colombia. today i would like to repeat that there is no doubt that illegal crop activities are damaging the natural heritage of mankind. it is therefore the duty of all our countries to put an end to this destruction in order to defend at all costs the human rights of future generations to live on a habitable planet. we share the european concerns about global warming, deforestation and the need to conserve tropical forests. we also understand that we need to address the issue of polluting emissions. that is why we intend to propose to europe an environmental alliance bringing together the countries of the european union and colombia in order to achieve this noble objective together. in the face of the real situation in colombia, it is clear that the hard work of peace building must go beyond dialogue and negotiations with the insurgents. we need to look for deep solutions to our problems. we must build a new nation where respect for human rights, the administration of justice and the reconstruction of our social fabric are the solid foundations that will enable us to form a society in which the factors of violence are eradicated once and for all. that is why i have come here, to propose to those who share these ideals to deepen their commitment to us and to consolidate a beneficial alliance for all. timely cooperation is one of the best ways to protect human rights; cooperation is about preventing what can be avoided; cooperation is opening the door to hope. it is with this aim that i have drawn up the plan colombia for peace, prosperity and the strengthening of the state. this is not a military plan. it is a comprehensive and unified strategy to strengthen the country's fundamental objectives, such as the pursuit of peace, the recovery of our economy and the creation of jobs, the protection of human rights, the strengthening of justice and the increase of social participation. the final result will be the strengthening of our state, which is essential for achieving peace and progress. we need your participation in all these areas, but we especially need you, your nations, the whole of europe to invest in peace for peace's sake, to open its markets so that we can create jobs for peace. colombia is therefore presenting to the international community an alternative policy for the eradication of illicit crops based on an alternative development offering the peasant population, currently involved in illicit cultivation, a stable solution to its economic and social problems, by replacing its illegal crops with commercial, mining, agricultural, agro-industrial and service enterprises, equipped with the necessary infrastructure to be sufficiently competitive in a globalised economy. colombia hopes to be able to finance the infrastructure of the project with countries that are in some way linked to the drug trafficking chain and also hopes to link private capital, both domestic and foreign, to economically productive enterprises so that they can integrate advanced technologies and new capital. madam president, ladies and gentlemen of the european parliament, i wish you, on behalf of the colombian people, every success in the enlargement and deepening of european democracy. you represent those who have chosen life, peace and the defence of human rights; you are the expression of those who believe in democracy, freedom and a healthy environment for future generations. it is up to you to play a major role in bringing the nations closer together, those who are building up their own hopes and who are eager to see the third millennium filled with the realities that are good for them. i am here before the representatives of european democracy to make it clear that i have placed my trust in peace; i offered the guerrillas peace in dignity and security. we need a great national agreement, backed by the international community, to live in peace. as a democrat speaking to democrats, i say to you today: bet on peace in colombia. doing so means investing in humanity and in prospects for development, well-being and social justice. thank you very much. - mr president, general de gaulle said that good politics is not a politics of good feelings. in this respect, the tampere council marks a further step in the denial of reality. the report of this conference suggests that the peculiarities of the peoples of europe should be fused in a kind of global melting pot where, i quote, 'the rights and obligations of migrants should be similar to those of citizens of the european union, the status of third-country nationals should be closer to that of nationals of the member states', and this in accordance with a so-called principle of non-discrimination. all these positive feelings will of course only increase the migration flows, i.e. unemployment and insecurity. a realistic immigration policy should, on the contrary, be to make the situation of migrants in europe more difficult by, among other things, abolishing all social aid - a policy which is also that of the us congress - by reducing economic aid to countries which encourage immigration and by systematically organising border returns. but to do this, we must break with the prevailing ideology, punish the media which, like the arte television channel, disseminate this ideology and, in general, no longer be afraid of our social and cultural superiority. we cannot shoulder the misery of the world, the inability of some to organise themselves or the vengeful thirst of the former colonies. it is natural for groups of men to seek to dominate others. it is up to our european peoples to be the strongest in this fight. if we fail to do so, europe, like any other organisation which stops fighting, will be forced to disappear into the crowd.
- mr president, despite all the good words we have just heard, it seems to me obvious that the mountain of tampere has given birth to a mouse. the only resolution adopted was to take the resolution to adopt a resolution later to solve the problems raised. yet there is urgency. while all the member states were pledging their commitment to human rights in tampere, the belgian government was sending back to slovakia, manu militari and by charter, several dozen gypsies. in france, because of changes in legislation, nearly 70,000 immigrants are undocumented, illegal. in saint-denis, in the paris region, six of them have been on hunger strike for more than 30 days. the question remains: how can member states be obliged to respect the rights and dignity of immigrants and asylum seekers ? in concrete terms, this means the right to free movement, the right to vote, the right to family reunification, the abolition of double punishment, the regularisation of the undocumented, the end of all racial discrimination. the approach taken by tampere is therefore wrong. instead of harmonizing repressive laws in a europe that is increasingly looking like a fortress, let us establish at community level real statutes and rights for immigrants and asylum seekers.
- mr president, commissioner, the europe of nations group considers that the dehaene report on the institutional implications of enlargement is not satisfactory either in its methodology or in the main conclusions it draws. the method he used: the cologne council last june refused to appoint a small working party to prepare the work of revising the treaty. he wanted the discussions to be more open from the outset. now, what have we seen? the commission, despite not being able to close the debate, hastened to appoint a small working party on its own behalf, a group which was immediately described as a group of wise men, although its members are no wiser than the average person in the chamber. all this in an attempt to force the council to stick to the agenda of the conference as desired by the commission. it is not surprising, therefore, that the dehaene report seeks to strengthen the powers of the commission and to circumvent the rights of the states. first of all, this text concludes - what a curious coincidence! - that the commission will have to present a complete draft treaty to the council as soon as the intergovernmental conference begins. so it's the same method of enforcement that continues. in the same spirit, the group is advancing the old federalist proposal for the generalization of qualified majority voting in the council. this proposal, combined with the maintenance of the commission's monopoly of initiative, would, as is well known, result in a considerable strengthening of the commission's powers and a corresponding reduction of the rights of the states. it is interesting to note that in a good example of nine european languages, the majority decisionmaking system is described in the report as 'consensus-based', although the opposite is clearly true. majority rule requires minority to comply, especially small states, while unanimity requires negotiation until consensus is reached. in the same spirit of circumventing the states, the dehaene report proposes that the treaty may in certain cases be amended by a simple decision of the council, or even by a decision taken only by a qualified majority. this is absolutely unacceptable, because it is totally contrary to our conception of a europe which respects its nations. however, this report, alongside the usual federalist pontificals, timidly outlines a new idea, that of the institutional flexibility necessary for an enlarged europe. it recognizes, as we have always said, that the enhanced cooperation of the amsterdam treaty can do nothing to solve the double problem of growing heterogeneity and the total impossibility of relinquishing sovereign powers to qualified majority decision-making procedures, and even more so in a europe of thirty or more states. that, ladies and gentlemen, is the real subject to be included on the igc's agenda, and the second subject, 'how to bring europe back under the control of its peoples', is similar to the first, since it too calls for the free exercise of national sovereignty.

in writing. - this is not the first time and certainly not the last time that i have spoken about the issues connected with the development of e-commerce services. i believe that while we should be pleased that trade is being facilitated by the advances in information technology, we must nevertheless remain extremely vigilant and ensure that there is a fair balance between the interests of service providers and consumer protection. we must take account of new developments: electronic communications and transactions are growing and becoming more widespread. the products and services of the sector generate a rapidly expanding global market, with growth expected to exceed 100% by 2001. this means that rules to regulate this new market must be adopted as soon as possible. while it creates new opportunities for profit for businesses of all kinds, it also creates a certain degree of insecurity for consumers. it is therefore imperative to develop standards for the security and legal recognition of electronic signatures and authentication services (authenticity of origin and data integrity). this is what the directive we are discussing today proposes. the european parliament had proposed several amendments at first reading. we were pleased to see that many of them were taken up in the common position. the same must be true of the amendments proposed today. this directive should be a first step in the development of a european framework in the field of electronic commerce, while being aware that we will not be able to avoid discussing this topic at world level for a long time.
in writing. - i voted against the european parliament resolution on the 1998 annual report of the european central bank (ecb) because it approves of this report, which itself is in the perspective of the transition to a fully unified european monetary system. i agree with the economists in the association for monetary independence in france that this is not a desirable objective and that, on 1 january 2002, national currencies must be maintained alongside the euro as a common currency. the european parliament resolution also deals extensively with technical measures to improve the ecb's transparency. this may seem a noble goal, but it is unattainable. the european parliament has just proved this itself by getting itself into a tangle from which it has not been able to escape. the original text of the resolution called for the meaning of the votes of the various members of the governing council to be made public after each monetary decision. mr duisenberg, president of the ecb, argued that he did not agree with this idea for all sorts of reasons, each one worse than the last. in particular, he said that publicity of votes would encourage pressure on council members. professor buiter, a member of the bank of england's monetary policy committee, has rightly said that if the votes are kept secret, the pressure will be on in secret, and that will be even worse. the european parliament's committee on economic and monetary affairs has finally withdrawn the relevant part of the draft resolution to avoid any trouble with mr duisenberg, and the european parliament has just given its approval to this resignation. this is a bigger deal than it looks. firstly, it shows the timidity, even complacency, of the european parliament's control. secondly, it should be remembered that voting advertising is permitted in all the major central banks of the world, particularly in the united states and japan. why should the european central bank be an exception? why should she play a more opaque game ? the answer is simple: the central banks i have just mentioned work each within the framework of a single nation, whereas the european central bank works with several nations and peoples. because of this difference in situation, it is much more afraid than the others of the exploitation of its internal conflicts by one or another of the member states. and to counter that danger, it's forced to be half as transparent. the european central bank, because it has jurisdiction over an area which is too heterogeneous, must distance itself even more from social reality. in doing so, it may calm the game in the immediate on this or that vote, but it is condemned in the long run by cutting off from the people. it is understood that under these circumstances i cannot approve either the european parliament resolution or the ecb's annual report for 1998.
in writing. - as a former member of the economic and monetary affairs committee, i have read the first annual report of the european bank with great attention and i try to follow its work closely. i - the agenda calls for the commission's statement on the restructuring of enterprises in the face of globalisation. i give the floor to mrs diamantopoulou, who will speak on behalf of the commission.
commission - (el) ladies and gentlemen, the michelin case is an opportunity to bring the crucial question of industrial restructuring back into the spotlight. we are indeed living in a period of profound change in industry and in business in general, due to various causes, starting, of course, with the complex phenomenon of globalisation. the liberalisation of capital, the removal of economic frontiers, the transformation of patterns due to advanced technologies and the information society, global competition are all elements which are frequently factors in restructuring and violent upheavals of industrial production. it is certain that this restructuring is foreseeable and that it can be carried out in many ways. the michelin press release and the announcement that 7 500 jobs will be lost over the next three years have raised a deep concern which i share and which concerns not only the company in question but what is happening and will now be happening in all european companies, large and small. realism leads me to say that no restructuring can be smooth sailing and without problems. but restructuring can be prudent, in other words it can take into account the social and economic cost, or it can be short-sighted, i.e. consider the immediate economic cost and pay the social cost much later, because there are many factors that have a negative impact on a company that neglects the social dimension. our objective, of course, is what i have just called prudent restructuring, and there are three key elements that many companies have taken into account, because we have dealt in the past in the european union with the two types of behaviour i have just mentioned. a prudent restructuring first of all involves providing for the employability of the persons concerned. obviously, this is both a right and a duty of the company itself. the company must have a strategic plan for the employability of the persons concerned. secondly, there is no reason why workers should not be warned in time, informed in detail and consulted on possible restructuring which could, at a lower social cost, produce the same results. the european union currently has an institutional framework which consists of two directives: one on collective redundancies and the other on the european works council. they represent a minimum set of requirements to which a company intending to restructure can refer. as far as today's debate is concerned, there is nothing to indicate at this stage that the company in question has broken the rules in force. we have a long time ahead of us to consider the next initiatives. but it is clear that, as in the present case, in view of the very important changes taking place around us, we can only change our way of dealing with them. existing rules often need to be improved, changed or replaced by new rules. that is why in november 1998 the european commission put forward a directive on information and consultation of workers which has so far received the support of parliament, and i think that the current debate on michelin will give rise to further action on our part in support of this directive. but it is certain that we are living in a time when legislation alone cannot solve the very large problem of restructuring firms, especially at a time when european industry is not only facing competition within the union's borders but must successfully face competition on a global scale. in earlier cases, such as the renault case, the commission had asked experts to examine the question of restructuring in the light of job losses. the gillenhammer report, which parliament has read, has been drawn up and contains a number of proposals which we could follow. the first concerns the creation of an observatory, on which a final decision will be taken in january, and i reserve the right to discuss this with the european parliament to see whether it is necessary to set up an observatory for smes which would inform about the changes to be made but would also have, at national level, a liaison function with local observatories so that companies are as prepared as possible for the signs of the times. the point i wish to raise now is that of social dialogue. the responsibility for social dialogue lies with the social partners and there are certain initiatives that they could take as part of their collective social responsibility. the first is that employability of workers is an aspect of national policy as well as of the workers and the enterprise itself. the employer is obliged to preserve the employability of the worker, the worker is obliged to participate in continuous information and in the continuous development of his abilities and qualifications. negotiations between employers and workers on continuing training mechanisms are one of the major aspects of the social dialogue. i would like to point out that i will have my first official meeting with the european social partners at the beginning of november and that this issue is one of the main items on the agenda. finally, i would add that, drawing again on the proposals and ideas of the gillenhammer report, i intend to send a letter to all companies employing more than a thousand people at european level, asking them to draw up, on a voluntary basis, a report entitled 'managing change' which will serve as a kind of reference point for large companies on how to plan restructuring without causing acute social problems. i think it is important to recall a number of measures which have been taken at european union level in the field of company restructuring. i will mention very briefly: the decision taken a few days ago on the implementation of the plan for high-risk capital investment, which the commission approved last week and which is an important tool, especially for newly created small businesses; measures to promote cross-border innovation; measures to encourage the mobility of employees by transferring their rights and pensions; special programmes for their training; the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos at work is a good example of the need to ensure that the directive is applied in all member states. we are dealing with a particular case today which is not a model to be imitated. a particular case where we are told of profits and a large number of job cuts at the same time. it is clear that the european union will do everything possible, as it is obliged to do, and at all levels, to help free competition, the area of free and healthy competition in which european companies operate. but it is equally clear that the union must defend what it can be proud of in the face of history - the european social model. restructuring and modernisation of enterprises cannot take place without victims. as i said earlier, while restructuring cannot be easy, it can be controlled, planned and carried out at a passing social cost. i am convinced that the proposals in the legislative field and especially the proposals in the field of cooperation between the social partners constitute a basis for tackling these major problems of our time.

- mr president, commissioner, i am glad that this debate on the wave of company restructuring we are witnessing and the accompanying job bleeding has been able to take place in the european parliament. my group had expressed this wish in the 'michelin' case. in other words - and this has just been repeated - the simultaneous announcement by the management of this large company, in front of financial analysts, of substantial profits on the one hand and the decision to cut 7,500 jobs in europe on the other. if this initiative was immediately welcomed by the stock exchange - where the stock took a leap forward - it has, on the other hand, aroused a very strong indignation in large sectors of public opinion, particularly in france but also elsewhere, as i have been able to see for myself. in a way, the cynicism of the michelin method has had the effect of multiplying tenfold the phenomenon of rejection which is increasingly caused by this very modern capitalist strategy, the so-called shareholder value strategy, the creation of value for the shareholder, which consists in subordinating everything in the first place to the bulimic demands of the financial shareholders of the company, these costs which are unbearable in their eyes, which are represented by jobs. unfortunately, michelin is far from being an exception in this respect. its provocative announcement is part of a real gangrene which we cannot allow to develop without reacting, unless we ourselves renounce all control over economic and social development and consequently the ambition to promote a european social model in globalisation. this is the case for olivetti, which, after finding the capital necessary for its juicy takeover bid on télécom italia, planned to cut 13 000 jobs; for alcatel, which, in order to regain the confidence of its financial shareholders, announced in the same move 15 billion francs, or 2.3 billion euros of net profit and 12 000 job cuts; for the banking sector, where the arrival of the euro has given a real blow to job-devouring mergers and acquisitions and moved the banking business to financial activities, if not speculative. the sad record is held by renault, which, by liquidating nissan jobs, is satisfying its shareholders and is about to export europe's most odious image to japan, not without, by ricochets, eliminating several thousand jobs in the european union itself. so what can we do ? there is the matter of governments, and in particular the reform of the laws on so-called "economic" redundancies. under no circumstances should a thriving company be allowed to reduce its workforce or even lay off employees. then there is the matter of the european union. our parliament amended the directive on information and consultation of workers last january, madam commissioner. we are still waiting for the commission to take up these amendments. but i think that today we have to go further. for example: a six-month grace period for any restructuring plan should be imposed on companies to allow for independent union expertise; if the company has received public aid - it has been said - including european aid, non-compliance with the established rules should lead to their reimbursement; in the same spirit, the role of the european works councils directive and the protection of staff delegates should be considerably strengthened. it is therefore up to the commission to submit to us as soon as possible two revised proposals for directives. finally, on the eve of the opening of the wto negotiations, i would like to stress the need for europe to assert its political will, including in the field of industrial policy, with 'employment, wealth creation and territorial development' at its centre. in the face of new technologies and the information revolution, there is room for a new conception of productivity, based not on the rationing of social spending but on the promotion of human capacities. contrary to the current tendency to deregulate everything, the european union can, if it wishes, provide itself with the instruments to promote such a policy, from taxation of speculative operations to the introduction of selective credit to encourage job creation and deter mass job cuts. my group will be contacting the main european trade union organisations to exchange our experiences and, if necessary, launch a european petition to allow our fellow citizens to influence future decisions. there has been a vilvorde effect, mr president, and we all remember the magnitude of it, but it has not translated into new rules. we want the michelin effect to bring about real change. i think that it is at this stage that our fellow citizens, faced with the restructuring we are discussing today, will be able to gauge the real extent of our solidarity. - mr president, in this debate i want to speak against the scandalous decision of michelin to lay off 7 500 people, when its profits are high. of course, i am equally appalled by the plans to cut jobs at renault-nissan, alsthom, rhône-poulenc and hoechst marion roussel, and many other companies. they all have in common that they make huge profits and still throw workers out on the streets, or they cut jobs, which has almost as serious consequences, because a job lost is another unemployed person. the companies that do this, their bosses, their large shareholders, are the main ones responsible for the seriousness of unemployment and the material and even moral misery it causes. we are in favour of a ban on redundancies in all profitable enterprises, or else we will be forced to resign. to promote the enrichment of a handful of large shareholders by pushing tens of thousands of women and men towards unemployment and poverty is a criminal act, and i weigh my words. the profits of enterprises are the result of the work of all: they must be used as a priority to maintain existing jobs and create new ones, by distributing the work without reducing wages.

counsel. - (fi) mr president, the european union wants the treaty on the prohibition of nuclear tests to enter into force as soon as possible. all eu countries whose ratification is required for entry into force have done so - including france and britain, states with nuclear weapons. the eu believes that the ctbt (comprehensive nuclear-test-ban treaty) is an important step towards nuclear non-proliferation and disarmament and that its entry into force is in the interest of all states. the european union therefore deeply regrets the decision taken on 13 october by the united states senate not to ratify the nuclear test ban treaty. this decision has a detrimental influence on multilateral efforts to promote nuclear non-proliferation and disarmament. the disappointment caused by this decision was expressed in the statement made on 13 october by the president of the european union. the tampere summit also issued a declaration on the prohibition of nuclear testing. we have underlined the support of the european union for the nuclear test ban treaty in the eu-us political dialogue. in the light of what has just happened, it should be noted that mr clinton has assured that he will do his utmost to ensure that the united states ratifies the treaty as soon as possible. mr clinton said that the united states would refrain from nuclear tests in the future. the international credibility of the nuclear test ban is strong. efforts to ban nuclear testing have a long history dating back to the 1950s. after difficult negotiations, the un general assembly accepted the comprehensive nuclear-test-ban treaty (ctbt) in september 1996. the treaty has been signed by 155 states and ratified by 51. of the 44 states with nuclear technology, whose ratification is, according to article xiv of the treaty, a condition for the treaty to enter into force, 26 have ratified it. the strong international reaction to the nuclear tests by india and pakistan last year showed that nuclear tests are strongly condemned by international opinion, regardless of the country that carries them out. the european union adopted a common position in july 1999 with the aim of strengthening eu cooperation in international efforts related to the entry into force of the ctbt. on the basis of this common position, the eu actively participated in the conference in accordance with article xiv of the treaty, which took place in vienna from 6 to 8 october. in addition, the eu has held bilateral talks with all countries that have not yet signed or ratified the treaty, but whose ratification is necessary for its entry into force, with a view to its entry into force. these efforts to bring the treaty into force must be pursued with determination. the eu calls on all countries, and in particular those, including the united states, whose ratification is a condition for the entry into force of the treaty, to accede to the treaty as soon as possible. the european union considers the treaty on the non-proliferation of nuclear weapons to be a central instrument of the international security system, which provides a comprehensive framework for the non-proliferation of nuclear weapons, as well as for nuclear disarmament. the nuclear test ban treaty supports this non-proliferation system. the european union is preparing to participate constructively in the conference on the non-proliferation treaty to be held in april-may 2000. the nuclear test ban treaty is unique in its nature. it prevents all nuclear tests, anywhere, even "peaceful" nuclear tests which were the subject of a heated theoretical debate in the 1960s, at the time of the birth of the non-proliferation treaty. compliance with the nuclear test ban treaty is monitored by a comprehensive verification system, the central part of which is a global monitoring system consisting of 321 technical measurement stations. the verification system shall also include instructions for carrying out on-the-spot checks where there is reason to suspect that the treaty has been violated. the verification system is efficient and allows for a high degree of reliability in monitoring compliance with the treaty. the verification system strengthens the maintenance of confidential relations between the contracting parties. the european union is actively involved in vienna in the preparatory work for the establishment of the organization for the application of the treaty and the monitoring system. the union supports the efforts of the preparatory commission of the ctbt to establish, in a timely and effective manner, a monitoring system, as provided for in the treaty.
the commission shares the disappointment expressed by the presidency of the council at the decision of the us senate not to ratify the comprehensive nuclear-test-ban treaty. as honourable members know, this treaty, which dates back to the non-proliferation treaty of the late 1960s, is the result of decades of hard work, decades of determined work to stop the proliferation of nuclear weapons. it is a key element of the international strategy to control, reduce and ultimately eliminate the risk of nuclear conflict. the ratification of the treaty by the present nuclear powers is essential to support our efforts to stop the proliferation of nuclear weapons to other countries. as the presidency has stressed, the european union is and remains fully committed to the pursuit of these objectives. we have endeavoured to bring this treaty into force as soon as possible. with the exception of one member state, the fifteen have already ratified the treaty and the ratification procedures are being completed in the fifteenth state. i know the american administration shares our goals. president clinton and his team redoubled their efforts to get congressional approval to ratify the treaty. they, like us, have understood how important it is that we are at the forefront of the movement to get the 44 ratifications needed for the treaty to enter into force. it is therefore all the more regrettable that the senate has voted against ratification. he seems to have acted as much for reasons of us domestic policy as for his assessment of the value of this treaty to us and international security. as reflected in the proposal before us today, i think he has made a very serious mistake. by refusing to approve the treaty, it is giving a chance to the states which we wanted to join the commitments laid down in the treaty and whose ratification is a condition for its entry into force. what is the message to russia and china? will this vote help to convince countries such as india and pakistan to ratify the treaty? this unfortunate vote could even encourage other countries' nuclear aspirations and push them to go over the line by testing their own nuclear devices. at this stage, any such nuclear test could ruin all the work that has gone into this treaty. it would undermine international support and confidence in multilateral arms control efforts. more seriously, it could lead to reciprocal action in other countries via nuclear testing or the strengthening of nuclear programmes. the senate's refusal to approve the treaty's ratification is a setback, not an irreparable defeat. we must demonstrate more than ever our commitment to the treaty and redouble our efforts to promote its early entry into force. this is essential to maintain the international momentum towards a permanent arms limitation and a stricter global non-proliferation regime. the commission has shown unwavering support for an ambitious community policy on non-proliferation issues. wherever possible, we have supplemented cfsp initiatives in this area with actions falling within community competence. for example, we have contributed to the development and strengthening of an effective nuclear safeguard system in europe, including the russian federation, under the euratom treaty. activities in this field are financially supported under the phare and tacis programmes. we are now considering extending these activities to other areas such as safeguards for chemical and biological weapons of mass destruction. the common strategy towards russia also includes specific provisions on non-proliferation. in this context, we are examining the extent of cooperation with the united states on the initiative to weaken the threat thus strengthened. accession to this treaty is also a crucial element of our policy towards south asia, as the presidency has stressed. following the nuclear tests carried out by india and pakistan, the commission took part in the international task force set up to increase confidence and develop security measures and to bring these countries to constructive discussions on regional non-proliferation and arms control. in recent years, remarkable progress has been made in international arms control, non-proliferation and disarmament, whether through bilateral or multilateral efforts. in the multilateral context, the ratification of the treaty and the revision of the non-proliferation treaty scheduled for next year will be of crucial importance in reaffirming past commitments and building a platform capable of supporting future progress. to achieve this, we must work with the united states and other major partners. the united states' leading role has been essential in the development of the global non-proliferation regime. i hope that we can encourage our american friends to take up this role again. we should do everything we can to convince congress of the importance of the ctbt to us, to the united states and to international nonproliferation efforts. i can assure you that the commission will continue to contribute to this objective. i also think that all members have a special role to play in this respect. i hope that you will take every opportunity to explain and demonstrate to your colleagues in the us senate why they should reconsider their vote on this treaty and how a renewed commitment to international non-proliferation and arms control will serve the security of the united states and, more broadly, international security and stability. in this wonderful newspaper, the international herald tribune, you can read today the abridged version of a recent speech by sandy berger, the president's national security adviser, to the council on foreign relations. he points out that american opponents of treaties similar to the one we are debating have overlooked the fact that the united states has already stopped testing and that the treaty has helped to freeze the global development of nuclear weapons even though the united states enjoys a huge strategic advantage. to paraphrase it in an unattractive but appropriate way, i hope that the fallout from this regrettable policy decision can be contained. i know that's the american administration's intention. that's what we all want. u.s. senators and congressmen should assume the responsibilities that come with their country's position in the world. this position emphasises bipartisanship on foreign policy in general and nuclear security in particular. failure to recognize it condemns us all to live in a world that is far less safe.
- mr president, mr council representative, mr commissioner, you have just very fully recalled the importance of this ban treaty, which is essentially aimed at strengthening the provisions of the non-proliferation treaty and, with it, at keeping the development of nuclear weapons under control, and thus limiting the proliferation of these weapons and the technologies necessary for their development. the treaty, which was opened for signature three years ago, was signed on the first day by the five permanent nuclear powers on the united nations security council. but to enter into in writing. - the europe of nations group supported the joint resolution on corporate restructuring in the face of globalisation, as it shows the beginning of a new spirit, distancing itself from free trade, and calling for international trade to be conceived "in the context of the more complex objective of sustainable development". i believe that while it would be very inappropriate to call into question international free trade, it is now necessary to force it to take account of a number of unstated costs to our societies. you have to continue to reap its benefits while counteracting its drawbacks. the unstated costs include social costs resulting from the relocation of enterprises. it is true that international asset reallocation can contribute to better use of assets and thus ultimately benefit everyone. but at the same time, wage competition is marginalizing the least qualified people in developed societies, which we cannot accept. the michelin company, which has just carried out controversial redundancies in france, is in precisely such a situation, since its main competitor produces tyres in eastern countries at wages five times lower. the french minister for social affairs, mrs aubry, has put forward the idea of making michelin pay an exceptional unemployment contribution. this proposal seems absurd, because in this case the company is the victim. i would suggest the opposite: that companies manufacturing in low-wage countries should be obliged to pay an exceptional unemployment contribution when importing into france or europe. this contribution would be one element - but probably not the only one - of a system of rebalancing social costs which could better regulate international trade between heterogeneous areas, without, however, depriving us of the advantages of free trade. we believe that this proposal should be put on the table at the next round of the millennium trade negotiations which are to be held in seattle. i would also like to take this opportunity to recall the main objectives of the europe of nations group at the outset of these negotiations. we want to emphasize the importance of the problems not resolved by the uruguay round, and the harmful effects of which we are now beginning to see, in the areas of social costs, which i mentioned earlier, but also in those of the environment, public health, food, etc. it must be remembered, however, that we alone, or almost all of us, refused to approve the uruguay round, both in the french national assembly and in the european parliament, for precisely this reason: we considered it very dangerous to accept substantial reductions in customs tariffs without first resolving the essential collateral problems. so now we have to try to make up for lost time by putting these social, environmental, health cost issues on the seattle agenda. (2) the we want an objective and comprehensive assessment of the uruguay round, based on transparent consultation of governments and specialised non-governmental organisations. we refuse to negotiate in the present darkness. the opening of negotiations is inappropriate in such circumstances and a moratorium should be decided pending the establishment of the balance sheets. 3) the we are even more opposed to the inclusion in the seattle agenda of certain subjects proposed today by the european union, the consequences of which we have absolutely no control over. i would mention in particular the question of international investment, which would lead to a repetition of the attempt at the dismal multilateral agreement on investment (mai). i would also mention the definition of a global competition policy which, as it is presented today, would lead even more surely to a challenge to public services than the current european policy. (4) the finally, we demand that future negotiations should at the outset recognize a fundamental principle: that each people has the right to choose its own laws and that international trade must respect them. the logical consequence is that each people has the right to express choices and preferences. preferential zones, whether expressed on a regional basis (european community) or on a functional basis (lome convention), must be recognized as legitimate when they are based on democratic decisions of the peoples concerned.

mr president, i would like to remind you that by deciding not to lift the embargo on british beef, france is merely applying the treaty which allows each state to ban or restrict its imports for reasons of protection of the health and life of people and animals. i am personally pleased that the precautionary principle takes precedence over free trade. the reasons given by france for its decision are not false pretexts masking some kind of protectionism. they are based on sound scientific arguments from afssa, a completely independent association of scientists. his studies show that the bse epidemic is far from under control. so of course, i'm not going to get into a numbers war, there are still a number of them that are here to demonstrate that. the british committee of experts does not dispute these figures, which were echoed by the director of public health in scotland, who said: 'i remain sensitive to the fact that there is a risk to human health in this country'. too many bse cases are occurring in cattle born after the ban on animal meal. how can this be explained without acknowledging that the eradication programme in britain is not yet fully developed? furthermore, the traceability of animals is not guaranteed. there is no guarantee that only animals born after 1 august 1996 and between 6 and 30 months of age are to be placed on the market. france is not the only country in this position. without having formally decided to lift the embargo, germany is dragging its feet in applying it: did not the minister for health just announce that the embargo would not be lifted until christmas? it seems to me that the european commission's decision to lift the embargo is more political than scientific, as the divergent analyses and views within the european scientific committee show. past experience with the european commission's dysfunctions and shortcomings in this bse case does not lead me to have blind faith in its decisions, to say the least. so obviously, in view of the campaign that has developed in the british press, i do not think we should fan the flames as some colleagues do. i think we must be right, and help to restore calm, with the aim of ensuring the best possible protection of the health of our fellow citizens by limiting the risks to the greatest possible extent. the question of food security has become a matter for our societies, and i would even say a requirement of our fellow citizens. i therefore think that more scientific examination should be carried out within the scientific committee, taking into account all the most recent data, pending the screening tests which could be applied to live animals and by strengthening controls at all levels. only then will france be able to lift the embargo safely.

lifting of the embargo now, when britain has no beef to export and these tests are about to be validated? the french government's attitude is not consistent. if, instead of abstaining in the council, it had voted, as germany did, in favour of maintaining the embargo in the absence of the essential elements of traceability, the embargo would be in force, consumers would be safe, the tests would be about to tell us something, the outbreak of chauvinism in the channel would have been avoided for the honour of the great british people and our conservative friends would not have had to renounce the principle of sovereignty to which they are rightfully attached. however, questions as crucial to human health as those of bse could not, of course, be dealt with by majority decisions. the whole question of the health and food protection of our people is at stake. the crisis is rooted in the obstacles to the implementation of the precautionary principle by both the european union and the wto, and it is by returning to genuine subsidiarity, not by subverting it as has been done in the name of free trade and federalist ideologies, that the precautionary principle can be properly implemented. in the field of food security, the european union is what it is, and we know that we can only expect a minimum level of protection and a value in the box rather than an added value. subsidiarity therefore imposes the urgent need to recognise that states have the right to derogate from any harmonisation measure if they intend to adopt more protective rules in the field of public health, as well as in the field of the environment. this is a key point which must be urgently included on the agenda of the next igc and, as a corollary, it is a point which must be renegotiated within the framework of the wto, otherwise any application of subsidiarity at european level could be circumvented. in marrakesh the commission made us give up our freedom of health protection. the burden of sufficient scientific evidence on the actor concerned to protect the health of his population in practice hinders or prevents the application of the precautionary principle. these provisions must be revised if the present crisis is to steer us firmly in these two interlinked directions. we cannot, as is currently the case, ask seattle to take the precautionary principle into account at wto level and refuse member states to do so. the crisis, mr president, commissioner, will not then have been unnecessary.

commission. - these days, almost nothing surprises me. i think, however, that the clarifications requested by the french authorities are not unreasonable. they concern the date-based export regime. they cover five subjects: traceability, additional testing, questions about derived products, additional information on controls - inspections and controls by the food and veterinary office at the only facility in truro, devon, which slaughters and exports this product - and finally, labelling. as regards labelling, there is currently a draft european legislation, which is due to come into force on 1 january 2000. these provisions were delayed by one year because the member states had not completed the preparatory work necessary for the application of the legislation. in the meantime, the uk authorities have introduced their own system of labelling of beef quality assurance programmes and have indicated that the voluntary labelling system would work for exports to france or other countries. this, i must stress, is done voluntarily. this is not the subject of legislation at european level. i have neither the competence nor the pretensions to do so. as a transitional measure, pending the final application of the european labelling system, this proposal was put forward by the united kingdom voluntarily and it will work in this way. i agree with you, mrs roth-behrendt, that the french authorities have not produced any new scientific evidence. the scientific steering committee confirmed it last week. this was more recent information but not new evidence to change the opinion of the scientific steering committee. as for the agency, i can only refer you to my reply to mrs jackson that i think the creation of a centralised food safety authority at commission level will have a long way to go before this kind of difficulty is eliminated. there may be some initial difficulties, but it will be a challenge for all of us who have committed ourselves to creating legislation for this agency to ensure that the competences of each of the different institutions - policy. the debate on the macroeconomic dialogue yesterday showed that monetary stability policy is enough. no one has yet demonstrated the validity of the postulate that monetary stability and full competitiveness are sufficient for employment to follow. our last debate in strasbourg on michelin and company restructuring was an opportunity to amplify our doubts on this point. once it has been said that the aim of european economic policy is employment, and that this has been decreed and loudly proclaimed, without ever realistically and pragmatically checking the validity of this assertion, a link of subordination between the economic and the social is engraved in the marble of the treaties, which ultimately reduces the latter to the management of competition for everyone and everyone for a place on an increasingly contracted labour market. the consequence of this economicist, minimalist approach is that the debate on the means of creating employment, which deviates from these liberal-inspired dogmas, is evacuated, almost forbidden. it is hard to believe that out of 22 employment guidelines, not one concerns the actual reduction of working time. none of them concerns public there is coordinated and permanent cooperation throughout the macroeconomic policy process. secondly, the important question of indicators and the harmonization of statistical services and indicators in the member states. this is a question, as has been very rightly said, which is neither technical nor technocratic but fundamentally political. the fact that we have a monitoring base for the member states is both extremely important and extremely difficult. this is one of our priorities and we are working on the harmonization of the indicators. the third point is lifelong learning. despite our efforts, it is clear from our recommendations to the member states that this issue has not received the attention it deserves. our objective for the coming year is to have a stronger and better information society. i think we can be more ambitious and set common european objectives in the field of information, because there can be no convergence of the member states without convergence in this particularly sensitive area of the information society. i would also remind you that at the cologne council the heads of state and government set targets for school internet access. i would like to emphasize the essential issue of development in the member states and its translation by local authorities into policies at regional level. the finnish presidency has given impetus and priority to this area, and we believe that the council will endorse this approach. the proposal for closer cooperation between the commission and the european parliament to give new impetus to the european employment strategy has been put forward on a number of occasions. it is clear that there are concrete procedures in place since cologne - those adopted in the spring and autumn - but i am waiting for - madam president, this is a brief reminder of the rules of procedure on the basis of rule 29. it has been clear to everyone that a number of our colleagues in one group voted differently from the majority of their group. this is in the normal exercise of the freedom of mandate, which is that of parliamentarians. this therefore means that one can have voting independence, without, however, the group being deprived of political affinities within the meaning of article 29 of that regulation. if the same rule applies to small groups as to large groups, or to large groups as to small groups, i do not think that the conclusion will be drawn that the epp group should be dissolved on the grounds that this or that national group has voting independence in this parliament. but then, for the sake of consistency, our parliament would have to reverse the decision which its majority felt it had to take in respect of a group which had observed the independence of its members' voting rights and had included this in its rules of procedure, which does not exclude the existence of political affinities within the meaning of article 29.
- madam president, i would like to make an explanation of vote on the menrad report, in particular on amendment no 31, on which the french socialist delegation and i abstained, although it was rejected. i would like to make it clear that the radical wording is the main reason for this. indeed, if we can share the idea that aid or employment incentives cannot be subjected to strict and rigid technocratic control conditions which risk excluding some of the jobseekers in difficulty from these aids, our approach encourages us to propose not control but positive and constructive support in the procedures to be carried out, which, as we know, remain difficult. the practices already in place for this type of support, especially for the most disadvantaged, show us that it is not enough to grant financial aid which would relieve us of everything else. this is ultimately a matter of the good conscience of the person who gives the money. but a genuine social accompaniment of the objectives to be set with people in difficulty in the context of contractual procedures is the only way for aid and incentives to seek employment to produce their full effects, not only for access to employment itself but also for what is closely associated with it, namely a lasting reintegration of people totally weakened by the destructive processes of unemployment. it is also in this spirit that we tabled an amendment on positive action which, unfortunately, was not adopted.
in writing. - i spoke last week about the michelin case and the real scandal of collective redundancies in an otherwise successful company. i would like to speak today on the employment guidelines for the year 2000. it is the treaty of amsterdam which gives me this opportunity and i take this opportunity to say how important it seems to me that the european parliament should be formally consulted on this subject. the current aim is not to add new guidelines, since the basis adopted in 1997 seems to be working, but to amend them, building on the 1999 joint employment report, and adapting them to the new socioeconomic situation. what this report shows is that progress has been made since 1998, with unemployment rising from 10.1% to 9.9% and 1.8 million more people in the labour force. but these positive figures should not obscure the serious disparities and problems which persist. thus, youth unemployment remains close to 20%! half of the unemployed in the european union are longterm unemployed. many jobs remain precarious, and 60 million people live below the poverty line. the european employment strategy must therefore be given new impetus and ambitious targets set, such as halving unemployment within five years. this can only be done by acting on several fronts using active preventive and corrective methods. this requires, in particular, a reform and modernisation of education and training, which must benefit everyone, without discrimination based on social background or person, and which must incorporate technological and information technology changes, and a vigorous fight against all forms of unemployment and precarious work. it is essential to prevent people from 'settling down' in unemployment. the unemployed need support, guidance and motivation to enter the world of work. imaginative measures must be found which can adapt to the diversity of national situations and respect the dignity of jobseekers. but be careful! we must not fall into the trap of certain politicians who say that under the pretext of being unemployed we must accept any job because it is better to have a precarious job than no job at all! the aim is to integrate the unemployed into the world of work in a sustainable way and with rights!
in writing. - this report is the very type of debate where political consensus is excluded. this is a highly political issue, with the conservative right flirting with precariousness and the left seeking to achieve social convergence, emphasising the link between employment, quality of employment and social protection. the amsterdam progress gives us the opportunity for the first time to join this discussion on the employment guidelines through mr menrad's report. that is why we must set ourselves targets, with a timetable. hence the importance of the amendments tabled by my group calling for (1) that the combined efforts of the member states and the european union converge towards an employment rate of 65% in the next five years, (1) that preventive measures aim at the long-term reduction of unemployment by 50% in each member state over the next five years, (2) that positive measures be taken to encourage young unemployed people to take up employment and facilitate their integration into the labour market, (3) that a new deadline of 2002 be set for equipping schools with computers and allowing students to access the internet. employment is not only measured in terms of job creation, but above all in terms of the quality of employment, education and training for all. we will be judged on the overall quality of this project, on the quantitative results, but also on the qualitative results, on a new way of life, on working life and life outside work, on a shared time. let us dare and put all our weapons on our side, on the side of life and integration.
in writing. - i welcome the fact that the treaty of amsterdam recognises the european parliament's ability to be more closely associated with the implementation of the european employment pact and that our assembly has therefore been able to express its views on the guidelines for the member states for the year 2000 in the fight against unemployment. improving vocational integration, developing entrepreneurship, encouraging the adaptability of enterprises and their workers, and strengthening equal opportunities for women and men are the main pillars of this policy. beyond these ambitious principles, we have asked the council and the commission to turn the guidelines into concrete proposals to be translated into practical and effective measures in the member states. although i welcome the fall in unemployment at european level (9.4% of the working population in 1999 compared with 10.1% in 1998), the hard facts must not in any way obscure the very difficult human and social economic situation in the most disadvantaged regions of the community. the fruits of growth are not shared by all, far from it! the french overseas departments, for example, have dramatically high unemployment rates: martinique 27%, guadeloupe 30%, réunion 37%. this situation, far from being resolved, has been steadily worsening in recent years, with the aggravating circumstance that every year tens of thousands of young people are thus struck by the ban on hope! at 25 years old, having, as they say, "life ahead of you" but without any chance to conceive a life project, with no other prospects than unemployment and a minimum subsistence income, is this not worse than a death sentence? in these circumstances, should we be surprised (or outraged as some are) at the temptation to violence that is plaguing our youth and, in episodes, shaking the lid of our social cauldron? this situation is all the more worrying because it is not due to cyclical phenomena: it is our remoteness, our insularity, the very structure of our societies, with their demographic dynamism, that are causing this situation. it is not enough for growth to return and become sustainable to bring about the prospect of full employment again! but this present reality must not be regarded as a fatality! nothing is inevitable, which is why imagination as well as heart is needed to find specific answers to equally specific problems. in this respect, the new article 299 (2) of the treaty of amsterdam, by enshrining the particular nature of the french overseas departments as the outermost regions of the union, gives us the possibility of adopting measures derogating from community law in the interests of their development. it should be recalled that the european council in cologne last june invited the commission to present, before the end of this year, a set of proposals to give substance to this new legal basis. this is where our congregation must be vigilant, so that these actions are marked by boldness and ambition. this is the only way to cope with the difficulties facing these regions, the only chance of not disappointing the immense expectations of their people, who are the advanced points of europe in the heart of the caribbean and the indian ocean.
in writing. - i cannot vote for the whole report on the guidelines for the employment policies of the member states. these guidelines do not intend to change the dictatorship of the market and multinationals over the economy. however, the european union has 20 million unemployed and 60 million poor people and there are no binding measures in the guidelines to prevent redundancies and job-cutting schemes. the only remedies proposed are aid to enterprises which, in most cases, are not job creators. the so-called employment policy will at best be reduced to a few empty phrases, at worst it will continue to be used as a pretext for subsidizing the employers, at a loss of funds, unless authoritarian measures are taken to prohibit large european companies which are making profits from cutting jobs at the same time. the fact that the european states grouped in the union refuse to take binding measures in this particular area shows that its main concern is to remove all obstacles, including social obstacles, from large enterprises in order to maximise their profits and by no means to put an end to unemployment.
