- mr president, ladies and gentlemen, it is a happy moment to see the daphne programme renewed. the determination of the members of parliament, from 1996 with the report by marianne eriksson, to today's report by maria antonia avilés perea, has therefore made it possible for violence against young people, children and women to be the subject of political action. i weigh my words when i speak of politics, because this violence is unacceptable in the eyes of countries which have been built for fifty years on the principle of human rights. let me stress the dignity of the victims of violence, the need for a proper understanding of their health and their mental and physical integrity. prevention seems to be the right word. if we restore to it all its richness, which is to act on the causes as well as on the consequences, then the question is indeed political, in the sense that we want the causes of violence, which are mostly male - and i regret, as mrs gröner does, that men are so little present here in the chamber tonight - to be analysed and combated in the framework of the programme to come. we also hope that the consequences of violence and the effectiveness of a remedy, and more, will be taken into account in order to put an end to this violence. that is why we must give this programme its full scope, both for the children on the one hand and for the women on the other. these are two categories of victims which must be distinguished. europe must dedicate a day to the rights of the child, as is happening in france, for example, and as the european parliament has been calling for some time. are we not celebrating the tenth anniversary of the international convention on the rights of the child today? therefore, the dignity of women must be unambiguous. if the word 'sexual exploitation' means the trade that can be made with the body of another, then there is no good trade, nor is there any human trafficking or prostitution. states as states cannot accept, even organize, or even promote the commercialization of women. the awareness is recent with regard to rape, for example, which was only so recently considered at best a crime, whereas today we know well that it is a crime. the awareness is recent; i am glad that violence against children and women is no longer a taboo. if this programme is to be seen as an experiment, it must be understood in the strong sense, as a model, and not just as a one-off experiment for the future enlargement of europe, as for the responsibility of democratic europe throughout the world. i believe that we europeans have a responsibility. i hope that the new daphne programme will be implemented as soon as possible and, if possible, with more resources in time and budget. but i would like to see that, beyond a health approach, we know that this is a fundamental human right; i would like this programme to be guided by the objective of combating all forms of violence against children and women.
- mr president, raising public awareness, exchanging information, and thus trying to protect children, adolescents and women from all these situations of fracture and despair - that is the great mission of the daphne programme. behind these texts are recitals, the broken individual fates of children and women who suffer physical violence but also and more insidiously moral harassment. this is the physical and mental health of europeans. direct or indirect violence against any person deemed weak must be condemned without complacency. i personally feel that violence is on display in the marriage, in the family, in business, on television, or even in political and social life. perversion, aggression, predation are all the more fascinating and the victims are treated with little regard in this world of the law of the stronger. our time refuses to set standards. it tolerates perversion because to set a limit today means an intention to censor. we have lost our moral or religious boundaries and we don't regain our capacity to be outraged unless the facts are visible, like bruises on a face, or appear on the public stage, relayed by the media. information campaigns are therefore needed and the daphne programme will support them. violence belongs to a world without borders and not to barbaric and distant times. we are indeed in 1999 and we are sitting in this chamber in strasbourg and discussing violence against children and women in europe. we are not living in a cruel and obscurantist mythical middle ages but at the dawn of the 21st century. i strongly support the establishment of the daphne programme; - (de) mr president, dear mrs haug, first of all i would like to thank you. looking at your report has been a political as well as an intellectual pleasure. i certainly think that the report describes what is currently considered politically feasible, but i think that in view of the challenges ahead, we have a responsibility to consider fundamental reform which is not measured by what is politically feasible but by what is politically necessary. when we want to change a system, we have to be clear about the benefits of the current system, and i think these are the four fundamental points. firstly, the framework of the current eu own resources system is very rigid. the revenue is limited, in partial regression, and additional expenditure can only be financed if other expenditure is eliminated. in the meantime, however, european integration has reached such a level that we are simply running up against the limits of the framework. this means that this framework can no longer cover the expenditure necessary for enlargement of the union, the respect of human rights in the world and the creation of a context capable of countering the rise in unemployment. secondly, if we are to discuss reform in this parliament, we must finally be able to give a detailed opinion on all this. in this respect, the european parliament's budgetary rights are quite inadequate. thirdly, the existing structures for budgetary decisions make any deep reform extremely difficult. it is quite natural that member states should remain below the ceiling when they are being urged at national level to be budgetary strict and to respect the stability criteria. fourthly, while the discussion of fair distribution is justified, it is also absurd. absurd because the member states' interpretation of the concept of equity means that, in the end, they want to get back what they pay into the budget of the european union. if that is the case, i think we could really do without the european union. there can be no question of fairness in the european union unless the original objectives of economic development, prosperity and the reduction of development disparities are the founding criteria of this fairness. finally, every budget represents the financial implementation of political strategies. the task which the european union has set itself for the years ahead is considerable. if at the same time we try to cut expenditure systematically, we simply cannot meet the political needs. add to this cuts, corrections and other similar measures, and any company that does so will be bankrupt. this means that we must now look at the possibilities for improvement on the revenue side. europe needs a financing system that is independent of gnp resources and the particular interests of the member states. in short, we need our own tax revenue. the first report published in march mentioned a whole series of positive measures in this respect: an ecological tax, a co2 tax, a levy on the profits of short-term speculation, the use of the ecb's profits. this is the way we must go so that the european parliament and the european union will still have sufficient own resources in the future.
mr president, the haug report, which has been submitted to this house, raises a highly political problem, namely the question of financing the union from its own resources. in other times, french leaders have not hesitated to practice the empty chair policy on such an issue. unfortunately, our country is now the big loser at the berlin summit, where the fifteen agreed to revise the union's resources system. in berlin we did indeed accept the principle that some rich countries, those in the north of the union, were paying too much, which is why the financing quotas of the member states have been re-weighted, with the result that france will have an increased share, up to several billion francs. it is also clear that the limitation of the contribution of certain member states to the financing of the united kingdom rebate will have the effect of increasing the contribution of the others. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. we are opposed to the haug report, which proposes to reduce gradually the dependence of the system on contributions from the member states and eventually to achieve financial autonomy. financial autonomy, fiscal autonomy, are we not, without admitting it, moving towards the creation of a european tax? in any case, this financial autonomy always follows the same logic, which we obviously condemn. more and more integration, more and more federalism in this europe, always at the expense of the nation states, taking away what is left of their sovereignty, their fiscal sovereignty. we cannot therefore accept that and we shall vote against this report.
- mr president, the proposal is to increase the european union's own resources and to allocate them differently between the member states. the real problem of distribution is not between states, or between states and the european union, but between social categories. of course, the draft resolution hypocritically states that this need not lead to an increase in the burden on the european citizen. but it seems clear that this is a wishful thinking and that future european taxes will be added to the others. i am all the more opposed to any idea of increasing taxes, since the burden of taxation, both national and european, falls mainly on the lower classes. in all of europe, indirect taxes are the main source of taxation, but they are particularly unfair because they are paid at the same rate by the poorest and the richest. the lowest paid employees and even the unemployed or homeless, by paying vat on their food, contribute to the financing of the european institutions, which have not taken a single measure in their favour. the fundamental raison d'être of the european union is to favour large enterprises by removing the obstacles they face, unifying their market in europe and supporting them in the world market. so if we have to pay more for the european institutions, for their services, let it be these big companies that pay, let us tax their profits and the shareholders' dividends and make them pay.
mr president, a system of own resources raises four questions: who should pay, on what basis should we pay, what should we pay and who should decide to charge? neither the commission nor parliament has the power to answer these four questions. we are in this case the imaginary actors of a play written by others. mrs haug, and her report has the great merit of doing so, raises a number of problems and is going in the right direction. who 's paying ? the states, or the individuals and economic agents? the current trend is towards the states and not towards individuals and economic agents. this is a dangerous trend towards intergovernmentalisation, towards the articulation of our resource system. what are the grounds for paying? proportionality, progressivity, what is that? we can hesitate. what we are seeing today is that if there is a step in the right direction towards proportionality, we are inventing a new system which is to base the contribution on the expenditure. i pay, therefore i receive; i receive, therefore i pay; i'll give you grants, provided you pay them. this is absurd ! we're in the middle of surrealism. what do we have to pay ? does anyone think we can go on for a long time with such a limited rate of borrowing, while the european union is taking on more and more new responsibilities linked to the extension of monetary union, the enlargement of the union, the taking into account of foreign and security policy responsibilities? we are in the throes of schizophrenia on this point. who's to say who's gonna pay? for now, it's the states and the states alone. it is absolutely necessary to reform this mechanism. it is imperative, ladies and gentlemen, that the question of own resources should be at the heart of the next intergovernmental conference.
- mr president, madam commissioner, madam rapporteur, ladies and gentlemen, following the berlin agreement, the interinstitutional agreement, it was necessary to revise the european union's own resources system in order to correctly weight the quotas of each member state. the jutta haug report recalls the objective of this revision. it has four objectives: to simplify the system, to make it more transparent and thus more understandable, to strengthen the financial autonomy of the european union and to reduce the imbalances between the budgetary contributions of the member states. the proposed rebalancing of the four types of resources, and especially the reduction in the vat share to the benefit of the part linked to each country's gnp, is particularly interesting, because it is much more equitable. it better represents the real contributory capacities of each citizen. we are holding on to that and we must continue. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament. first, it is essential that the imbalances in current budgetary contributions due to returns which may be historically explained be gradually, progressively but stubbornly dismantled and that the contributions of each country be brought back to what they should be objectively, accounting-wise. this simplification is essential for the fairness of the system and the transparency of management, both imperatives for securing the future of europe. especially on the eve of enlargement, the current practices of discounts or rebates are no longer justified and must therefore be abandoned. the second point i would like to draw your attention to seems to me extremely strange. this is the request made by the member states to withhold management and collection costs, which could rise from 10 to 25%. what justification is there for this usurious increase ? the strengthening of control and monitoring missions for food safety; these activities are normal for states. it is therefore essential to maintain the basic rate of 10%, which will largely cover the costs of this function. on behalf of parliament, i expect the commission to take up the wishes mentioned above, as they are essential to our political objectives of clarity, transparency and fairness.

- mr president, the chichester report will certainly have important repercussions on european energy policy. the edd group voted for it because we are committed to the principle of subsidiarity. energy remains a strategic and sensitive area for states. it is essential to let them choose and define policy in this area, since europe and especially the commission have only a supporting role to play and not a censoring one. this report, which is very realistic, shows an undeniable openness of mind. it does not condemn or close any doors, especially the nuclear one. it identifies the different energy sources which are perceived as complementary and not as substitutes for the energies currently used. energy realism requires it. all leads must be explored, none must be ignored or sacrificed. the diversity of sources must be emphasized. finally, the greatest possible transparency must be ensured, while respecting the strategic safety rules. through serious and thorough studies and evaluations, each individual will be able to assess the relevance of a particular choice, which will make it possible to make any corrections in our management that are necessary as a result of the knowledge evaluation. we want energy and the environment to coexist intelligently, but we must avoid sacrificing energy on the altar of the environment. the consequences would be catastrophic for the member states.

to do so. in my view, one of the important tasks of the helsinki summit will be to decide what this military force should be, how it should be developed and how the union should decide on its use. was not a final destination but a starting point and i am convinced that helsinki will be a new, very important step in this process. we have gradually moved closer to a goal which i believe is of ministers want the union to have the appropriate means to assess crises and to have equally adequate and clear procedures to take decisions if action is needed. i think that is a very important element. we must also take account, madam president, of the contributions and interests of the allied countries which are not members of the union. this will mean that we have arrangements for them to express their views when we assess a crisis situation and adequate mechanisms for them to also participate fully in operational decisions if we invite them to join us. ladies and gentlemen, madam president, all these measures must also be taken - and it is important to stress this - for reasons of credibility. first, to be credible in the face of our own public opinions. we cannot be credible if we simply improve the institutional and bureaucratic mechanisms. if we want our citizens and public opinion to support a european security policy, we must convince them of our willingness and ability to provide ourselves with the appropriate means. secondly, to be credible to our transatlantic partners and nato allies who are not members of the union. if we want to be taken seriously, we have to prove it. this means that we must strengthen our military forces. if we are serious, and we are, our allies will be more willing to provide us with their resources. thirdly, ladies and gentlemen, to be credible at international level. we must prove our capacity to respond in times of crisis, perhaps not when our survival is at stake, but when something else equally important is at stake, our moral stature, our moral greatness as europeans. i believe that the defence of our values, our way of life, our freedoms and our well-being will be more effectively ensured jointly than by each of our countries in isolation. finally, ladies and gentlemen, to be honest with ourselves. we will not be able to achieve this successfully unless we commit ourselves clearly, energetically and decisively to this goal. however, i would like to stress that security is not limited to military aspects. it's obvious. the cologne european council asked the council to examine all aspects of security with a view to strengthening and coordinating all non-military instruments to respond to crisis situations. in this respect, the finnish presidency has done an extraordinary job, which will be reflected in a report to the helsinki european council on non-military instruments for crisis management. i think it is very important to continue along this path. we need to establish mechanisms that cover the full range, the full spectrum of crisis management instruments, from the strictly humanitarian and civilian ones to the other extreme, more related to the military aspects. ladies and gentlemen, in this spectrum, this range, we must make an effort to strengthen the instruments of protection of citizens and of law enforcement, namely, the police instruments, whose urgent need has been brought to light during the last crises. you will recall that both in bosnia and in kosovo at the present time the problem of international policing remains crucial, it finds no solution and it persists. and i am well aware that this parliament is particularly sensitive to this problem. ladies and gentlemen, i'm almost finished. if we take these steps and solve these problems properly, i am cooperation with our partners and allies. madam president, i would like to conclude by reiterating my firm intention to work closely with this parliament in all areas. the main task and priority of in writing. - this daphne programme has been welcomed by all of us, the members of the european parliament, but also by all the non-governmental organisations and other organisations and associations working in the sensitive field of violence against children, adolescents and women. the council has reduced the duration of the programme - four years instead of the five originally planned - but the budgetary allocation remains unchanged. the rapporteur has done an excellent job of negotiating with the council and as a result our three key amendments are accepted by both the commission and the council. these amendments concern first of all the necessary reference to the notion of the physical and emotional integrity of the person and to that of his dignity, so that the exercise of physical, sexual or psychological violence amounts to depriving the person of his human rights; secondly, the definition of 'public health' as conceived by who, i.e. not just as the absence of disease or infirmity, but as a state of physical, mental and social well-being, is included in the report; thirdly, the encouragement to be given to organisations and associations in general working in this sector is emphasised. fourth, but not least, it refers to the information and awareness of the public and the media on these painful social issues. the expectations are high, therefore, and it is imperative that this house should take a decision on this matter, and since codecision is required, we must mobilise the 314 votes needed to adopt the daphne programme. i can therefore only urge you to vote unanimously on this report, to avoid further delays in the conciliation procedure and to allow it to enter into force as from january 2000.
- mr president, mrs haug's report on the european union's own resources system seems to us to be quite contradictory, and that is why we opposed it. on the one hand, it affirms excellent principles of economy, in particular the idea that the union's resources must be limited to 1.27% of the gnp of the member states, a ceiling which the commission's proposal was precisely seeking to circumvent in a in writing. - the proposal for a council regulation on which we are voting today seeks to make certain changes made necessary by the decision of the european council of heads of state or government in berlin in march. the european commission is taking this opportunity to introduce new rules which express a new conception of budgetary discipline and extend its management powers, and we cannot accept that. it is also proposed that these rules should now take the legal form of a decision rather than a regulation. the french delegation of our group opposes this change in the legal nature of the act, in the sense that the regulation makes it possible to take better account of the impact of budgetary discipline on the member states as well as on the community institutions. the commission's initial proposal was unanimously opposed in the committee on budgets. another element also strengthens the powers given to the european commission in the framework of the proposal under consideration: the possibility of reducing the amount of direct aid or suspending the payment of monthly advances. since the reduced or suspended amounts are expected to be borne by the community budget by the following financial year at the latest, this intervention will necessarily result in more stringent measures in the following years, with the risk of undermining the principles of the common agricultural policy. the french delegation of the union for a europe of nations group is therefore opposed to the proposal for a regulation, as is the averoff report.

commission. - mr president, with your permission, i was just thinking for a moment about these motions for a resolution. i am sure that members can easily imagine my feelings about the events of the inform parliament of our most recent contacts with the russian authorities concerning chechnya. i will also be able to take part in the discussions planned in istanbul on this subject, with a much clearer idea of the views of the european parliament. i think it is fair to say that there is a general consensus in the european union - council, parliament and commission - on the following two principles. firstly, whatever the understandable outrage over the terrible acts of terrorism in moscow, the north caucasus and elsewhere - acts which i condemn unreservedly, as i, whose country has been the target of terrorism all too often - the russian reaction in recent weeks has been marked by a repeated and disproportionate use of military strikes, a constant disregard for the search for a political solution and a sustained indifference to the tragic human consequences. secondly, most people - and i think this is also the prevailing view throughout the european union - consider that it would be a historic mistake to start the new century by leaving russia out of european affairs as we did at the beginning of this century. it is because it wants to avoid repeating the mistakes made after 1917 that the european union is sincerely trying to establish a strategic partnership with russia. we can only see this in the dialogue we have established under the partnership and cooperation agreement and the common strategy adopted at the cologne european council. it is equally clear that the situation developing in chechnya is putting considerable pressure on our relations with russia. the russian authorities must understand that their current behaviour affects their recognition by the international community and the credibility of russia as a political and economic partner. they are trying to justify their action by the pressure of russian public opinion. it is exactly the same when they refuse to respond to the legitimate trade concerns of the european union, despite the €10 billion surplus in their trade balance with us. however, we live in democratic countries with democratic institutions such as this parliament. we must also expect pressure from the public, which is understandably horrified by what is happening in chechnya and does not always understand that we can be just spectators. so far we have reacted by trying to increase diplomatic and political pressure on russia. we took every opportunity to get the message out to all levels. at the beginning of october i participated in the troika led by foreign minister halonen. the chechen issue was omnipresent at the eu-russia summit on 22 october and dominated the discussions of the general affairs council on monday. at each stage, we have tightened the tone and radicalised the operational proposals. the message from the council this week could not be clearer. the european union strongly condemns any disproportionate and indiscriminate use of force in chechnya and urges the russian government to respect its humanitarian commitments in accordance with humanitarian law. there is no alternative to seeking a negotiated agreement based on dialogue with the elected leaders of the north caucasus countries, including chechnya. the council stressed that russia would be making a serious political mistake by imposing a military solution on chechnya. what would the situation be in a month or two, in a year or two? there seems to be no long-term russian strategy for ensuring lasting peace. more specifically, the council urges a role for the osce and the opening of an osce assistance group office in chechnya in nazran and ingushetia. the council concluded that the istanbul summit on thursday and friday could serve, among other things, to convey these messages to the russian authorities. i would certainly like to come back to this house after istanbul to give an account of the message as we have delivered it and the reactions that have been received. i am asked more and more often whether the european union should not step up the pressure and move from forceful talk to more direct action. what do you mean by that? some are proposing to close the financial aid tap under the tacis programme. do you think this will stop the military intervention? such a measure would not have a direct impact on russian public finances, as all funds follow the chain of contractors mainly located in the european union. it would, however, undermine the process of economic and social modernisation which we have so vehemently defended. what if we suspended the food aid? the current program is coming to an end. by september, more than 90% of the planned food aid had already been delivered to russia. it is now up to the russian authorities to distribute them. our priority is to ensure that the proceeds from the programme are actually used to pay pension arrears and other social projects. as far as the future is concerned, we have serious doubts about the need and economic justification for a new food aid programme. recent events in chechnya provide a further strong political argument against any further request for food aid from russia. i already warned madeleine albright last week that i did not think this parliament would approve any new food aid to russia this winter. it was also suggested that the imf assistance and the ebrd loans be suspended. these are clearly not matters for the european union to deal with directly. that said, would it really be in our interest to provoke a backlash against the international community on the eve of the duma elections in december? the osce meeting in istanbul offers an opportunity to move forward, although i am not very optimistic. the russians have made it clear that their public opinion comes before any other consideration in their handling of the crisis. our job must be to convince them that their current approach, which lacks vision, will never lead to lasting peace in the caucasus, and that we must be able to provide quickly and in sufficient quantities the food aid that the people so desperately need with the coming of winter. we will be more effective on both fronts if we keep the channels of communication open. that is why, as the presidency and the high representative, i wish to remain in close contact with igor ivanov, the russian minister for foreign affairs. we met last week in helsinki on the sidelines of the conference on the nordic dimension and have spoken by telephone since then. as regards the urgency of the humanitarian situation, i have repeatedly stressed the need to guarantee access and security for international aid agencies. some progress has been made following recent evaluation missions by external experts and donors. these have provided a better measure of the scale of humanitarian needs. it is reported that ingushetia is now hosting up to 200,000 chechen refugees, most of whom live with families and the rest in camps. many of the displaced - mr president, commissioner lamy, this morning the president-in-office of the council recalled the importance of agriculture in the wto negotiations, and i thank him for that. you already know that european farmers will have to make a great deal of effort to adapt to the implementation of the berlin compromise, which was the acceptable balance for the 15 member states of the european union last march. you know that the developing countries must be able to count on europe to guarantee the legitimate growth of their own agriculture, which is often the major sector of their economic development. you know that the united states is now demonstrating that the market alone can hardly provide agricultural income. so you should also know that we are counting on you in particular to lead these wto negotiations to the results we want. as regards market access, how can we fail to recognise that europe is not the fortress it is unjustly accused of being, when we are the world's largest importer with a deficit in the agri-food trade balance? - mr president, on the eve of seattle, i still think it is regrettable to embark on a new round of negotiations without taking a serious look at the previous one. the fact that millions of people are affected by the consequences of the decisions that will be taken, however, makes it a necessity. the adherents of trade liberalisation as a driver of prosperity are all the more reluctant to accept this assessment because it is indeed difficult to deny that the situation has worsened in recent years with the increase in inequalities between the backward developing countries and the advanced countries, as well as the growth of inequalities within the developed countries themselves. when there is a concentration of wealth at one pole and an increase in unemployment at another, one can indeed ask whether the wto has not first served to institutionalize the law of the strongest. there is an urgent need to promote a new approach to trade between nations, based on solidarity, cooperation, democracy, the promotion of employment and social rights. but if all this is not to remain a pious wish, decisions must be taken, i think, in three directions. firstly, to give substance to the principle that these negotiations must be of benefit to countries and peoples in difficulty, by affirming the right of the union and the member states to defend their development policy and the specific agreements with the acp and by refusing to see the lomé agreements called into question by the wto. secondly, to affirm the primacy of the interests of the people over commercial and financial criteria. i shall make three proposals in this connection, provided that they are not exhaustive. first, to subordinate the rules of the wto to the international charters and conventions governing human rights, social, health and environmental issues. i am thinking here of kyoto, beijing and copenhagen. secondly, to refuse further liberalization of services and, on the contrary, to help develop cooperation in public services of education, health, transport. finally, to maintain the principle of cultural exception, which recognises the possibility for the union and the member states to preserve their capacity to define freely their audiovisual cultural policy in the name of the development of a living and enriching diversity. another proposal is to make the precautionary principle of the environment, health and food safety a top priority. thirdly, a thorough democratization of the wto structures is essential. democratic control of the negotiations and the implementation of the agreements is necessary. it is necessary to accept the presence of ngos, representatives of civil society and trade unions, with observer status, at these negotiations. it is also necessary for all the points negotiated at the wto to be ratified by the european parliament and the national parliaments. today, the wto makes laws, enforces them, and settles disputes. i believe that one cannot be both judge and party. the dispute settlement body needs to be radically changed.
- mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, by 2005 at the latest, the trade negotiations opened in seattle will be completed. mr lamy, you will be back in 2005, sitting in the same seat, and you will tell us that the european union has been a global success because it is a global negotiation. you will have obtained, in the final act, a mention on the precautionary principle, on sanitary, even phytosanitary, an ilo-wto forum, a recognition of environmental principles, especially since they have already been recognized in kyoto. we'll have improved the dispute resolution process. the developing countries will have obtained positive discrimination, which the european union will finance, as for the acp banana. the hens will have even gained a few inches in their cages, in the name of animal welfare that we will recognize, and the world of film and television will have secured the maintenance of a few helpers. in exchange for peace, a new peace clause, you'll have made some concessions to seattle. the 'european market' will thus be reduced from 5% to x%, internal support will become residual, export aids will have been condemned, customs duties and tariff peaks will no longer exist, direct investment will have been obtained thanks to lamy, because of ami, and the market will have become global, a kind of commercial fukuyama, the end of gatt history. so, what are we gonna do? - mr commissioner, mr president, i believe that in this millennium cycle europe must affirm three major principles. the first is that this cycle must aim at reducing development inequalities, unlike what has happened as a result of previous cycles. today, the african continent accounts for less than 3 percent of world trade. the rules of the multilateral trading system must take account of differences in situations, resources and levels of development. free trade without any other consideration is to strengthen the strong and weaken the weak. we cannot therefore accept that the principles of our cooperation with the countries of the south, and in particular with the acp countries, and i am of course referring to the lomé convention, should be called into question. i believe, on the contrary, that we must reaffirm the commitments we made at the acp-eu joint assembly a few weeks ago. europe must go to seattle with a vision of globalisation that is opposed to that of a unilateral world dominated by a single power. europe must instead promote a vision of a multipolar world and encourage the creation of economically and politically integrated regional groups, as we have been trying to do for the last 40 years. how can we deny others what we granted ourselves after the war to rebuild our industry, our agriculture, our economy? secondly, the wto must be confined, its role strictly limited and areas which are at stake in the very identity of companies, which must remain under the sovereignty of citizens and their elected institutions, kept out of its sphere of competence. education, health, public and social services, public transport and culture are all areas which cannot be included in the balance of trade negotiations and cannot be the subject of an international trade court. we must reject the race to the general commodification. thirdly, we must uphold the principle of a hierarchy of standards. the 1948 universal declaration of human rights, the international labour organization conventions, the environmental conventions, are of more importance than the standards that govern trade. a state cannot be condemned for applying the precautionary principle, for protecting its environment or for refusing to import goods which are proven to be the products of child labour. on the contrary, it must be possible to appeal against a wto decision to the international labour organisation or to the competent bodies of the united nations. on the eve of this new cycle, it is striking that civil society and international public opinion have entered the debate. i think this is an excellent development because it is the best guarantee that these issues will not be able to be eliminated during these negotiations.
- the wto, created to accelerate trade liberalization, has become one of the essential pillars of the new international order. it not only accompanies globalisation but also seeks to give it form and legal force, in order to impose the dictatorship of the markets. it actively contributes to the implementation of neoliberal policies that result in attacks on public services, employment rights, health, food security, and the environment. unfortunately, the european delegation in seattle is part of the liberal logic. it is in favour of extending the powers of the wto, which is totally rejected by the associations and organisations which have called for both an assessment of the last five years of the wto and a moratorium on future negotiations. we support this approach as the first step towards a radical challenge to the international capitalist order. that is why we cannot vote on this schwaiger report.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, in marrakesh we were promised an assessment of the previous round of negotiations before we started new negotiations. today, this balance sheet does not exist for a simple reason: it would not be positive. he would say that we must break with liberal dogma, the old theory that by expanding trade we create wealth. in 50 years, trade has increased 17 times, while we have produced only twice as many goods on our planet. he also rejected the idea that the situation in the third world would improve. inequality has been rising, both there and here. he would say that we must change course, and that is what we are asking you to do, commissioner. changing course means first of all getting real social and environmental regulations out of the existing package, the one already negotiated, instead of vague references to standards that have never been applied. yes, it means opposing ecological and social dumping with real logic. the balance sheet would say 'prudence', so as not to open pandora's box in other sectors, and i am thinking in particular of investment. this parliament has said no to the ami. he said 'no' for substantive reasons and you, commissioner, must take up these arguments to avoid the investment sector experiencing the disasters we have seen in other areas. finally, this balance sheet would condemn the patentability of "the living", the fact that life, plants, everything becomes a commodity. the 20th century has been marked by a fundamental crisis of humanism through xenophobia, genocides. i do not want the 21st century to be marked by a crisis of humanism because the all-purchasing, all-money approach would take precedence over human development, over the fundamental values that make up human life.
- mr president, no, the seattle conference is not a summons by the united states to the rest of the world to impose the vision of absolute and unfettered free trade. it's the exact opposite. the world trade organization is a european idea, to which the americans converted in marrakesh after long-standing opposition. for seattle, it is the europeans, not the americans, who are proposing the broader agenda: the millennium cycle is our idea. it was the europeans, not the americans, who benefited most from the previous negotiations. since 1995, the us trade deficit with us has increased dramatically, to almost $30 billion last year. finally, the challenge is not trade without rules, but rather to ensure that the tremendous growth in trade serves the sustainable development of all, not the predatory enrichment of the strongest. we want more trade, we want to remove the many barriers which still exist in some countries for certain products and for most services. we want fair trade for all, that is to say, equal conditions of competition. they are not in agriculture, nor in the cultural industries. we need competition rules and a court to enforce them, including by the strong against the weak. finally, we want trade that benefits sustainable development, by linking trade agreements with our other major international commitments on fundamental labour rights, food security and environmental protection. we must, in essence, take the same approach at global level as we succeeded in doing in europe when we moved from the customs union to the single area, and that is why europe can contribute the most to the negotiations and has the right to expect the most from them.

in writing. - we do not intend to put our backing into the european anti-fraud office. although this office was created under the pretext of control of officials and elected representatives of the european institutions, neither the manner in which it was appointed nor the absence of any indication of how it would be controlled inspires the slightest confidence in us. we are in favour not only of full transparency in the functioning of all the european institutions, but also of the election and recall at any time not only of all those who are elected today, but also of all those who have responsibility at any level, from the bottom up, including the brussels commission. given the undemocratic nature of the decision-making bodies of the european union, the creation of olaf seems to be a ridiculous measure designed to pretend to control when there is no real and democratic control.
in writing. - the national front members of the european parliament condemn in the strongest terms corruption, whether it is that of elected officials, civil servants or members of governments. they also condemn fraud or misappropriation of public funds, money stolen from european taxpayers. and we know something about this, as french people who have to deal with the daily developments in the affairs of the mnef, the paris city council, elf or gifco. the list is unfortunately far from exhaustive. they will, however, vote against the napolitano report. because they are tired of this parliament's self-flagellation, alternating with lessons in morality and an equally unbearable morgue. because they think that with olaf, we are recruiting yet another team of officials, whose cost will be higher than the amount of fraud. because they believe, above all, that there is already a structure capable of assuming the role that olaf is intended to play. the solution is obviously to give the court of auditors jurisdictional power and the human and material means to carry it out. this is the case for many national accounting courts, not only in france but also in other member states. it is true that the court of auditors does not have a good reputation in this parliament, since the president has refused it a press conference room, a room which is nevertheless readily granted to the most fanciful associations, to personalities of the most dubious representativeness, or to any watchdog of the single thought provided that he barks loudly. in this case, as in many others, parliament has made a fool of itself.
in writing. - there is corruption. from the left to power and the right to government. names sum it up: agusta in belgium, urba in france, palermo in italy, fictitious jobs at the rpr in paris, the national mutual of students in france or dominique strauss-kahn. but because we in the national front do not have the anxiety that affects potential defendants from other parties, we reject the extension of the police powers conferred on the brussels commission's annex under the name of olaf. - firstly because olaf violates the separation of powers, the foundation of western democracy, with officials without legitimacy controlling the representatives of the sovereign. - secondly, because olaf is the thief who controls the gendarme, since the european commission, at the centre of the suspicions of corruption, will in fact control, via olaf, the parliament which should be the controller and not the controlled. - finally, olaf fails to tackle the root causes of corruption, which lie in the removal of national borders allowing drug money, fraud and financial crime to move freely. if we really want to combat the mere symptoms of corruption, while respecting the foundations of legal societies, there are only two ways: either the technical way, by transforming the european court of auditors into a court of jurisdiction and budgetary discipline; or the democratic way, by creating within the european parliament, as in britain and the united states, the equivalent of the british national accounting office (nao) or the american general accounting office (gao). these are two powerful, autonomous control bodies, but within the parliament, with up to 5 000 staff. the expert body exists, but with a link to the representatives of the people who alone have the right to demand an accounting of the use of their tax money.
- the preparations for the next round of international trade negotiations are not satisfactory from a procedural point of view for at least three reasons. firstly, we see, in a familiar process, the european union itself being weakened by its own internal discussions, even before the negotiations begin. for example, the final mandate given by the council on 22 october makes no mention of defending the principle of community preference, which had been retained by the agriculture council of 27 september, which was already only half satisfactory because it forgot the principle of europe's food independence. every step you take, you go down a notch. we could go on and on. so, with regard to our privileged system of importing bananas from overseas, the commission has just made proposals which satisfy the american demands even before the opening of seattle. in all areas it seems that our internal concessions, in order to arrive at a unified european position, declared a priori desirable, lead us to reduce our pretensions before we have even started discussions with our competitors. secondly, the commission has been given a mandate to negotiate globally on a whole range of issues, some of which are community competence, but others, such as services or investment, clearly fall within national competence. it is true that this is a mandate on the framework of the negotiation and not on the outcome of the negotiation itself. nevertheless, without saying so clearly, the council is putting its finger in the wheel which may lead it, if no one stops it, to give the commission a full negotiating mandate and thus, in application of the new article 133.5 of the treaty of amsterdam, to deprive the national parliaments of their power of ultimate ratification, again without clearly saying so, of course. we are drifting in the fog, not knowing exactly when we will cross the fatal line. then we'll be told it's too late. these methods are completely reprehensible. thirdly, we note that despite our requests, the seattle negotiations are going to be launched without a clear, precise and contradictory assessment of the consequences of the uruguay round. we'll go blindly there too. the commission has indeed made a concession on one point, since it is going to carry out an impact assessment on sustainability, i quote, that is to say, on the environmental consequences of liberalisation. that's very good. but this study should have been carried out on many other points, for example the consequences of liberalization, in its present form, on the preservation of cultural and social models. for these three reasons, we cannot approve the opening of the seattle negotiations in these conditions.
- mr president, the green group, european free alliance, abstained on a report which it found a little soft. for us, the aim of this report was to give commissioner lamy a precise negotiating mandate for the cycle which opens in seattle. however, this specific mandate has not been sufficiently affirmed. we would therefore have liked parliament to propose a very political set of demands to the commission, instead of drawing up a more diplomatic report which deplores, emphasizes, gives an opinion but does not give a mandate. the tone of the text is therefore too liberal for us to agree with it, especially since none of our amendments has been adopted. this report, as amended, has major weaknesses in comparison with the trips agreement. there is nothing we agree on about the right to intellectual property related to trade. as regards the ami, which was rejected by the oecd and is returning, a strengthened code of conduct for investment and strict rules in this area are needed, and this also applies to dispute settlement. however, this report contains fundamental principles which we consider to be essential, such as the precautionary principle and the rules on production methods and processes; it particularly emphasises food labelling to ensure the implementation of food security, and the need to adopt a more favourable position towards developing countries. in any event, we shall be watching very closely the way the commission is negotiating, and even if this amended report still seems too liberal in its tone, we greens would be the fiercest defenders of this text if commissioner lamy went below the recommendations made here.
in writing. - the european delegation to the wto negotiations is seen as a defender of europe's interests. it is only the representative of the most powerful industrial and financial groups in the european union, rivals of the american or japanese trusts in the controlled cutting of the planet, but all exclusively concerned with increasing their profits at the expense of the workers of their own countries and the peoples of poor countries. by referring to the 'basic rights of workers' and their 'protection', especially in poor countries, the schwaiger report adds a dose of cynicism to the rest. but where is the protection of workers, especially against the drama of unemployment, even in the richest countries of the european union, those very countries which would have the means to eradicate unemployment if their governments were not primarily concerned with the profit of large companies and the enrichment of their owners and shareholders? the claim that we are interested in the inhumane working conditions and wages in underdeveloped countries is pure hypocrisy. many multinational companies in africa and asia, which employ workers who are barely paid and who have no social protection, have their headquarters in france, germany or england. instead of requiring these multinationals to respect a minimum of social legislation, it will be enough to invite a few ilo officials as observers to the wto negotiations. we will not vote on or amend the report presented, because the capitalist organization of the economy, with or without the wto, is fundamentally unchangeable.
in writing. - the millennium cycle, which will soon begin in the world trade organisation, must be an opportunity for europe - since we are obliged to speak with one voice - not only to show unity throughout the negotiations, but also to show the utmost firmness in the outcome, particularly as regards agriculture and cultural exception. however, if the fifteen have recently adopted a common negotiating policy for the new cycle, which is ambitious, it must be admitted that this basis, which appears to be the lowest common denominator for the member states, will necessarily be developed in the course of the negotiations. there is no doubt that this text of compromise, born of pain, will be the object of numerous american pressures during the negotiations, even though the union is only homogeneous in appearance and does not have a legal arsenal comparable to that held by the united states and capable, if necessary, of deterring the american side. while the organisation of free and fairer world trade must be encouraged and strengthened within a multilateral trading system, it must also ensure that all nations - rich and poor - and i am thinking in particular of african countries - are assured of the benefits that this round of negotiations is supposed to bring. although it is necessary to wait until the end of the negotiation cycle before a substantive assessment can be made of the results obtained, it is still the case, as regards the framework, that the overall result cannot be regarded as entirely negative if the european nations could obtain more binding regulation of the international competition rules. the introduction of universally accepted common minimum standards to prevent anti-competitive behaviour would already represent significant progress. the european union's initial negotiating position, ambitious in its objectives, is not likely to emerge strengthened from a cycle of negotiations which is likely to be prolonged and derailed, in particular because of the predictable attitude of the united states, which will not cease to try to put corners in the mandate given by mr lamy, which represents only a façade unit that poorly conceals the divergences of interests between the fifteen. moreover, the content of the final resolution adopted today by the european parliament contains many points which are unacceptable to france.
in writing. - the debate which has just taken place in this parliament on the wto on the occasion of the schwaiger report has clearly shown that, for europe, the negotiations which are about to begin concern at least as much the future of its social model as that of its trade. similarly, the question for the third world countries is whether they can still escape the grip of the mega-multinationals arising from mega-mergers and be in control of their own development. the problem is not whether we need rules for world trade. on that point, everyone will agree. the question is whether the policies promoted by the wto since its inception are conducive to fair and sustainable development for all regions of the world. i 'll make two observations: first, the liberalisation promoted in previous rounds and the increase in trade volumes have been accompanied by a worsening of global development inequalities. the leap forward was supposed to pull others, but the opposite happened. the african continent's share of world trade is less than 3%. liberal globalisation has proved incapable of providing an answer to the problem of development, let alone of promoting fair and sustainable development. this is why a review of the social and environmental effects of the previous rounds was essential before embarking on a new wave of all-round liberalisation. if it was rejected with such consistency, it was because the balance sheet would have been negative. however, for the european union, the establishment of a shared diagnosis with the third world countries could have been the basis for the alliance we seek to build with them in these negotiations. secondly, the dispute settlement body (dsb), set up within the wto, has demanded that the european union abandon its own standards in such fundamental areas as health and food safety and its policy of cooperation on bananas with the acp countries and the outermost regions. the question now is whether it can be accepted that, step by step, decision by decision, and all on the pretext of settling trade disputes, the esdr will eventually become a kind of world supreme court, imposing its views in all areas on governments and elected parliaments. we would then be witnessing a genuine democratic confiscation. this is why europe must, at the millennium round, promote a different approach to the organisation of world trade and economic exchanges. to do this, it should affirm three main principles: the first is that the objective of this round must be to reduce the development gap between the north and the south. to this end, the rules of the multilateral trading system must take account of differences in situations and resources between countries. free trade, without any other consideration, is the strengthening of the strong and the weakening of the weak. that is why we cannot accept the questioning of the lomé agreements and our policy of cooperation as we have built it up in the lomé agreements with the acp countries, which include 39 of the poorest countries in the world. we must reaffirm the commitments made to them at the recent acp-eu joint assembly. europe must go to seattle with a vision of globalisation that is opposed to that of a unilateral world dominated by a single power. it must promote a vision of a multipolar world and encourage the creation of regional groups which are integrated both economically and politically, as we have been doing for the last 40 years. how can we deny others what we have granted ourselves after the war to rebuild our industry, our agriculture, our economy? the second principle should be to 'confine' the wto to a strictly defined role and to keep out of its sphere of competence those areas which can only be the sovereignty of states and institutions created by citizens because they concern the very identity of each society. public and social services such as education and health, but also those where the safety of users and the collective interest are at stake, such as public transport or air traffic control, culture and artistic creation, cannot all be put on the balance sheet of a trade negotiation. we must reject the race to the total commodification of society. in intellectual property agreements, europe must refuse to patent living things, and it must guarantee that derogations from the general rules of trade for medicines to combat aids and other serious diseases identified by who are maintained. finally, we must defend the principle of a hierarchy of standards. fundamental human rights and the 1948 universal declaration, the ilo (international labour organisation) conventions or those on the environment are of a higher importance than the standards governing trade. we cannot condemn a state for applying the precautionary principle, for protecting its environment, or for refusing to import goods which are proven to be the products of child labour. on the contrary, wto decisions must be open to appeal to the ilo or to the competent un bodies. the imbalance arises from the fact that only multilateral trade agreements have led to the creation of a judicial type of body, whereas neither the environmental conventions nor the ilo conventions have. some of these concerns were taken into account by the rapporteur at the end of the discussions in the committee on industry and foreign trade. unfortunately, during the plenary session the rapporteur and the epp and eldr groups introduced a number of amendments to the text which mitigate its social and environmental requirements. in view of the unfavourable outcome of the amendments tabled by myself and my colleagues from the french socialist delegation and the gue/ngl and greens/efa groups, i have abstained on mr schwaiger's report. but i think one of the major facts on the eve of this new round, and which distinguishes it from the previous ones, is the entry of civil society, ngos and international public opinion into the debate. i think we should welcome this because it is the best guarantee that these issues will not be able to be eliminated during these negotiations. i am sure they will remain at the heart of the european parliament's debates throughout their duration.
in writing. - the new round of negotiations at the world trade organisation, which will open in seattle on 30 november, should be an opportunity to take greater control of trade liberalization. i doubt that's the case. this question concerns our ability - and our real will - to make the wto a regulatory instrument, to move from a globalisation desired by a few and suffered by all, to a truly regulated global trade that benefits the planet as a whole. it is from this doubt that my concern arises: that if we fail to achieve this, we will be condemned to break longstanding commitments to the developing countries, and in particular to the acp countries, to which we have been bound for 20 years by the lomé conventions. at the risk of breaking our good conscience, i would like to mention the example of the banana, where the multinationals (del monte, dole and chiquita) who, with the support of the united states, dump the bananas of slavery on the european market, produced under conditions of food security that are more than doubtful, have succeeded in bringing us to our knees; the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the commission's recent statements are not likely to allay this concern: 'the banana war must be stopped because it is poisoning the transatlantic relationship and because the union would send an unfavourable message to the world on the eve of new trade negotiations'. end the war, who can be against? - commissioner liikanen, for several years now i have been dealing with the issues and questions concerning industry and shipbuilding, first in the committee on economic affairs and now in the committee on industry. in particular, over the past three years, i have repeatedly raised concerns with the commission about distortions of competition at world level, aggravated by the fact that europe has always imposed on itself a rigorous approach that our competitors have not known. i have often received, from the commissioners and your services, requests not to receive. the commission seems to have become aware of the situation today and i welcome this, because, although we can regret the thousands and thousands of european jobs that have been eliminated in the meantime, as we say in french: "better late than never". today, it seems to me that it is no longer useful to go back to the past and that is why, this morning, i will ask you some specific questions about the future, which do not just concern korea. the first question concerns the united states. i have learned that an american shipyard - which had not built ships for more than forty years - has received an order for two cruise ships to serve the hawaiian islands, where the us law reserves ships for domestic transport to american shipyards. what are you going to do ? the answer seems obvious. this is the korean banking system, which is also supported by the imf and the korean state. so far, despite several reminders in this area as the issue is not new, the european union and the commission have done nothing effective to put an end to these indirect subsidies in korea. what concrete steps do you intend to take today to act quickly? - mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the question of shipbuilding must of course be approached in a global way, taking into account the different segments of production equipment. member states have recognised expertise in the field of military shipbuilding. this is an area in which the commission obviously does not have to intervene but in which it is desirable that intergovernmental cooperation should be developed more than it is at present so that the member states can maintain and increase their expertise, their independence, at affordable costs. it would be very dangerous to divest from this area and we cannot but regret the recent failures, notably in the horizon frigate programme and the abrupt withdrawal of some partners, which put the overall balance of the programme in question. as far as passenger and merchant shipping are concerned, which are highly competitive and labour-intensive segments, we must also preserve and develop the remarkable expertise and high-performance capabilities of the member states and not let them go outside europe. as regards heavy-duty units affected by significant technological change, member states must be able to pursue a policy favouring the technological conversion of their shipyards, so that they can occupy market segments which allow the exploitation of their know-how. any closure of a shipyard constitutes an irreparable loss of expertise for the member states and the union. the latter must not, therefore, in the name of inappropriate interpretations of free competition, prevent the states from encouraging the reorientation of production with a view to preserving both know-how and employment. in this respect, the example of the atlantic shipyards, whose brilliant relaunch after a period of crisis was particularly spectacular, and the role played by the french state in this development, must be considered. it will be necessary to ensure very carefully that the forthcoming wto negotiations will make it possible to put an end to the unacceptable dumping practices of a number of countries and will not endanger a sector which is subject to intense global competition, as it is a major employer of labour which is difficult to automate and therefore subject to strong pressure for relocations to countries where the cost of labour is much lower than in the european union. i would like to turn to the question of the construction of fishing boats. this sector, which may appear to be rather marginal from an overall point of view, nevertheless plays a vital role in the balance of the economic and social fabric of our maritime coastal areas. the european community has a key role to play in this area. the sector is almost entirely dependent on the common fisheries policy. for two years now, the european commission has been freezing community aid for the construction of new ships and, consequently, that of the member states, until the objectives set out in the multiannual guidance plans for ship destruction have been achieved. this blockade, with its serious consequences, was compounded by the refusal to take account of the sale of vessels to third countries in calculating the reduction in the capacity of the european fleet. by only taking into account shipwrecks, the commission is thus causing a significant loss of income to the detriment of fishermen and shipowners. the commission is also now proposing to prohibit any renewal on segments which are not progressing as fast as others and to require that 30% more capacity be found and destroyed than the renewed vessel on the updated segments of the pop targets. this situation and these proposals are causing a worrying ageing of the european fishing fleet, discouraging young people from investing, causing a significant loss of market for the specialist shipyard sector, dangerously weakening some of them, and placing our seafarers on board at a clear risk in terms of safety. we hope that the council will be able to convince the commission that it is right and that it will make the proposals made by the european parliament in its time, after close consultation with the member states, in the report by our colleague arias cañete, prevail. when a shipyard disappears, it is a particularly valuable know-how, accumulated over time, linked to the maritime history of a region, that disappears with it. we must do everything we can to avoid it. the commission must also be consistent. after encouraging the construction of driftnets because of the selectivity of the driftnet, it has, under pressure from certain lobbies and certain member states, banned the same driftnet in certain seas only, without scientific basis and in a discriminatory manner. it recommended experimentation with alternative engines, but did not provide for any specific financial component or a specific kilowatt envelope for the construction of ships adapted to the new regulations it had issued. however, after analysing the results of the first experiments, it was confirmed that the current trawlers could not be adapted to the new devices and that new boats would have to be built. i would therefore be grateful if you, commissioner liikanen, would point out to mr fischler that shipowners have a hard time understanding such logic, or rather such a lack of logic. the commission will obviously have to make the necessary arrangements to enable the shipbuilding involved in the change in regulations it has decided to introduce. in conclusion, mr president, commissioner, if the european commission really wants to contribute to the growth of the shipbuilding industry in europe, it needs only to defend clearly the principle of fair trade in the wto negotiations, to allow member states the freedom to intervene directly in this strategic sector to technologically reorient certain shipyards to market segments with potential, to promote cooperation between companies to help improve the overall efficiency of each of our shipyard types, and finally, within the framework of the common fisheries policy, to take the necessary decisions to allow a controlled renewal of our fishing fleet, the sustainability of the expertise of our shipyards and the vitality of our maritime regions dependent on fishing.
