commission - madam president, ladies and gentlemen, this is an important moment for sport in europe because it is the moment when sport is put on the agenda. why is he on the agenda? simply because it is a citizen's fact. europe is responsible to its citizens and must therefore look after what is good in sport, preserve it and try to solve the problems that arise. you may recall that in the first speech that president prodi made to this house he spoke of the fact that the new commission wants to have a special relationship with the citizens, and in this context he stressed the importance of fighting the scourge of doping. well, madam president, that is done: today the first stone is being laid for a building which will be built so that fair play can once again be part of sport. the fight against doping will be carried out in two stages. first, the commission helped to set up the world anti-doping agency. it wasn't easy, to say the least. it was very complicated, but we fought hard and finally got there. i was given a mandate by the commission to negotiate with the council and the president of the international olympic committee, mr samaranche, to ensure that this new anti-doping agency is established in a balanced way. what balance ? first, it must be transparent and independent. secondly, it must be shared, i.e. divided between the world of sport on the one hand and the world of governments on the other. thirdly, all its members worldwide must make a solemn commitment to implement, each in its own field, the decisions taken by the agency. secondly, this agency must, of course, draw up the list of prohibited products, monitor laboratories, set up control systems, establish non-competitive controls, take action, that is to say, fight the mafias that trade in prohibited products, but also take action to prevent young people from dissociating themselves psychologically and actively from the scourge of doping. madam president, i can tell you that both the council and the commission have been heard by the ioc officials. the european demands were written down word for word in the statutes of the new agency and on 10 november the statutes were signed. we will be represented on the agency's board of directors by two people in the future. similarly, there will be two people for the council of europe. the council of europe had asked us to negotiate on its behalf. we have therefore negotiated not only for the union but also for the council of europe. the agency was created thanks to the efforts of europeans. it is no longer up to us whether or not she succeeds in her mission, madam president, because we will be two of some 30 or 40 partners. we must all fight together, laying the foundations for an anti-doping campaign. we'll have done our best to make the first step possible. the other steps will have to be taken in conjunction with our partners at the global level. since we do not have the full latitude to make this world agency a success - we will do everything we can to make it so, of course, but others must follow us - we have decided to work on a european action plan against doping at the same time, and this time we will have full latitude to fulfil our obligations. this action plan was decided this morning by the commission, and this in a symbiosis between several commissioners, each responsible in his own field. the commissioner responsible for research will put the research programmes of the fifth framework programme, and other possibilities, at the service of the fight against doping, whether fundamental or applied research, to strengthen all the means of this fight. the commissioner responsible for education and youth will make the socrates, leonardo and youth programmes available for training, for cooperation between young people, so that the fight against doping becomes a reality for europe's young people. the commissioner responsible for health issues will ensure that existing directives, for example on the labelling of medicinal products for human use, are also developed in the anti-doping direction. and he promised to submit a recommendation which would cover all the issues concerning public health, the health of young athletes, the health of athletes in general, for a broad concerted action by the member states in the fight against doping. and then, of course, there is also the law enforcement aspect, and here the commissioner responsible for the third pillar, that is the internal policy, will make available the plans and programmes that already exist to raise awareness of the law enforcement and judicial authorities in the fight against doping. madam president, you understand that, on both these levels, the global and the european level, from next year onwards we will make the fight against doping a spearhead of our sporting policy. and then there's the secondary. at the vienna summit, governments asked us to present a document on sport as a social element, social sport, for the helsinki summit. and your parliament, i think it was on 17 december last year, adopted a resolution along the same lines. we are fulfilling our mandate today, madam president, ladies and gentlemen, because the commission has decided to present a plan for a communication on safeguarding the existing structures of sport and on maintaining the social function of sport in the community framework. to be clear, the commission and the union have no legal basis to start making regulations. we won't do it, because we don't have the authority. but we will use, in all the political areas where we have a legal basis, the existing means to operate in favour of sport. let me give you a very concrete example. in the structural funds, a good part of the money can be allocated to projects which are in favour of sport. but there is also something else, a new approach to the citizen. the commission does not consider itself to be sitting in its ivory tower, making up regulations which it imposes on the good people. no, i'm not going to. we believe that our role is to find a consensus between those in the member states who have political responsibility and those in the sports world who have the responsibility of making the sports world work. we will all sit down together, we will discuss, we will listen, we will find out what is wrong and together we will propose solutions which will respect the autonomy of sports federations and the subsidiarity which is being practised in our 15 member states. until then, we will look for what in european legislation can promote sport and what can be a hindrance. i take the competition rules as an example, to be specific: some practices have nothing to do with the rules in this area. for example, a football team with 11 players has nothing to do with competition. it is an element that is completely outside the competition. there are also practices which are in principle prohibited by the competition rules. i will give you another concrete example: if, during a major championship, tickets for the stadium are sold only to nationals and are refused to non-nationals, other european citizens, it is contrary to the rules of competition, so we must take action. however, where there is an apparent conflict about the competition rules, but the sports federations commit themselves in their action to use the funds collected for education and social action in sport, then certain practices may be exempt from the competition rules. i will give you a very concrete example. some federations have so far sold audiovisual rights collectively. well, if this monopoly action is only for trade, it clearly falls under the heading of trade and business. but if the money raised is distributed to clubs which provide education and training for young people, the action of collective interest allows an exemption from the competition rule. i have told you in a few words how we will act in the future in the new sports policy we will be introducing. from next year onwards, there will be a broad consultation with all federations, big and small, and with the political leaders in our member countries, to see together how to 'regulate', not to draw up new rules, but to put up barriers and safeguards so that all this becomes clear. and that we work together in the interests of our young people, in the interests of fair play in sport, in the interests of sport's commitment to society, its fight against racism, xenophobia, and so that sport is positive, friendly, as we all want it to be, but as, unfortunately, today, it is very often lacking. - the agenda calls for statements by the council and the commission on the preparation of the european council in helsinki on 10 and 11 december. without further ado, i give the floor to the president-in-office of the council, mrs halonen.
- mr president, the european council in helsinki on 10 and 11 december will launch the next intergovernmental conference to revise the treaty with a view to enlargement, but it seems to be setting a minimalist agenda, limited to or roughly confined to the three points left open by the treaty of amsterdam: the composition of the commission, the weighting of votes in the council, the new extension of majority decisions. we believe that this agenda will not help at all to solve the problems of the union in the face of enlargement, which may therefore be tackled in the worst institutional conditions. we certainly understand the council's disgust at the commission's shameless attempts in recent months to push through, along the lines of the dehaene report, the idea of a further major federalist leap. but on the other hand, the council is accepting the inclusion on the agenda of a similar proposal, the extension of majority voting, which was not even provided for in the amsterdam protocol on the institutions, but which was only included in an annexed declaration by three member states. this proposal, inspired by the idea of a uniform and unifying europe, is by no means the solution to make a europe of 27 or more members work. in our view, if the council really wants to do something new, it should both reject the commission's proposals and move beyond the amsterdam backlog. it should put a single issue on the negotiating table, decision-making in an enlarged union, a single issue which implies dealing together, in an inseparable way, with three logically linked consequences: qualified majority voting in certain cases, the officialisation of the luxembourg compromise for all cases and the liberalisation of differentiated cooperation. this means thinking about what really unites us, ladies and gentlemen, without blindly clinging to the taboo of the acquis communautaire, and thinking about how common institutions can function in a differentiated union. if we do not make this conversion effort, if we cling to rigid conceptions like oysters to their rock, well, mr president, either enlargement will be missed or the union will be swept away, of course.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i find it very regrettable that the intergovernmental conference does not take account of certain essential elements concerning the area of security, freedom and justice, since one cannot be done at the expense of the other. i also regret that our joint motion for a resolution does not mention the problems of eurodac, even though the council has just announced, in contradiction to the treaties, that this body should remain purely intergovernmental. this excludes parliament and the court of justice from any control over this matter. similarly, in view of the proliferation of data-filing systems (europol, eurodac), the european parliament should have reiterated its call for an independent commission on information technology and freedoms to be set up to safeguard our individual freedoms, in addition to democratic and judicial control. citizenship is also the great absent from this text. it is, however, a matter of the utmost importance, a key element in the negotiations on the charter of fundamental rights, on the one hand, and on the constitutionalisation of the union, on the other. at a time of enlargement of the union, it is this citizenship that must be at the heart of our european project to implement human and sustainable development. in conclusion, i think we must realize that a text so pale and dull is not likely to satisfy the citizens of the union. we must be careful not to stray too far from their aspirations if we are to build a more just, more united and more democratic europe.
- mr president, madam president-in-office of the council, commissioner, i too would like to welcome this first annual report of the european union on human rights. it is true that in the past there have been documents from the commission and many reports from our parliament, but this is the first time that the council of ministers has sent us a text of this kind. this is a welcome sign of concern for transparency and i hope it will improve the information available to civil society on the concrete actions carried out between june 1998 and june 1999 and on the instruments and means available to the union. the only criticism i have is that this report is probably too optimistic. the shortcomings, the shadowy areas are hardly mentioned. but the publication of this document encourages me to look to the near future, to the drafting of a charter of fundamental rights for the european union. this project, which is to be included in the igc's work and which could be completed by the end of 2000, is of great importance for the union, for all those who live on union soil and for the applicant countries. but today we have no guarantee that the text will live up to expectations. in particular, it is to be feared that the european council and the council of ministers have very limited ambitions, namely to draft a simple declaration without legal force, without binding force. if that were to happen, the european union would lose all credibility with itself and the world. in addition, there is a concern that there may be competition, or even contradiction, between this future charter and the texts which exist with unquestionable force. i am, of course, referring to the european convention on human rights of the council of europe. i hope, madam president-in-office, that the helsinki summit will reassure us on all these points. you know these questions admirably well yourself.
- mr president, in general terms, no one here dares to oppose the respect for human rights. that is why i propose that we move from talk to action. what is the situation with the right to work in a europe with 18 million unemployed and 50 million poor? where is the right to housing, health care or education when millions of people are deprived of it? what is the situation with the right of asylum and freedom of movement when countries such as belgium are expelling gypsies, or, just yesterday, some 15 nigerians? the same applies to my country, france, which refuses to regularize tens of thousands of undocumented migrants, often kept in detention centres, or which extradits basque refugees? where is the right to life when european armies agree to participate in the bombing of civilian populations in serbia or kosovo ? what about the member states which amnesty international has called upon to act with impunity in violation of article 5 of the universal declaration of human rights, which prohibits torture and ill-treatment? and finally, where are human rights when we allow, as we do today, the financial markets to license, exclude and pollute, and all in the name of profit and profitability?

the rapporteur. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, following the report published last year on turkey by our colleagues macmillan scott and swoboda, and the resolution of our parliament of 6 october last which concluded that it was important to deepen the european strategy for that country, our assembly should be able to adopt tomorrow two proposals for parliament and council regulations on the implementation of measures aimed respectively at: the first, the economic and social development of turkey, the second, the deepening of the customs union between the european community and turkey. the first involves the financing over the next three years of a total of eur 135 million based on article 130 of the treaty on european union and requiring the implementation of a codecision procedure, while the second, which provides for the commitment of eur 15 million over the same period, could be the subject of a simple consultation procedure. the union is thus preparing to resume economic aid decided in march 1995 under the agreements on the customs union, which has since been blocked because of the lack of unanimity in the council. i shall not go into the reasons for this deadlock, in which the crisis in the aegean played a leading role but in which european concerns in the essential areas of respect for human rights and the protection of minorities were also taken very seriously. in this respect, the forum which our parliament has asked to be set up should have an important role to play; the commission will be able to build on the existing structures, in particular within the economic and social committee of the european community. the proposals for regulations which we are now discussing, ladies and gentlemen, will therefore be an incentive to continue the political developments under way. they contain a clause authorizing the council to take appropriate action if it is proved that the most basic rights are being violated in turkey. it states that our parliament could then, like the commission, propose to the council that it be suspended. i would like to stress that if we want to ensure the coherence of the strategy we have adopted and approved over the last few months, we must avoid introducing measures in our amendments which would be tantamount to blocking the process we have started. let us not lose sight of the importance of a fruitful dialogue with turkey, if only for obvious geostrategic reasons. finally, i would like to point out that although the provisions for all the aid envisaged provide for a financing of eur 150 million over three years, the balance in favour of the union in the trade balance between turkey and the european union has doubled since the entry into force of the agreement on customs union on 1 january 1996 and has risen from eur 4 billion to eur 8 billion in four years. i sincerely believe that the community must now honour its commitments of that time, so as not to discourage all those in turkey who have resolutely embarked on the road to the customs union and who have thus decided to link their country to the european economic area.

- madam president, ladies and gentlemen, we voted in committee on the reform of the common organization of the market in fishery and aquaculture products. it is a sensitive subject, but this report was all the more necessary. the text we voted on is a good text and we have reached a good compromise. i believe that this is the kind of compromise that the european union can make when it is able to go beyond national interests and defend common interests at the same time. as we know, fisheries is a major european policy, even if it concerns few europeans, at least as producers, and much more obviously as consumers. since its creation in 1970, the community fisheries market has already undergone many changes. its regulations are adapted to this and this report should be seen as a further step in building a balanced organisation between protection and management of the fishery resource. today's report reinforces the role of consumers and producer organisations in the organisation of the market. however, it should be borne in mind that this reform will have consequences for the fisheries sector. i'll just briefly touch on two of them. what will be the role of our auctions, in particular, in view of the pre-sale contracts set out in article 12? this should not lead to a shift in our territories. secondly, what will happen in the event of a cyclical crisis in the fisheries sector if no provision is made for exceptional circumstances? it is better to plan ahead so that you can deal with all possible situations. this report does not dismiss the questions of the future, or any of them, but i believe that our committee has done a good job and deserves broad support for the report which, mrs fraga estévez, bears your name.

the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i have followed yesterday's debates with as much attention as you can imagine, and the unanimous praise for the form and substance of this report has not failed to cause me a slight concern, since it is true that it is impossible, whatever the qualities of compromise, to satisfy everyone and his father. today, as a last resort, we are being asked to postpone the implementation of these two texts on the basis of two pretexts which were raised yesterday in the debate. the first is that the european union has not been rewarded for its efforts and that there is absolutely nothing to be expected from the turkish government, since since the implementation of the customs union agreements, no significant progress has been made, according to some of our colleagues. i would point out to the house that in this agreement on customs union it is the european union which has been the beneficiary, by far, of the commitments entered into, since the balance of trade between the european union and turkey has doubled in favour of the european union since the implementation of these agreements. the second pretext is the confirmation of mr öcalan's death sentence by the turkish court of cassation and the fact that some of our colleagues now fear for mr öcalan's life. i would point out that there has been a de facto moratorium on the death penalty in turkey for 15 years, that the report we are voting on is precisely intended to encourage the turkish government to convert this de facto moratorium into a de jure moratorium, and that in any event i wonder what our colleagues would say if, in their country of origin, there were, as they wish, an intrusion of political power into the judiciary. because mr öcalan's case is currently before the strasbourg security court. so for all these reasons, i say that when you want to drown your dog you say that it has rabies and i naturally ask the house to disregard this request for referral back.
in writing. - despite its very limited nature, and its obvious inadequacy in relation to the problem, we shall vote for the directive on 'minimum requirements to improve the safety and health protection of workers who may be exposed to the risk of explosive atmospheres', since it can represent progress in countries where workers are least protected. but since there is no provision for real control - that is, exercised by the workers themselves and, more broadly, by the population - nor for sanctions against employers guilty of imprudence, the directive risks being left untouched. the resolution, while claiming to place the safety and health of workers above 'purely economic considerations' in article 3, contradicts itself in article 2 by refusing to 'impose constraints ... which would hinder the creation and development of small and medium-sized enterprises'. it will therefore be up to the workers themselves to impose the minimum protection to which they should be entitled and which the directive does not even intend to impose.
in writing. - turkey's application for membership of the european union will probably be on the agenda of the next european council in helsinki. a strong movement is developing, particularly in france, for turkey to be recognised as a candidate country on an equal footing with the other candidates for enlargement. i would like to draw attention to the risk of finding ourselves in the same situation as with the customs union. the eu-turkey customs union was supposed to promote democratic reforms and human and minority rights, according to its promoters. against the wishes of our group and of many human rights associations, such as "france liberté" chaired by danielle mitterrand, the customs union was ratified and put into effect. today we are discussing its deepening. it is clear that the violations of human rights have continued. the kurdish problem is still not solved. öcalan's death sentence has been confirmed. leyla zana is still in prison. the european commission itself has been forced to acknowledge that since the implementation of the customs union, 'no significant progress has been made in turkey in the field of human rights and democratic reform'. let us learn from the experience of the customs union. the european council in brussels on 18 november agreed to the need to strengthen the european union's external relations and to strengthen the european union's external relations. i am not proposing to rule out turkey's application for membership of the european union. but first we must demand firm and definitive commitments from turkey and ensure that they are respected: recognition of the rights of the kurdish people, abolition of the death penalty and a new trial for öcalan, the release of leyla zana and all political prisoners, the application of the un resolutions for the solution of the cyprus problem. the report of the committee on foreign affairs, human rights, common security and defence policy makes careful reference to the question of human rights. the commission has also proposed that the council should adopt a common position on the proposal for a directive on the approximation of the laws of the member states relating to the labelling of foodstuffs. i cannot support this approach, because it is time to send a clear signal to turkey by blocking or suspending the implementation of the customs union.
in writing. - i would like to congratulate mr morillon for making it clear that the purpose of these two reports is not to debate the eligibility of turkey. the aim is to prepare the country, which is officially a candidate, for accession by means of measures aimed at deepening the ec-turkey customs union (eur 15 million over three years) and at the economic and social development of turkey (eur 135 million over three years). these proposals for regulations, which were presented by the commission in october 1998 at the request of the general affairs council, are designed to unblock the european union's financial assistance to turkey. if the proposal for a regulation relating to the customs union, based on article 235 of the treaty, requires unanimous adoption in the council, the second regulation can be adopted by codecision and thus allows for a majority decision. the duplication of regulations is justified by the desire to break the deadlock in the council. it 's about time ! it is our duty to encourage turkey to continue the reforms it has undertaken to improve its economy, to restructure and increase the efficiency of its public service, to modernise its economic and social infrastructure, to develop its productive service and to strengthen the economic and social cohesion of the country. what i like about these regulations is that they provide for cooperation projects and actions to benefit local and regional authorities, public bodies and above all civil society: associations, ngos... i think it is essential to involve the turkish people in the changes taking place in their country. at the same time, it will be necessary to monitor the progress of these cooperation projects and actions and, of course, to involve the european parliament in these checks. it is foreseen, and i welcome this, that the council may decide to suspend all cooperation when obstacles to the implementation of projects and actions (particularly in the field of democracy, human rights and the protection of minorities) arise. this will require qualified majority voting on a proposal from the commission or the european parliament. it is indeed necessary to push turkey towards greater respect for human rights. it is not easy, as the death sentence against öcalan shows, despite the protests of europe and the world. but we must persevere, and i hope that giving turkey the prospect of membership of the european union will motivate the turkish authorities to better respect human rights, promote democratic practices and liberate the occupied part of the island of cyprus. ladies and gentlemen, as we approach the helsinki summit, where the status of turkey will be discussed, our parliament must send a strong political signal, despite the reservations i can understand on the part of some of you.
in writing. - we will not vote for the resolution of the committee on foreign affairs, human rights, common security and defence policy because, despite the confusing wording, the alleged concerns about human rights are badly concealed by purely commercial interests. the rapporteur himself stresses that the balance of trade in turkey is increasingly in favour of the european union. the point of our refusal to vote on the resolution is to protest at the same time against the conditions of the workers of this country, against the oppression of the kurdish people and against the failure of the turkish state to respect basic freedoms. however, the violation of workers' rights and basic freedoms is not unique to turkey. we do not regard membership of the european union as an honour that a state should deserve, nor as a patent for democracy. and while turkey's integration into the european union meets the requirements of the large industrial and commercial groups, mainly european and incidentally turkish, it will not improve the lot of the working masses in that country in any way, any more than the european union has protected workers in the countries already integrated from unemployment and the deterioration of their living conditions.
in writing. - this discussion is an opportunity to express our solidarity with the workers and the turkish and kurdish peoples. it is up to them to decide whether or not to join the european union. and if they decide to do so, it is not our place to oppose it. this will not prevent us from continuing to condemn the repression of this regime, which is a legacy of the military dictatorship of 1980 and which today threatens to execute öcalan and denies the kurdish people self-determination. before giving lessons in democracy, european governments should set an example and start by granting the right to vote to the three million turkish and kurdish immigrant workers living in eu countries. the same eu that exploits turkey through the customs union without financial compensation. the aid must be used to help the poorest people in turkey. the priority is not economic or customs relations, but relations between civil society and organisations in turkey and those in other european countries. i shall therefore abstain on the report on economic and social development and vote against the report on the ec-turkey customs union.
mr president, the european parliament's report on the duration of the transitional period for the physical introduction of the euro provides us with an opportunity to recall some disturbing truths. firstly, although there has been a great deal of publicity for the euro, particularly at the time of its launch, although it is now legally in force and has even had some exciting mishaps on international markets, citizens seem to have completely forgotten that it exists. they continue to use the national means of payment to which they are accustomed, and they use euro means only in an infinitesimal way; worse, they seem less and less prepared to use them in the future. opinion polls show, at least in france, that the percentage of people who are considering opening a euro account in the near future has been steadily declining since 1 january 1999 and now only affects a small minority. this is a very good figure, since the closer we get to 31 december 2001, the more this percentage should increase. clearly, our citizens do not see any practical use in the euro in their daily lives. but the european parliament wants to correct them and once again calls for an information campaign which, i quote the resolution, 'should cover both the practical aspects and the fundamental meaning of monetary union'. yes, that is where we are: once again reminding those who think the euro is useless of its usefulness. i, for my part, will ask an iconoclastic question: what if our fellow citizens were right? what if they could sense a simple truth firsthand? what if the euro really is useless in everyday life? the three-year transitional period has at least shown us that it is possible to live with a euro that lives its life - which is rather chaotic on international markets - on the one hand, and national currencies still in circulation on the other, to the greatest satisfaction of consumers. we are not going to be able to do that, because we are not going to be able to do it in the future.
in writing. - i welcome with great satisfaction the report by mrs torres marques. it provides a relevant analysis of the technical difficulties which remain to be resolved in order to prepare properly for the introduction of the euro. we must not hide our faces, the problems are far from being completely solved and public opinion is far from ready. that is why, today, like the ecofin council of the european commission and our rapporteur, i too believe that the reduction of the three-year transitional period could create very serious technical difficulties, which could jeopardise the smooth transition to the euro. the technical obstacles which would pose the greatest difficulties in reducing the transitional period include: the time taken to manufacture euro banknotes and coins; the considerable scale of the it adaptations to be carried out; the euro is also the currency of the european union, and the fact that the changeover to the euro for general government was planned for 2002 to take account of the complexity of the changes to be made in this sector. beyond these technical obstacles, shortening the transitional period would jeopardise one of the strong elements of the euro's success, namely the trust built with economic and social actors (who are still insufficiently prepared) around a precise and respected timetable. and i say this as someone who had initially campaigned for a tighter timetable. in the same spirit of smooth learning of the euro, the emac committee has made a proposal which i support, aimed at enabling consumers to start exchanging their national currency for euro coins and banknotes from the beginning of december 2001. similarly, bank supply of coins and banknotes is to start well before january 2002 and retail and government supply is to start as early as december 2001. in addition, from the second week of january 2002, retailers should only hand over currency in euro rather than in national currency. i also agree with mrs torres marques when she rejects a legal obligation and only recommends a recommendation to that effect. as regards the period from 1 january 2002 when two currencies will be in circulation simultaneously, which under the treaty could be up to six months, i share the view of the rapporteur and the ecofin council that this period should be reduced to two months. we must therefore strengthen active information campaigns to inform citizens. i would like to conclude by stressing an intolerably persistent problem, namely bank charges and exchange charges. this contributes to the citizens' concerns about the practical benefits of the euro. i have in fact informed the commission and the council of this by means of written questions, which have not yet been answered. this is a serious problem at a time when the euro is experiencing a crisis of confidence.
in writing. - under the pretext of technical measures (the manufacture of banknotes), the report proposes to carry out a campaign to promote the single currency. the point is not so much to talk about the 'practical aspects' of the euro as to stress its 'fundamental significance'. it is true that the virtues of the euro do not seem to speak for themselves! preliminary classification of skeptics as "illiterate, visually impaired, and hearing impaired" does not make the report any more convincing. the document notes that the european central bank has been using the euro for its monetary operations since 1 january without ever reporting on the criteria of its exchange rate policy. the single currency is therefore not a democratic achievement for the citizens of europe, but a powerful tool of monetarism, as the recent rise in interest rates shows. the euro has been in place on the financial markets since 4 january 1999. the ordinary citizens - those who have never speculated on currencies - continue to travel and make purchases, being blackmailed by the bank commissions. this is all the more scandalous since the exchange rate of currencies is fixed from now on. we are not really addressing the real questions: a single currency for whom and for what? for all these reasons, i shall vote against this report.

- the agenda calls for the commission's declaration on the wto millennium cycle (seattle, 30 november to 3 december 1999). i welcome the presence of mr pascal lamy and i shall give him the floor immediately.
mr. president, after the failure of seattle, all the problems remain, but nothing is as it was before. our first task is therefore to make a clear diagnosis of what has just happened, so that we can take our responsibilities in full knowledge of the facts. i have heard mr lamy's analysis, from within the institution, so to speak. i would like to offer an outside perspective. i had the opportunity in seattle, for a long time, to talk with these women and men of civil society - as we say - from all walks of life. i also had the opportunity to speak with some of the main organisers of this mobilisation. they were naturally measuring the radiance and support they received from around the world: they were therefore passionate and determined but not violent, populist or nationalist as some observers thought they should be caricatured. they were informed, thoughtful, mature. they wanted to be involved in decision-making as responsible citizens, no longer treated as passive consumers. it was not openness to the world that they were opposing, but globalised commercialism. far from identifying themselves with the champions of their own countries in the global economic war, they both denounced the capitalism of multinationals, the forced profitability, the commodification of nature up to the patenting of life, the leveling of crops, the deepening of inequalities practically everywhere and especially between the north and the south. they simply aspired to civilize the modern world, to humanize globalization. people before benefits was one of their favorite slogans. they must be heard, said mr somavia, the current director-general of the international labour organisation, who four years ago was the heart of the copenhagen international conference, where all the world's heads of state committed themselves to halving poverty by 2015. to hear them is to change the wto fundamentally. i think that this begins with the current wto framework: a framework which is falsely universal and really unequal, as my friend lannoye has very well imagined. this also applies to the current missions of the wto, which places the objective of gaining market share above everything else, including commitments made by the international community on social, environmental, health or southern development. changing the wto is finally about its current mode of operation, still based on summit diplomacy and secrecy at a time of citizen's intrusion into world affairs. that is why i am calling for a genuine work of critical evaluation of past experience, followed by an offensive role for the union in favour of a democratic organisation, open to civil societies, truly universal and resolutely overcoming the gap between commercial concerns and the requirements of solidarity and sustainable development. this is another good ambition for europe's nascent foreign and security policy.
- mr president, commissioner, the failure of the seattle negotiations represents a victory for all those who reject free trade, all those who refuse to reduce human activities and man himself to the status of a commodity. the europe of nations group had denounced the improper preparation of this conference, the absence of an objective assessment of the implementation of the uruguay round, the sneaky attempt to reintroduce the multilateral agreement on investment by the tape, the objective of accelerated liberalisation, without recognition of the legitimacy of the regional preference zones. the seattle protesters have put an end to this drift. they have stopped a conference prepared by the powerful for their own benefit and have thereby obtained the moratorium which my group was asking for. we welcome this, but we must now use this moratorium to prepare ourselves better for future negotiations. firstly, on procedure, we want the european parliament and the council to start thinking seriously about the democratic control of the commission during such international negotiations. we cannot forget that mr lamy, in a commission statement which did not have the council's agreement, proposed a working group on biotechnologies which risked bringing biotechnologies back into the negotiations, as the americans wanted and as we refused. the commissioner explained earlier, and last week before the european parliament's committee on agriculture, that he was going to get much more in return for this concession. we are not at all satisfied with this statement and we think it only makes matters worse for him, because in our view this was not a negotiable point at all. fortunately, in the end, seattle was a failure, or we don't know where we'd be taken. the commission, as is its custom, thinks it is above the council and tries to do what it wants. we have to change that. this needs to be changed, especially since the commission had been given a broad negotiating mandate on the agenda, including issues such as investment and services, which normally fall within the competence of the member states. we believe that this point too will have to be clarified seriously in the future, because it could have led to a final negotiating mandate which would have reduced or eliminated the powers of the national parliaments. on the contrary, in future negotiations, much stricter parallel control of national parliaments, such as the european parliament, will have to be introduced. the control over the commission will therefore have to be reformed, but we must also make use of the time we have to draw up a genuine and objective assessment of the uruguay round. above all, in the future, the functioning of the world trade organisation will have to be revised to establish this fundamental principle that peoples alone are sovereign, that they are free to choose their way of life and to express their preferences. finally, that multinational companies must adapt to the will of the people and not the people to the needs of the multinationals.
- mr president, the official delegation of the european union in seattle defended the principle of a broad agenda. it was mandated to include a wide range of new areas in the millennium cycle, but in fact it was intended to give the wto a wider range of responsibilities and powers. for us, it is not a question of better organising the continued liberalization of trade, but of giving priority to the defence of social and environmental rights and of enabling all the peoples to control themselves and decide their future. the delegation also implied that it had fought for the countries of the south. but it is not. as far as agriculture is concerned, the european union has only defended the european export agribusiness against its north american competitors and the exporters of the cairns group. it did not represent the demands of the family or associative farms of europe or the demands of the peasants of the south. the global protest that disrupted the seattle conference represents the first global response to the dictatorship of markets and financial profit. they are a source of hope for millions of workers, the unemployed, landless peasants and all the victims of the capitalist world order which the wto wants to impose on us. the interests of the people are in contradiction with the development of liberalism.
- mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i will not repeat what has already been said. the wto is a failure in its current form because the wto is no longer adequate, nor is it transparent. the first lesson we must learn is the one the ngos were asking for, namely fair trade and not free trade, and from this point of view we must say to ourselves that no international organization today can escape the eyes of the citizen and that this is normal. the next deadline is very close. geneva must not be conducted in a subtle way. of course we have marrakesh, of course we have no obligation to deliver results, but we must be vigilant that the separate agreements on agriculture and services do not bring in through the window what we have thrown out through the door. one of the lessons of seattle, and commissioner lamy has begun to learn from it, is to find allies. but, of course, there are already a few of these allies. the most important of these will probably be, as paul lannoye has stressed, the acp countries. if i take the example of european agriculture, it cannot continue to say that it is doing well, that it is multifunctional, that it is functioning in a positive way, that it is now defending its consumers, and at the same time remain selfish towards the countries of the south. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. everyone has the right today to be in solidarity and to have the means to live better, to get out of international selfishness.

- the next item is the recommendation for second reading (a5-0086/1999) on behalf of the committee on legal affairs and the internal market, on the common position of the council with a view to adopting a directive of the european parliament and of the council on the approximation of the laws of the member states relating to insurance against civil liability in respect of the use of motor vehicles and amending directives 73/239/eec and 88/357/eec (fourth motor insurance directive) (rapporteur: mr rothley).
the commission is aware of the fact that the fourth motor vehicle directive is an important step towards closing the gap in european directives on motor insurance and strengthening the internal market in this field. as you know, there are more than 500 000 road accidents in the community every year. the current system of compensation for victims of accidents occurring outside the member state in which they are domiciled is not working well. a quick and pragmatic solution is needed to protect the very large number of motorists who travel abroad each year. i would like to thank parliament very warmly for having asked for this directive. this was the first time that parliament had made use of its new competence under article 192 of the treaty. the commission supported this request and worked to ensure that its proposal was adopted swiftly. i would like to thank mr rothley in particular for all the work he has done, both in conducting the debate and in bringing the directive to where it is today. the commission is of the opinion that the common position defined by the council constitutes a balanced and coherent text. this is a true description of the problems which led parliament to call for regulation at european community level. the text incorporates the main elements of the commission's proposal and takes account in full or in part of 24 of the 36 amendments tabled by parliament at first reading. this is not insignificant. in its response to the amendments proposed by the committee on legal affairs and the internal market of the european parliament, the commission was guided by the search for a legal instrument that could respond as effectively as possible to the needs of those who take out a motor insurance policy. i now come to the amendments. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to cover the whole of the eu, including the european union, and to extend it to cover the whole of the eu. i can also accept amendment no 13, which calls for greater consumer protection, although the word 'immediately' as used in this text must be clarified to avoid contradictions in the application of this provision by the member states. i now wish to turn to amendments nos 1, 2, 8 and 9 tabled by the rapporteur, which seek to extend the scope of the directive to include accidents which have occurred in third countries and involve two parties who are both established in the european union and both of whom are covered by insurance companies in the european union. let me remind you of the reasons why the commission rejected these amendments at first reading. firstly, there is the compensation mechanism which is set out in this directive, as in the other previous directives on motor insurance, and which is based on the green card system. it is not possible to extend the mechanism to third countries which do not participate in this system and which do not recognise the validity of the european insurance conventions. insurance companies would not agree to cover these risks or would demand very high premiums. in any event, the authorities of third countries would require foreign motorists from the european union to take out insurance contracts with companies established in the territory of the countries in question. second, the application of the directive, in particular the provision which provides for the possibility of bringing an action directly against insurance undertakings, may run counter to certain rules of law in force in third countries concerning civil liability and private international law, in particular where direct recourse is not recognised in those rules of law. thirdly, these amendments lead to a lack of consistency with article 5 (3) of the information centre directive and article 7 concerning the impossibility of identifying the vehicle or the insurance company. in my view, these four amendments concerning accidents in third countries cannot be accepted at this stage and in their present form. in the event that a consultation procedure proves unavoidable, the commission could consider extending the scope of the directive to take account of the above. i would like to add something about this possible extension. as i have said, this directive is based on the green card system. 39 countries participate in the green card system. among these 39 countries, besides the european union, besides the 15 member states, there are six countries which are also parties to the multilateral guarantee convention. these countries are switzerland - which is very important because many accidents happen there - hungary, the czech republic, slovakia, croatia and slovenia. six countries therefore, which constitute a subgroup of all the countries participating in the green card system. the commission is prepared, in its desire to meet the requirements of the european parliament, to defend a compromise proposal in which the directive, or at least its scope, would be extended to the six countries already mentioned, but to no other.
- thank you, commissioner, for your precise answer. the debate is closed. the vote will take place at 12 noon on wednesday.
- doc. a5-0075/99 by mr aparicio sánchez, on behalf of the committee on regional policy, transport and tourism, on the proposal for a european parliament and council regulation on the allocation of licences for heavy goods vehicles in switzerland (com (99) 35 - c5-0054/1999 - 1999/0022).
commission. - (nl) mr president, i should like to begin by thanking the two parliamentary committees and in particular the two rapporteurs, mr aparicio sánchez and mr brunetta, for the time and effort they have devoted to the preparation of this proposal. the purpose of this proposal for a regulation is to define a method for allocating the two categories of authorization for heavy goods vehicles of the european union circulating in switzerland. the proposal therefore includes a regulation and two categories of authorizations, called heavy-duty authorizations. this proposal will for the first time make it possible to allow european union lorries with a maximum weight of 40 tonnes to be used on swiss territory, subject to a certain quota of journeys. the other category of authorizations, the so-called authorizations for empty or low-load vehicles, also entitles to a certain quota of journeys on swiss territory, at a reduced rate, for trucks with a maximum weight not exceeding 28 tonnes. i am pleased to inform you that the commission, which has greatly appreciated the excellent work done by the two parliamentary committees on this subject and their openness to compromise, can accept amendments nos 1 to 6 and amendment no 8. that is to say, all the amendments except amendment no 7, which the commission really cannot accept. the commission's proposal, mr president, aims to allocate 90 per cent of the authorizations to the member states which carry out the largest number of transports on swiss territory, while guaranteeing all member states a basic quota of 1 500 authorizations per year. with this amendment the minimum quota is reduced to 500. the benefit would accrue to the quotas of the three large member states which share a common border with switzerland. in other words: france, germany and italy. this would therefore be to the detriment of the other member states. since the authorization system includes a mechanism to allocate unused authorizations between the different countries, i can assure the house that there is no risk that authorizations allocated by quota will be wasted or unused. the commission therefore prefers to allocate an identical quota to all member states and cannot therefore accept amendment no 7.
- thank you, chief. the debate is closed. the vote will take place at 12 noon on wednesday.
- the next item is the recommendation for second reading (a5-0077/1999) on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy, on the common position of the council with a view to the adoption of a regulation of the european parliament and of the council on substances that deplete the ozone layer (5748/3/1999 - c5-0034/1999 - 1998/0228) (rapporteur: mrs hulthén).
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the environment is protected. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of biofuels. the commission certainly shares this objective, since these substances are making a major and increasing contribution to the depletion of the ozone layer. european smes, which play a major role in the development of alternatives, have demonstrated that a rapid phase-out of other ozone-depleting substances encourages sustainable industries and further protection of the ozone layer. following complex negotiations within the council, an acceptable common position was adopted in february. the commission's priority is the rapid adoption of this common position. the commission cannot act as quickly as it would like on certain issues now that certain dates which have been proposed for phasing out are fast approaching. it is important to avoid the introduction of new substances responsible for the depletion of the ozone layer. amendment no 27 introduces an accelerated procedure for the inclusion of new substances of this kind in the regulation, which would be useful in suspending unwise investments and would be beneficial for the ozone layer. the commission can therefore accept the amendments in principle. we can also accept amendment no 9 because it allows for limited time extensions for the use of very small quantities of cfcs in specialised medical facilities for the purpose of relieving the pain of patients. the commission may accept other amendments, in whole, in principle or in part. i am referring to amendments nos 1, 4, 11, 12, 15, 17, 24, 25, 26, 29, 31, 32 and 35. the commission cannot accept amendments nos 2 and 10 because they propose the first reductions in the production and use of methyl bromide within unrealistic time limits - 1 january 2000 and 1 january 2001 respectively. this would lead to procedural difficulties and problems for farmers. the commission cannot accept amendment no 3, which would prohibit any derogation beyond 2006. this would disproportionately penalise individual farmers or certain crops. the community's ozone policy includes strict controls on the production of and trade in hcfcs with countries which have not signed the montreal protocol. two weeks ago, at the meeting in beijing of the countries which signed the montreal protocol, the community succeeded in introducing these measures into the protocol. however, far too strict measures going beyond the common position could push markets to turn to overseas producers. we cannot therefore accept amendments nos 5, 6, 7, 8 and 23 because they call for an acceleration of the phase-out process and impose an immediate ban on the marketing of the substances in question. some amendments propose controls on the use of hcfcs. the current position strikes a careful balance between what is environmentally desirable, technically possible and economically feasible. the commission cannot therefore accept amendments nos 13, 14 and 16 because they would further limit the time limits in the context of phasing out the use of hcfcs in solvents, air conditioning systems and polyurethane foams. this would lead to more problems and serious cash-flow difficulties within companies. the commission cannot accept amendments nos 18 and 34 on the possible use of hcfcs as a substitute for halons in firefighting. the extension of the right is unnecessary and its limitation would have little or no practical effect. these changes would affect a key part of the compromise of the common position. amendment no 28 concerns article 5 and prohibits the direct use of cfcs and hcfcs as a manufacturing agent in a specific application. the commission cannot accept this amendment because phasing out requires a transitional period. the commission cannot accept amendment no 19 either, which prohibits the sale of second-hand equipment containing hcfcs within 5 years of the respective ban on use. this would increase the risk of illegal dumping and release of hcfcs into the atmosphere. the commission welcomes amendment no 20, which prohibits the production of products containing hcfcs for export within three years of the national ban on the use of these substances. however, we must maintain a balance between environmental requirements and the risk of manufacturing elsewhere. the commission cannot therefore accept this amendment. similarly, although we support the objective of amendment no 21, it would be incompatible with the derogation in article 5 (6) concerning special cases. we cannot therefore accept it. moreover, the commission cannot accept amendment no 22 since the derogations would in any case be granted by the member states after full consultation. we cannot therefore accept it. the commission cannot accept amendment no 30, which seeks to extend the scope for derogations to substances which have already been phased out. it is important to send a clear signal that when a substance has been phased out, no further derogations can be accepted except for substances whose use is recognised as essential. finally, i thank parliament for its work and for its careful examination of the common position.

- the next item is the motion for a resolution (b5-0313/1999), on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer protection, on the follow-up to parliament's opinion on the labelling of foodstuffs produced from genetically modified organisms.
- mr president, this 1% rate of non-labellable gmos, presented here from a purely technical point of view, seems very high compared to commitments already made by large retailers. then why the 1% rate? in our view, the companies that produce and use gmos on a massive scale are seeking to create a de facto situation, achieved by generalising the presence of gmos to the entire agri-food market. they make it virtually impossible to establish supply chains capable of offering consumers products without gmos. secondly, there is no guarantee that gmos will not have any long-term consequences for public health and the environment, especially as mass production causes their dispersal into nature. the social impact of the spread of gmos is well known: the growing dependence of producers and consumers on the giants of the agri-food sector. in our view, to overcome the policy of the fait accompli, it is necessary to ensure that complete production chains are maintained without gmos. finally, producers and consumers need to know whether the products they use contain them or not. there are means of control, and they are effective if the public authorities have the political will to do so. we now see no reason for a tolerable threshold for gmos below which the risk would be zero or at least acceptable.
the commission is aware of the difficulties facing the community in the field of the internal market. the committee on the environment, public health and consumer protection has already discussed this matter on 15 november. i said then that it is not just a question of whether we approve or authorize gmos or not or whether we should label them or not. we are simply trying to implement the existing legislation and make it operational. we are responding to the council's mandate on the labelling of genetically modified food by means of the proposal to amend regulation no 1139/98, which establishes a minimum threshold for the accidental presence of authorized genetically modified substances. the commission was forced to do so when the regulation was adopted. this project aims to solve the problem of food labelling where farmers have tried not to use genetically modified substances and can prove it but small amounts of these substances are still detected. this accidental contamination may occur during crops, harvesting, transport, storage and processing. we have had several consultations with the joint research centre and the member states and have come to the conclusion that a rate of 1% is the best compromise in two respects: firstly, for the objective of establishing a very low tolerance threshold involving efforts on the part of the operators; then it shall consider the feasibility required throughout the production chain. we shall soon have methods that will not cause any undue difficulty to the competent enforcement authorities. i would also point out that this value is stricter than the thresholds applied by other countries such as switzerland, norway and japan. as you are aware, the united states of america and canada have no obligation to label genetically modified food, and the european union does not. the environment committee wants us to re-evaluate this issue. i am prepared to make a commitment on behalf of the commission: the commission will review the draft regulation amending regulation 1139/98 within one year of its entry into force. the commission will propose any amendments which may prove necessary in the light of improvements in quantitative detection techniques and practical experience gained from the implementation of the proposed 1% rate. in addition, the white paper on food safety will also give us the opportunity to hold a wide-ranging debate on the question of labelling if the european parliament so wishes. the commission has not exceeded its executive duties in proposing these regulations. the two proposed measures are consistent with the current legislation. we will follow the codecision procedure when parliament asks for a programme on products not containing gmos. mr byrne's department is preparing a proposal for a regulation on novel foods.

conventional armed forces in europe, to adopt the 1999 vienna document and to sign the european security charter, which highlights the common challenges and foundations of european security in the new millennium and proposes new instruments to enable the osce to meet these challenges. president ahtasaari and i signed the charter for the european union and i am pleased to see that it takes up the platform for security cooperation proposed by the eu. i now return to the helsinki summit and the third major theme of the discussions, the igc. i think it is very wise that the european council has best policy to follow in the fight against unemployment. the fact is simply that tax evasion is unfair and harmful to employment. we must fight it by all means possible. if we fail to find effective methods of taxing capital, the entire tax burden will have to be borne by labour, which will only aggravate the problem of unemployment. i will therefore be following very closely the negotiations on lot to be done as a result of this european council. we must work together and, for the first time, we have a wide scope to do so. we shall do so with determination, in good faith and in a spirit of great cooperation. i thank you for the spirit that has prevailed. counsel. - (fi) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i have the great pleasure and honour today to present to you the results reached by the council at the second reading of the draft budget for 2000, which take account of the amendments and proposals for amendments tabled by the european parliament. i would also like to take this opportunity to explain in more detail the council's proposal on the financing of aid to kosovo in 2000. we know that some of you think that the funding prospects for the years 2000 to 2006 are too narrow and that the maximum rate for category 4 is too low. we do, however, consider that the maximum rate for the year 200 which we are now deciding on is appropriate. in view of the unexpected needs arising from kosovo, the council believes that a flexible approach can be used provisionally. we fully understand parliament's concern about this year's budgetary procedure. i think, however, that our common objective is to give the people of kosovo the help they need without further delay. our common objective is at the same time to maintain our aid for the other beneficiaries, especially the poorest countries. the new interinstitutional agreement is of interest because it provides for the possibility of using an extended conciliation procedure, which has given parliament several opportunities to present its views and to hear the views of others. we have been in contact on several occasions with members of parliament, in particular with mr wynn, mr bourlanges and mr naval, in order to reach a balanced compromise which will allow a stable economic policy in the year 2000 and which will preserve a good spirit of cooperation between the institutions for the years to come. after these contacts, the council is prepared to accept the flexibility 4 issues, such as the eastern balkans. we have not, however, considered it necessary to revise the maximum rate for category 4 otherwise than by means of a flexible instrument. the main reason is that over 90 billion, and as the commission has not yet had the opportunity to define the needs for each year after the year 2000, there is no technical need at present to revise the funding prospects. the to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. we must show that we, the leaders of the european union, are doing a serious job, that we are taking decisions with a sense contains in respect of category 4 and why it meets the european parliament's requirements financially. the first advantage of the package presented by the council is that it proposes, for the aid to million from the 2000 budget. in addition, 60 million from the obnova programme and 20 million from the echo programme were already provided for in our first review, and they were to be used for we also know that the european parliament wants to give 20 million to east timor. 180 and 20, that's 200. this is precisely the amount which could be used, according to the council's proposal, by european parliament in drawing up the budget. this was not just a statement without substance, it also had practical consequences. the council, for example, has accepted almost all the amendments concerning the administrative expenditure of the european parliament, most of them relating to domestic policies which, to our knowledge, are of particular interest to you. the sums which parliament also been accepted. the council also accepted the new guidelines for the determination of the costs of managing action programmes and for the control of technical assistance offices. this was also one of the main objectives of the european parliament this year. the council also accepted the increase of 50 million, which parliament considered important, for appropriations relating to food safety. i would also like to mention olaf, the european anti-fraud office, as an example of what can be achieved through interinstitutional cooperation. the regulations and, in general, the legal framework for the founding of olaf as a whole, despite their complexity, were, thanks to the close cooperation of parliament and the council, the first codecision procedure to be successfully completed in a single examination and in the record time of five months. in addition - also thanks to the close cooperation between parliament and the council - supplementary budgets 4 and 5 for 1999 were accepted quickly and amendment no 2 to the 2000 budget is now ready for acceptance. all this makes it possible to almost double olaf's staff during the year. in addition, the european parliament and the council seem to have to agree today on the new director of olaf, which makes olaf entirely reliable. we all know that a solitary path and the apparent freedom it offers can sometimes seem more appealing than the obligations imposed by cooperation. we believe, however, that cooperative strategies normally produce a better outcome from the point of view of the community as a whole and that they are normally more advantageous for each party involved than aggressive strategies. the council thus proposes cooperation as a means of financing aid to be granted to kosovo and east timor in the year 2000. this solution provides, without unnecessary delay, resources for those in kosovo and east timor who are in urgent need of assistance. under this proposal, all these needs will be financed through a flexible means for those parties exceeding the upper limit of the financing prospects, without taking anything away from anyone. the council is also ready for a solution where payment appropriations are cut by two billion euro by adding compulsory and non-compulsory expenditure. the council has already shown that it is willing to respond to parliament's wishes by accepting many amendments which are important to you and by presenting this offer on kosovo and east timor, which seeks to take account of your concerns. the council therefore wants the european parliament to take its decision on the budget on the basis of the council's proposal.

in writing. - i welcome this proposal to amend regulation (ec) no 093/94 on the production and use of substances that deplete the ozone layer. i believe that it is high time that new measures were taken to protect the ozone layer. the situation is indeed alarming! the decline in stratospheric ozone levels is one of the most serious environmental problems we face. a decrease of 6 to 10% has been recorded since 1980. in 1996, the hole in the ozone layer over antarctica extended over 20 million square kilometres for more than 40 days. in addition, the depletion of the ozone layer over scandinavia, greenland and siberia has reached an unprecedented level of 45%. this has a negative impact on human health, causing a decrease in immune defenses and a resurgence of skin cancers. in addition, it is causing particularly worrying disruption to ecosystems. we need to act quickly, especially as we know about the substances that deplete the ozone layer (hydrochlorofluorocarbons (hcfcs) used mainly in refrigeration and air-conditioning systems, as solvents and for the production of synthetic foams used for insulation purposes); methyl bromide, primarily used for the fumigation of agricultural land to control pests and diseases of plants, classified by who as 'highly toxic', chlorofluorocarbons (cfcs), used in refrigeration systems and previously used in the manufacture of synthetic foams, solvents and propellant gases for aerosols; halons are used for firefighting, particularly in sectors with very high fire-extinguishing requirements (in aircraft in particular) and as non-hazardous substitutes. every effort should therefore be made to eliminate the substances concerned and to use substitutes. this is what the proposal under discussion today proposes, even if it is not as voluntary in terms of timing as we might have hoped, as the rapporteur has pointed out. that is why amendments to this effect were tabled, which were, in most cases, rejected by the council. the council's attitude is truly regrettable. i think the objectives proposed by the committee on the environment are achievable, since there are alternatives. for example, the council proposes that in 2008 production of the substances in question should not exceed 35% of 1997 production. the commission also proposes that the production levels be reduced to the following levels: below 75% in 2001, below 55% in 2004 and below 30% in 2008. the commission is also proposing that the ceiling for 2014 should not exceed 15%, while the council's proposed ceiling is 20%. i deplore the council's lack of ambition. this is all the more regrettable in this area where it is not only a question of protecting the environment, but above all of protecting people's health!
in writing. - the swiss people had spoken out a few years ago in favour of controlling the transit of heavy goods vehicles through their territory. the conditions for the movement of heavy goods vehicles are strictly regulated, which allows a choice in favour of a real quality of life in the alpine valleys, a positive measure for the environment and for the people. far from welcoming this effort to protect the environment, the european union has only one objective in its bilateral negotiations with switzerland: to get switzerland to abandon its regulation, under the pretext of hindering free competition and unequal treatment between european territories. the logic of profitability therefore takes precedence over ecological and social considerations. we have examined with great interest proposals to develop alternative, non-polluting transport, such as railways. the report, in its present form, is strongly in favour of the all-truck in switzerland to the detriment of other modes. we therefore do not agree with this logic and will vote against this report.
in writing. - i can only agree with what has just been said, namely, that seattle's failure is far from a victory! the balance sheet we have to draw from these abortive negotiations is very mixed! we should welcome the emergence of civil society concerns in international trade discussions, thanks in particular to the mobilisation of ngos, trade unions and other associations. in this respect, the seattle ministerial conference was a real turning point in the functioning of the wto. while previous rounds have been conducted in the utmost discretion between informed negotiators who have regard only to the commercial interests of their country, the next round, the start date of which remains unknown, can only be conducted in a transparent manner and by integrating into the debates all the themes that have a connection with trade, namely social standards, the environment, consumer protection, culture. and it is to deal with these changes that the wto needs to be revised. it was not set up to manage so many portfolios. furthermore, it was created by nations to serve their own interests. the new situation requires full participation of the developing countries and the least developed countries, which was not the case in seattle, hence their legitimate discontent. good intentions must be reflected in the way the wto works. we must therefore start thinking seriously about the revision of the wto. the european union must play a leading role in the forthcoming discussions. as we have seen, it has established itself as an indispensable link between the united states and the developing countries. we should also highlight the initiative of the european parliament delegation to create a parliamentary body within the wto. this will be only one element in the reform to be carried out, but it will reduce the democratic deficit which characterises the wto. the european union must also prepare for further negotiations which will begin as early as next year! the european union, which had prepared very well for the discussions and whose position remained very consistent, did not give in to the agenda it wanted to see adopted, namely a broad agenda beyond the agriculture and services themes, as the united states wanted. however, it is on these two issues alone that discussions will have to start as early as next year, in accordance with the marrakesh agreements. we must therefore be very vigilant in these negotiations, which are proving difficult. lastly, and this is a very positive point, our negotiator, pascal lamy, has been able to win with his foresight, sensitivity, knowledge and authority. this is extremely positive for the future.

in writing. - i voted against the draft resolution on the labelling of food produced from genetically modified organisms, because its sole purpose is to give the commission a green light to propose a regulation establishing that when gmos are present in a food below a threshold of 1%, labelling indicating their presence would not be compulsory. this would be contrary to the position adopted by the european parliament on 14 may 1998, when it called for mandatory labelling in the event of the presence of gmos, irrespective of the percentage of gmos. today the council is asking the commission to be more flexible on the grounds that in some cases industries cannot avoid a minimal accidental contamination of their products by genetically modified material during transport or processing. the problem is real, but the solution proposed to us seems unacceptable, even temporarily. the real solution lies not in tolerating a lack of consumer information, but in increased efforts to separate genetically modified products from conventional products throughout the production process. i maintain that labelling should be compulsory, regardless of the amount of gmos in food, and even if it is minimal. if the manufacturer has any doubts, the following must be added: 'this food may contain genetically modified organisms'.
