- madam president, my dear british colleagues, we are faced with a scientific, political, legal and moral problem. first, scientifically, the disease is caused by an unknown agent. it's not bacterial, it's probably not viral, although german professor diringer thinks it is, it's due to a mysterious prion. second, there is no ante mortem test. thirdly, the disease did not disappear despite the ban on flour. fourth, we found mites on the feed that are full of prions. so the disease can be spread through fodder or grass, which may make your land cursed and may ban cattle ranching forever. so, for now, science can't tell. you're sending the ball back to the political camp. politically, it's a question of hierarchy between commerce and health. what's the priority? sell or live? most countries in the world, including your american cousins, your canadian cousins, including your australian friends, your new zealand commonwealth friends, they tell you they want to live first and sell second. so you're asking for sanctions and making it a legal problem. legally, there are two problems. the hierarchy of norms, first. should we give priority to the principle of free movement or to the precautionary principle? it is true that in the case of bst, which is not dangerous to human health, we have given priority to the precautionary principle, which we also advocated in seattle. so there remains the second legal problem, a problem of legal liability. you are guilty because you created the disease in the first place. we have taken the financial risk for two years, but we cannot take the health risk. there remains, then, a moral or theological problem, which is already found in st thomas aquinas, antigone and creon: must the natural law take precedence over the law of men? well, it turns out that with the law of men, you've created both an epizootic and a zoonosis. i remind you that the last child to die from your disease was 13 years old. well, we don't want to die. so, on the last level, the religious level, your minister of agriculture came to us two years ago in the agriculture committee and said that this was due to god. well, as christmas approaches, rely on god, hope that santa will offer us a test to diagnose and try to ask god for forgiveness, but in this case you have to repent... sakharov, we pay tribute to a man who fought hard for freedom of thought. nothing characterizes a human being more than his ability to think. to deny anyone the freedom to think and express his ideas is to deprive him of his human dignity. freedom of thought is a fundamental right of every human being. in europe, it has become one of the fundamental pillars of citizenship. in totalitarian regimes, oppressors suppress and suppress freedom of thought. in indonesia, our experience has shown that the regime of orde baru, led by suharto and his generals, which occupied my homeland for more than two decades, the methodology of repression and suppression was based on the imposition of a doctrine, pancasila, which standardized thought and, therefore, human action, in an attempt to destroy the ability to think individually, collectively and, above all, freely. this doctrine permeated the whole of indonesian society and was also carried over to east timor, accompanied by a systematic action of physical torture and mental conditioning. but ironically, these actions had the opposite effect: they strengthened the identity and determination of our people. after the fall of suharto in may 1998, the way was open for a solution to the east timor conflict and for the democratization of indonesia. i would like to take this opportunity to pay a sincere tribute to all the sakharov prize winners, first and foremost to aung sang suu kyi, one of the great figures in the struggle for freedom and democracy throughout the world. mr president, if the commission had wanted to prove that france was right to maintain its embargo on british beef, it could not have done better than to present today's dossier on labelling. we have been told at times that the embargo is not really necessary and that it is enough for beef to be well labelled so that the reasonable consumer does not buy beef from britain. this is a strange line of reasoning, since it would be tantamount to agreeing to send consumers to their deaths if they misread the labels. that would be an unacceptable resignation of the state. but in any case, this excuse is overruled by today's dossier, since we are learning that the obligation to label beef is going to be postponed again. what is it ? at the beginning of 1997, in the midst of the mad cow crisis, the council decided to introduce a system of identification of bovine animals from the place of production and meat labelling, which was initially optional but was to become mandatory from 1 january 2000. however, as the fateful date approaches, the commission admits that nothing is ready and that the obligation cannot come into force for another year. this means that today, after years of neglect, we are still unable in the european union to ensure effective traceability of beef. a french consumer importing ravioli from italy cannot possibly know that they do not contain british mad cow meat. it is astonishing that the commission should dare to take france to the court of justice for maintaining its embargo in the face of such negligence. never before have we seen more clearly than now how, in the single market, the free movement of goods takes precedence over all other considerations. it is true that the french government has allowed itself to be legally trapped by accepting the treaty of amsterdam, which tends to deprive it of its right to protection. but this right is sacred. it is never too late to take action and take it back to the commission. in writing. - we are dealing here with the labelling of beef, as we were dealing with the labelling of gmos. in fact, labelling has become the tool to do everything. thanks to the label, food safety would reign supreme, the consumer would be protected and our green colleagues would be satisfied that they had ensured the survival of food for mankind... in reality, labelling is one of those deceptions which european leaders use to appease the anxieties of our fellow citizens without actually solving any problem. the labelling of gmos should have been a warning. we don't know what to put on the label. for example, should we put "product of biotechnology"? - mr president, in 1998 the european commission launched a procedure concerning the crossborder agreement on book prices concluded between germany and austria. by means of this procedure, which was based on compliance with european competition rules, the commission was in fact seeking to challenge the single price for books system, which is used in particular to support literary creation and to ensure the survival of small publishing houses and small bookshops. the european parliament reacted strongly by adopting, by almost unanimous decision, on 20 november 1998 a resolution defending the single book price and calling on the commission to adapt its community policy on the agreement on book prices to cultural requirements. on 8 february 1999, at the instigation of the french and german governments, the council adopted a resolution, based on the european parliament's position, calling in particular for the continuation of the existing book price systems. the council and parliament's firmness led the commission to recognise that the competition rules could not be applied mechanically in the book sector. it therefore confirmed that it did not intend to challenge either contractual agreements concluded in certain member states or national legislative provisions such as the lange law in france. however, a few months later, after the new commission was set up, the directorate-general for competition again pressed the commission to take action against cross-border agreements and the single book price. in the face of this new offensive by the commission, which cannot help but express its desire to deregulate, it was important to react very quickly. i therefore welcome this debate and the new position of the european parliament on this issue. in its motion for a resolution, my group stresses that books are first and foremost cultural goods and should therefore not be subject to the rules of competition in the same way as all other goods. their specificity must be fully recognised in the framework of the cultural policy of the european union which we wish to see developed. we therefore hope that the european parliament will confirm its position of november 1998 in order to defend crossborder agreements and the single book price. why does the commission not accept our proposal to extend the possibility of the single book price system to all member states? in order to take account of technological developments, the e-commerce directive should also include the requirements of the various national laws on the single price for books, in order to prevent it from being circumvented. in conclusion, i hope that the council will show the same determination as the european parliament in safeguarding and promoting the single book price system which, as our resolution notes, improves the production and distribution of literary works better than any other system without eliminating competition.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, we are particularly concerned about the human rights situation in djibouti. political prisoners are held in worrying conditions: crowded in cramped cells, isolation, lack of hygiene and medical care. the outbreak of tuberculosis has been reported on several occasions. two prisoners have already died from lack of medical care. political prisoners have started hunger strikes to protest their conditions of detention, to demand access to medical care and their release, in the absence of a fair trial. it should be noted that the majority of prisoners are in pre-trial detention without any judicial review. among the sick prisoners is mohamed kadamiousouf, the european representative of the front for the restoration of unity and democracy, who was illegally extradited from ethiopia in 1997 and who, in the absence of medical treatment, is in danger of losing his sight. since respect for human rights is an essential element of cooperation and development between the european union and the republic of djibouti, we call, in accordance with these principles, for the release of all political prisoners, access to medical care for all detainees - and in particular the provision of emergency care to mr mohamed kadamiousouf, who is at risk of blindness - the guarantee of freedom of expression and political pluralism, which are essential to any democracy, and an end to the repression of dissidents. we also call on the commission to use all the means at its disposal to ensure that human rights are respected in djibouti.
mr president, i am indignant at the conditions of detention of political prisoners in djibouti, but i am equally indignant at the hypocrisy of the leaders of the french state who could, if they wished, put an immediate end to the authoritarianism and the abuses of the djiboutian regime. because, after all, everyone knows that the french state is holding the djiboutian regime in check. without the financial support of paris, without the presence of one of the main bases of the french army abroad, the regime there would not last a month. the leaders of the french state, whatever their political label, insist on human rights in paris but support regimes in africa or asia which trample on the most elementary rights and freedoms. so, to blame the government of djibouti alone is, at best, to hide the responsibilities of the french government, but it is, in reality, to endorse a policy of support for an authoritarian and repressive regime. we can only join the protest against the conditions of detention of prisoners in djibouti by making it clear that, if the prisoners are there, the real ones are in some of the official palaces of the french republic.
- mr president, i shall speak about the natural disasters which struck the south of france on the night of 12 to 13 november 1999 and which were quite exceptional in their violence and the unusual scale of the damage: 35 victims and some three to four billion in damage. i know that the budget of the european union does not provide for a credit line for natural disasters occurring on the territory of the union. i must say that it is not lost on me that parliament itself wanted to abolish this credit line. i would ask you to intervene and ensure that the european union is still present, because it has the opportunity to do so. she can do it two ways. on the one hand, by allowing france to reallocate the remaining structural funds not committed under the 1994-1999 programming. we know that there are still a lot of appropriations: 54% of appropriations not committed under leader, 38% under interreg, 49% under urban and 88% under retex. it is now sufficient for the commission to authorize france to redeploy part of these appropriations so that it can intervene very quickly. on the other hand, it can do so by ensuring that, for the new programming of the structural funds 2000-06, the zoning for reconstruction is in place and that the most affected areas are covered by objective 2. i would like to conclude by saying that it is a bit paradoxical that our european union can intervene, which is perfectly legitimate, in countries outside the union, but that it does not have the means or the possibility to do so within the union. at a time when everyone, and especially mrs fontaine, is putting this parliament under the sign of bringing the citizens closer to the union, it seems to me important that the union should be able to make a concrete statement when our citizens are in difficulty.
- mr president, ladies and gentlemen, if we want the citizens of europe to feel attachment to the european union, then the european union must show solidarity with them when they are in trouble, as in the south of france. this region, in fact, experienced heavy rains and floods on the night of 12 to 13 november, which caused casualties, devastated its daily life, its economy and its agriculture. as soon as these events took place, i wanted parliament to express its solidarity with the victims by tabling an emergency resolution on 15 november. the rules of procedure have unnecessarily delayed it, so i have added my proposal to those tabled at this part-session on the same subject by other groups. i hope that this resolution will be followed up in practice and i ask the commission to consider measures which could bring relief to the people of tarn, aude, the eastern pyrenees and the hérault. i think that this situation should be taken into account in the zoning of european union aid. in future, i will of course vote for the emergency resolutions tabled by our colleagues when similar tragedies occur. i hope, of course, that there will be few of them, but in any case it seems to me essential that we, the elected representatives of the peoples of europe, should show solidarity and humanity.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, my speech is in line with that of mrs de veyrac, because the catastrophic floods in the south of france result in a very heavy toll of human lives: 39 dead. the turmoil in this region is immense. in the four departments affected by the floods of 12 and 13 november, aude, hérault, the pyrénées orientales and tarn, the bill is heavy. it exceeds eur 0.7 billion and the compensation to individuals will reach eur 0.5 billion. damage to public property is estimated at over $200,000,000, with extensive damage to roads and railways, electrical and telephone lines, public buildings, and utilities. all sectors were affected, more than 200 craftsmen were affected, 260 businesses suffered heavy damage and 1518 employees were penalised. i would draw parliament's attention to the fact that this is indeed a natural disaster, that these floods and rainfall have been 20 times greater than in normal times. the problem is not, as some would have us believe, the result of imprudent local planning. this is a real natural disaster. that is why i would draw parliament's attention to the need to intervene in these areas.
mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i naturally support the joint motion for a resolution tabled by my colleagues and i would like to draw your attention once again to the floods in my region, the far south of france. the natural disaster, of course, which caused the death of almost forty people and whose consequences continue to test the lives of some of our fellow citizens to this day. a month later, the decline, with the spectacle of devastation it revealed, confirmed the scale of the disaster, beyond human lives that require a prevention effort to be rethought. the needs are enormous, both in terms of private and public assets in terms of heavy construction and infrastructure and in terms of economic instruments, and - as has been pointed out - in the order of ff 6 000 million. faced with such an urgent demand, the state, local authorities and associations are mobilizing throughout france. as an example, and among many others, the general council of the eastern pyrenees voted for aid of 42 million francs, the languedoc-roussillon region for 50 million, the senate for 400,000 francs, and finally, the french government announced aid of 1.2 billion. you are no doubt aware of the proposals made by commissioner barnier on structural policy. they will help to ensure better long-term risk prevention, but i am speaking again today to ask the commission to show its willingness to show solidarity in an emergency. the legitimacy of our institution with regard to the european citizens is at stake, and the president, like all of us, is very attached to that legitimacy. finally, i would like to draw your attention to the pollution which is once again threatening the breton coast and which will require, as a matter of urgency, a complementary financial effort by the european institutions.

the rapporteur. mr president, as a member of the bordeaux elected body, i thought you were giving me the floor to answer my bavarian colleague on the subject of bordeaux wine. but no, it is on tajikistan that you are inviting me to speak and as i have five minutes, i will try to be as clear as possible on a subject which is perhaps a little esoteric and difficult. this is exceptional aid to tajikistan, which, as you know, is a small country situated between uzbekistan, kazakhstan, china and afghanistan. this case has a history and, in fact, today, what i am proposing to you is to close a case which was opened in 1991 on a loan of €1 billion 200 million to the newly independent states, at the time of the disintegration of the soviet union. it turns out that all but three of the member states have repaid this loan. in 1997, three states were in difficulty and had large arrears: georgia, armenia and tajikistan. in 1997, parliament was therefore presented with a commission proposal to reschedule and restructure the debt of these three countries. it was therefore decided to set up two types of financial assistance: loans, at the time €245 million had been earmarked for loans to these three countries, and a donation of €130 million, the main objective of which was to reduce the debt burden and improve the repayment capacity of these countries. 1997 is also a year, ladies and gentlemen, and we are entering the heart of the matter with a civil war in tajikistan, a horrible civil war between the ruling government and the islamic opposition. so parliament, on the basis of our colleague mr kittelmann's report, had proposed to defer aid to tajikistan and that is why, after two years, now that the situation has normalized, we are being asked today to reopen this dossier. the situation in tajikistan, which has remained extremely critical and worrying, both politically and economically, has been gradually stabilizing for the past two years. there was a peace agreement between the various parties, which was implemented and is generally respected, although security in that country remains in doubt because of the presence of warlords and a strong push of wahhabi fundamentalism in afghanistan. in economic terms, it is a country that has made very great efforts under the aegis of the imf and benefits from a structural adjustment facility from the latter. we are therefore asked, as the european union, to re-establish contact with that country and to re-schedule the debt, which is now about eur 73 million. what the commission is proposing is to replicate what was done for georgia and armenia, that is to say to provide a new loan to repay the previous one, but on much more favourable terms so as to give that country a little bit of oxygen, and to provide a donation of eur 35 million for the period 2000-2004 to alleviate the debt burden. however, i regret to say that the commission's proposal is highly contradictory. we are asked to make a loan of €75 million and a donation of €35 million, only to find that there are no more budgetary resources for donations and that in 1999 we only budgeted for donations to armenia and georgia, which are due to end in 2001. consequently, and quite logically, the committee on budgets pointed out to us, the committee responsible for industry, that we could not, under any circumstances, endorse donations which are not budgeted today and which are not in the financial perspective, in particular category 4, which you know is already under pressure to try to finance kosovo. so, ladies and gentlemen, the compromise we reached with the committee on budgets is, in effect, to retain only the loan of €75 million, while agreeing - a position of the committee on industry which was understood, i believe, by the committee on budgets - that tajikistan should also be able to receive additional aid to alleviate the monthly debt burden of €200,000, which is unbearable for that country. tajikistan is the poorest of the newly independent states, and it is essential to stabilize it, because, like chechnya and for other reasons, it is a country which can endanger the whole region, particularly because of its strategic position in relation to kazakhstan and uzbekistan, which are very rich countries. we have therefore tabled a number of amendments. first, amendments that validate the gift. then there are the amendments which refer the council and the commission to their contradictions by telling them that it would be desirable to grant direct aid, but by financing it through another line, i am thinking of tacis. finally, there are amendments on conditionality: control of the use of funds, political and democratic conditions and parliamentary control.
- mr president, we shall not vote on the savary report. this is due both to the choice of country and to more general considerations surrounding financial assistance. while we are of course not opposed to the sovereign state of tajikistan, we do not consider that the european states should abandon their priorities, or more precisely, the priority they have long set for themselves in the field of cooperation. this priority was implemented more than a quarter of a century ago by the lomé agreements. for obvious reasons, geographical but also historical, it became necessary for the europeans to engage in a major cooperation action with the african, caribbean and pacific countries in the 1970s, in a very original form known as the lomé agreements, to enable our partners in the south to benefit from stable prices for the foodstuffs from which they derive the bulk of their resources, this being protected from all-round free trade, which we see too much today, how it ruins the most fragile economies. however, under the blows, not of globalisation but of the globalist ideology, which the european nations have accepted without further examination, we have seen for several years the acp agreements slowly dismantled, their basic principles denied and, above all, we see the contribution of several european countries to the edf decreasing. at the same time, however, the number of financial aids, so-called exceptional, to the most diverse countries on the planet is increasing, without any overall plan emerging, so that our cooperation policy is no more than a vague and vast sprinkling, that is to say, in short, it is no longer a policy. to this particular consideration, a second is added. if tajikistan is now experiencing the economic difficulties mentioned in the report, as are so many other countries in the world, it is certainly the result of the reckless opening up of borders and the excessive play of empires. we see no better solution than the restoration of a new international trade order which respects the sovereignty of states, their pace and their development methods, and also their traditions, traditions which we will not be able to dissolve with a magic wand because we will have imposed elections, human rights and what we are too hastily calling democracy.
